# Sexuality- and Gender-Based Crackdowns Under Egyptian Law

[Alyssa Bernstein](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/contributors/abernstein)

Thursday, December 28, 2017, 9:00 AM

Share On:  [Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3a%2f%2fwww.lawfaremedia.org%2farticle%2fsexuality-and-gender-based-crackdowns-under-egyptian-law)   [Share on X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3a%2f%2fwww.lawfaremedia.org%2farticle%2fsexuality-and-gender-based-crackdowns-under-egyptian-law)   [Share on LinkedIn](http://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3a%2f%2fwww.lawfaremedia.org%2farticle%2fsexuality-and-gender-based-crackdowns-under-egyptian-law)   [Share on BlueSky](https://bsky.app/intent/compose?text=Sexuality-+and+Gender-Based+Crackdowns+Under+Egyptian+Law https%3a%2f%2fwww.lawfaremedia.org%2farticle%2fsexuality-and-gender-based-crackdowns-under-egyptian-law)   [Share on Threads](https://threads.net/intent/post?url=https%3a%2f%2fwww.lawfaremedia.org%2farticle%2fsexuality-and-gender-based-crackdowns-under-egyptian-law&text=Sexuality-+and+Gender-Based+Crackdowns+Under+Egyptian+Law)   [Print this article](#)

Homosexuality is [not technically illegal in Egypt](https://antigaylaws.org/regional/middle-east/). But Egyptian authorities are [cracking down on the LGBT community](https://eipr.org/en/publications/trap-punishing-sexual-difference-egypt), its supporters, and advocates for social liberalization more broadly. In September, the Lebanese band [Mashrou’ Leila](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NF__cpsDmZk) played a concert to an audience of 30,000 in Cairo, led by openly-gay singer Hamed Sinno.

* ![Alyssa  Bernstein](https://lawfare-assets-new.azureedge.net/assets/images/default-source/contributor-images/2488.png?sfvrsn=ad3e051a_0)

  ## [Alyssa Bernstein](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/contributors/abernstein)

---

[Meet The Authors](#postContributors)

[Subscribe to Lawfare](/subscribe)

Homosexuality is [not technically illegal in Egypt](https://antigaylaws.org/regional/middle-east/). But Egyptian authorities are [cracking down on the LGBT community](https://eipr.org/en/publications/trap-punishing-sexual-difference-egypt), its supporters, and advocates for social liberalization more broadly. In September, the Lebanese band [Mashrou’ Leila](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NF__cpsDmZk) played a concert to an audience of 30,000 in Cairo, led by openly-gay singer Hamed Sinno. Fans waved rainbow flags in support of LGBT rights, leading to a [media outcry](https://www.reuters.com/article/us-egypt-rights/rainbow-raids-egypt-launches-its-widest-anti-gay-crackdown-yet-idUSKBN1CB1HE) against homosexuality and perceived immorality.

The government [immediately arrested](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/middle_east/with-midnight-raids-and-chat-room-traps-egypt-launches-sweeping-crackdown-on-gay-community/2017/10/17/6a8397fc-b03e-11e7-9b93-b97043e57a22_story.html?utm_term=.efc1316d2be5) over 60 men and women for suspected gay conduct or for waving the flag. Police [performed](http://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-41482001) anal examinations on some, a scientifically-debunked procedure to determine whether they had engaged in anal sex. Sarah Hegazy, one of the women arrested, says guards abused her and allowed cellmates to [beat her](https://www.reuters.com/article/us-egypt-rights/rainbow-raids-egypt-launches-its-widest-anti-gay-crackdown-yet-idUSKBN1CB1HE). Sixteen had been [convicted](http://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/middle-east/egypt-lgbt-crackdown-men-jailed-gay-debauchery-charges-africa-latest-homophobia-government-a8083016.html) by the end of November. The New York Times happened to be filming a documentary report about Esraa, one of the women waving the flag, and she is [now on the run](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/12/03/insider/egyptian-woman.html?action=click&pgtype=Homepage&module=timesinsider&region=c-column-bottom-span-region&_r=0) from law enforcement. The government simultaneously banned media statements [supporting](https://egyptianstreets.com/2017/10/01/all-forms-of-support-to-the-lgbt-community-to-be-banned-on-media-outlets-scmr/) homosexuality. Since August, Egyptian law enforcement has intensified entrapment campaigns against LGBT folks, using fake profiles on dating sites and social media and arresting those who show up for dates.

No law criminalizes homosexual conduct in Egypt. Instead, the government uses [Law 10 of 1961](https://www.hrw.org/reports/2004/egypt0304/9.htm#_ftnref470) to prosecute suspected gay and trans people. The law forbids prostitution and “debauchery,” and carries up to three years in prison and three years of supervised daily release. The administration has also begun using the same law, colloquially known as Law 10/1961, to silence and punish media commentators and artists.

**Law 10/1961’s History and Use in Egypt**

[Law 10/1961](https://www.hrw.org/reports/2004/egypt0304/9.htm) forbids engaging in, soliciting, or providing facilities for “debauchery and prostitution.” Legislative history demonstrates that parliamentarians [added](https://www.hrw.org/reports/2004/egypt0304/9.htm#_Toc63760433) "debauchery" to refer to male sex work specifically. Because the blanket term for debauchery, “fujur” (الفجور), is not defined in the statute, the law is broad enough to allow the police and prosecutors to use it against LGBT-identified Egyptians and their supporters.

From the late 19th through early 20th century, prostitution in Egypt was [legal, regulated, and widely patronized](https://books.google.com/books?id=-Dr7CwAAQBAJ&pg=PA59&lpg=PA59&dq=law+no.+68/1951+egypt&source=bl&ots=8EdEdveVdF&sig=hmBDkXgVI5xr9R9gjeEpWSEpUvQ&hl=en&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwjim9quob_XAhWJ54MKHcdMCqsQ6AEIPDAE#v=onepage&q=law%20no.%2068%2F1951%20egypt&f=) by colonial British soldiers. During the 1950s, however, international and local sentiment turned against legalized sex work. Responding to increasingly religious sentiments, parliamentarians originally [created Law 10](https://www.hrw.org/reports/2004/egypt0304/9.htm#_Toc63760433) [in](https://www.hrw.org/reports/2004/egypt0304/9.htm#_Toc63760433) [19](https://www.hrw.org/reports/2004/egypt0304/9.htm#_Toc63760433)[5](https://www.hrw.org/reports/2004/egypt0304/9.htm#_Toc63760433)[1](https://www.hrw.org/reports/2004/egypt0304/9.htm#_Toc63760433) [against debauchery and prostitution](https://www.hrw.org/reports/2004/egypt0304/9.htm#_Toc63760433). Lawmakers updated the law in 1961 to include Syria, then unified with Egypt as the [United Arab Republic](http://www.aljazeera.com/indepth/opinion/2013/02/201321985412606377.html), so it is now called Law 10/1961. Though 10/1961 responded in part to increasing Islamicization, it was not part of the country’s Islamic law, which [only applies to family law](https://books.google.com/books?id=-Dr7CwAAQBAJ&pg=PA59&lpg=PA59&dq=law+no.+68/1951+egypt&source=bl&ots=8EdEdveVdF&sig=hmBDkXgVI5xr9R9gjeEpWSEpUvQ&hl=en&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwjim9quob_XAhWJ54MKHcdMCqsQ6AEIPDAE#v=onepage&q=tolino&f=false). Rather, it was a secular codification of the [United Nations’ Convention for the Suppression of Traffic in Persons](http://www.ohchr.org/EN/ProfessionalInterest/Pages/TrafficInPersons.aspx) and of the Exploitation of the Prostitution of Others, to which Egypt [acceded in 1959](https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetails.aspx?src=IND&mtdsg_no=VII-11-a&chapter=7&clang=_en#7).

Law 10/1961 prohibits inciting, soliciting, or maintaining premises for debauchery or prostitution. [Article 9, for example, imposes](https://www.hrw.org/reports/2004/egypt0304/9.htm#_Toc63760433):

> Punishment by imprisonment for a period not less than three months and not exceeding three years and a fine not less than 25 LE [Egyptian pounds, approximately $1.40 today] and not exceeding 300 LE in the Egyptian administration and not less than 250 Lira and not exceeding 3000 Lira in the Syrian administration or one of these two punishments applies in the following cases:
>
> (a) Whoever lets or offers in whatever fashion a residence or place run for the purpose of debauchery or prostitution, or for the purpose of housing one or more persons, if they are to his knowledge practicing debauchery or prostitution.
>
> (c) Whoever habitually engages in debauchery or prostitution.

It also permits that:

> Upon the apprehension of a person in the last category, it is permitted to send him for a medical examination. If it is discovered that he is carrying an infectious venereal disease, it is permitted to detain him in a therapeutic institute until his cure is completed.

Under President Hosni Mubarak, the Egyptian government began imprisoning men suspected of having sex with men under 10/1961 [in the mid-1990s](https://www.hrw.org/reports/2004/egypt0304/1.htm#_Toc63760380). But there were no large-scale crackdowns until the [Queen Boat raid in May 2001](http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/middle_east/1493041.stm), when 52 men were arrested on a Nile party boat. Several dozen men were [taken into custody](https://www.hrw.org/reports/2004/egypt0304/3.htm) and brutally beaten. The arrests and charges were accompanied by massive media coverage. During two trials over the course of five months, several men were subject to anal examinations, and 21 of the 52 put on trial were sentenced to the maximum sentence, [three years in prison and three years of probational observation](http://www.nytimes.com/2003/04/03/world/cairo-once-the-scene-cracks-down-on-gays.html). [Scholars and observers](http://hollis.harvard.edu/primo_library/libweb/action/display.do?tabs=detailsTab&ct=display&fn=search&doc=TN_informit046278021628400&indx=2&recIds=TN_informit046278021628400&recIdxs=1&elementId=1&renderMode=poppedOut&displayMode=full&frbrVersion=&) point out that the months-long scandal, the media outrage, and general mania around the raid allowed Mubarak to [distract](https://www.jstor.org/stable/20097954?seq=1#page_scan_tab_contents) public attention from his government’s economic and democratic deficiencies.

Mubarak’s security services continued to entice and sentence gay and trans people [following the Queen Boat raid](http://www.nytimes.com/2003/04/03/world/cairo-once-the-scene-cracks-down-on-gays.html), often by using police or informants as lures. In 2008, the government [arrested](https://www.hrw.org/news/2008/02/14/egypt-spreading-crackdown-hiv-endangers-public-health) more than a dozen men suspected of contracting HIV, and, as 10/1961 permits, forcibly tested them and convicted some of them.

The 2011 protests and Tahrir Square revolution interrupted the government’s suppression of the LGBT community. Despite some protesters’ pro-LGBT message, Mubarak’s forces did not use 10/1961 during the few weeks of protests before his government’s collapse, and the community [began to thrive](https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/egypts-gays-hope-for-change-in-culture-after-revolt/2011/08/15/gIQAOiskQJ_story.html?utm_term=.fd0fd82b0f22) following the revolution.

Perhaps surprisingly, Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi , the Muslim Brotherhood member who was democratically elected, did not [enforce 10/1961](http://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/middle-east/how-distaste-of-lgbt-people-in-egypt-has-turned-into-state-sponsored-persecution-10256869.html) [heavily](http://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/middle-east/how-distaste-of-lgbt-people-in-egypt-has-turned-into-state-sponsored-persecution-10256869.html) —perhaps because he lacked strong control of the state security apparatus. The LGBT community in Egypt became more [out and vocal](https://www.thedailybeast.com/egypts-growing-gay-rights-movement), hosting large parties and generating social media campaigns, as fear of repression decreased.

**Why the Crackdown is Coming Now**

The LGBT community’s newfound openness was short-lived, however. Gen. Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi, the military officer who deposed Morsi in 2013 and then won elections with [96 percent](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2014/jun/03/abdel-fatah-al-sisi-presidential-election-vote-egypt) of the vote, quickly broadened campaigns and arrests. His regime [has quadrupled](https://eipr.org/en/press/2017/11/trap-punishing-sexual-difference-egypt) arrests of gay and trans people under various Egyptian laws. On Nov. 4, 2013, the same day that Morsi first appeared in court after being overthrown, riot police [raided](https://www.thedailybeast.com/al-sisis-egypt-is-worse-for-gays-than-the-muslim-brotherhood) an LGBT party and arrested ten men, nine of whom were sentenced under 10/1961 and other laws such as those against “insulting public morals.” The following year, 26 men were [arrested at a bathhouse](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2015/jan/12/defendants-cleared-cairo-bath-house-debauchery) but were later acquitted in a surprise verdict. In 2015, [more than 100 people](http://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/middle-east/how-distaste-of-lgbt-people-in-egypt-has-turned-into-state-sponsored-persecution-10256869.html) were sentenced to time in prison for “debauchery” or “inciting sexual perversion.”

Sisi has a no-holds-barred approach to repressing dissent, [imprisoning](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/03/14/magazine/how-egypts-activists-became-generation-jail.html), [disappearing](http://www.bbc.com/news/av/world-africa-33740651/enforced-disappearances-on-the-rise-in-egypt-activists-say), and [publically killing](http://www.nytimes.com/2013/08/15/world/middleeast/egypt.html) activists from both the [Muslim Brotherhood and Egypt’s](http://www.aljazeera.com/indepth/features/2017/07/egypt-worse-indicator-2013-coup-170702072016494.html) left. His government has [confined](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/03/14/magazine/how-egypts-activists-became-generation-jail.html?_r=0) [over](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/03/14/magazine/how-egypts-activists-became-generation-jail.html?_r=0) [60,000](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/03/14/magazine/how-egypts-activists-became-generation-jail.html?_r=0) [political prisoners](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/03/14/magazine/how-egypts-activists-became-generation-jail.html?_r=0) since August 2013. The U.S. has criticized Egypt’s state policies in its [2016 Human Rights Report,](https://www.state.gov/documents/organization/265706.pdf) and has withheld some military aid to Egypt over its rights abuses, even as President Donald Trump praises Sisi. New anti-civil liberties laws, such as [limitations on NGO activity](https://www.hrw.org/news/2017/06/02/egypt-new-law-will-crush-civil-society), restrict both [Islamist and human rights organizing](https://www.state.gov/documents/organization/265706.pdf).

However, it appears that suppression of the LGBT community comes from a different motivation than silencing dissent: Sisi is demonstrating to the Egyptian populace that though he deposed an Islamist president, his government [still upholds](https://www.huffingtonpost.com/entry/the-politics-behind-egypts-lgbt-crackdown_us_5a00926ae4b0d467d4c226fa) conservative religious values. Egypt’s morality police [widely publicize their raids on the LGBT community, sometimes notifying the press beforehand](https://www.thedailybeast.com/al-sisis-egypt-is-worse-for-gays-than-the-muslim-brotherhood). The arrests [get positive press coverage for the security forces, who otherwise have a poor reputation](https://theintercept.com/2017/12/06/egypt-gay-lgbt-rights-apco/). In the words of one young Egyptian named Amr, the president is trying to [prove](http://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/middle-east/how-distaste-of-lgbt-people-in-egypt-has-turned-into-state-sponsored-persecution-10256869.html) that “though the Islamists are out of power, the new regime is not letting go of public morals, it is not less Islamic.”

Presidential elections are planned for early spring 2018, and while Sisi [faces a number of potential](http://www.egyptindependent.com/who-might-run-egypt-s-2018-presidential-elections/) [competitors](http://www.egyptindependent.com/who-might-run-egypt-s-2018-presidential-elections/), it is likely he will [win by a landslide](https://muftah.org/next-middle-east-election-watch-egypts-2018-presidential-election/), despite not being able to boost the [continually-struggling economy](http://www.newsweek.com/2017/03/10/egypts-economy-crisis-government-spending-millions-new-space-agency-561743.html). But Sisi must still [campaign](https://www.al-monitor.com/pulse/originals/2017/10/egypt-election-polarization-government-sisi-suez-canal.html) for a respectable margin of victory, and preserve his government’s acceptability. Protecting conservative social values is one means to boost his government’s legitimacy, and even when he nods to liberalizing tactics such as more women leaders, he jokes “I do not want any man getting me wrong here, particularly since the [elections are approaching](http://mesryon.com/story/1121240/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B3%D9%8A%D8%B3%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B1%D8%AC%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A9-%D9%87%D9%8A%D8%B2%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%88%D8%A7-%D9%85%D9%86%D9%8A-%D9%88%D8%A5%D8%AD%D9%86%D8%A7-%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%AE%D9%84%D9%8A%D9%86-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%AA%D8%AE%D8%A7%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%AA).”

Members of the Egyptian Parliament are vocally supportive of the government’s repression of the LGBT community, and some hope to see it increase. They have floated two new bills, one that will [strengthen the existing debauchery and prostitution law](http://www.youm7.com/story/2017/11/14/7-%D9%85%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%88%D9%85%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%B9%D9%86-%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%88%D9%86-%D9%85%D9%83%D8%A7%D9%81%D8%AD%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AF%D8%B9%D8%A7%D8%B1%D8%A9-%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AA%D8%AD%D8%B1%D9%25) by lengthening sentences and including messages on electronic media, and another that will [outlaw homosexuality and increase sentences to five years](http://www.masrawy.com/news/news_egypt/details/2017/10/25/1178761/%D9%86%D9%86%D8%B4%D8%B1-%D9%85%D8%B4%D8%B1%D9%88%D8%B9-%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%88%D9%86-%D8%AA%D8%AC%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%85-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AB%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AC%25D). International human rights groups have [condemned the bills](https://intomore.com/into/More-Than-60-Legislators-Have-Signed-Onto-Egyptian-Bill-Criminalizing-Homosexuality/d9fc1b3d1a0547f9).

**10/1961 Enforcement Against Media Figures**

Aided by active citizens, the government is also using Law 10/1961 against media personalities and authors who speak out about social liberalization. The law allows individuals to [refer cases to the state prosecutor if they feel they have been harmed by obscenity](http://www.rollingstone.com/culture/features/cairo-novelist-imprisoned-for-obscenity-in-egypt-tells-story-w468084), similar to the procedure that allows American citizens to file a Federal Communications Commission obscenity complaint in the U.S. The complaint procedure stems from an inherited French legal procedure, but also [responds to pressures](https://books.google.com/books?id=5a_-DAAAQBAJ&pg=PA135#v=onepage&q&f=false) implemented by conservative Muslim activists who have pressed the Egyptian government to embrace traditional Islamic social morality enforcement mechanisms.

Following a private citizen’s petition, television presenter Doaa Salah was [sentenced to three years](http://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/africa/egypt-woman-jailed-pregnancy-doaa-salah-public-decency-charges-a8036376.html) in prison for suggesting on network television that single women should be allowed to have children. The state prosecuted her for a monologue on where she [appeared to be pregnant and spoke in support of unwed mothers](https://www.thetimes.co.uk/article/egyptian-presenter-doaa-salah-jailed-over-show-about-single-mothers-q77j702rj), going so far as to suggest that they hire men to serve as sperm donors. Her sentence is being appealed and may be overturned. Law 10/1961 and other obscenity laws are also being used to clamp down on pop stars’ racy [Instagram posts](https://www.elwatannews.com/news/details/1337545) and [music videos](http://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-42328428), and on [authors like Ahmad Naji](http://www.rollingstone.com/culture/features/cairo-novelist-imprisoned-for-obscenity-in-egypt-tells-story-w468084), imprisoned for “violating public morality.” Khaled Ali, a left-wing human rights lawyer, has announced a [competing presidential campaign](https://www.reuters.com/article/us-egypt-politics/egyptian-rights-lawyer-says-hell-run-for-president-in-2018-idUSKBN1D6249) against Sisi despite a [three-month](http://www.menafn.com/1095899473/Egypt-Court-sentence-Khaled-Ali-to-3-months-in-prison-on-charges-of-blatant-act?src=RSS) [sentence](http://www.menafn.com/1095899473/Egypt-Court-sentence-Khaled-Ali-to-3-months-in-prison-on-charges-of-blatant-act?src=RSS) [for public](http://www.menafn.com/1095899473/Egypt-Court-sentence-Khaled-Ali-to-3-months-in-prison-on-charges-of-blatant-act?src=RSS) indecency and a raid on his office to seize election materials. Enforcement against public speech and obscenity has veered into the absurd: Singer Sherine Abdel Wahab has been indicted for making a joke about [parasites in the Nile](https://egyptianstreets.com/2017/11/16/egyptian-singer-sherine-abdel-wahab-to-face-trial-for-offending-the-river-nile/), and toy sellers were arrested for selling [retro toys](https://www.alaraby.co.uk/english/news/2017/11/8/sisis-balls-egypt-cracks-down-on-popular-childrens-toy) [that children have](https://www.alaraby.co.uk/english/news/2017/11/8/sisis-balls-egypt-cracks-down-on-popular-childrens-toy) [recen](https://www.alaraby.co.uk/english/news/2017/11/8/sisis-balls-egypt-cracks-down-on-popular-childrens-toy)[tly](https://www.alaraby.co.uk/english/news/2017/11/8/sisis-balls-egypt-cracks-down-on-popular-childrens-toy) [re-dubbed](https://www.alaraby.co.uk/english/news/2017/11/8/sisis-balls-egypt-cracks-down-on-popular-childrens-toy) “Sisi’s balls.”

Egypt is, of course, not the only country with extensive anti-gay and anti-free speech prosecutions. The United Nations [recently condemned](https://www.reuters.com/article/us-un-rights-gay/u-n-condemns-anti-gay-crackdowns-in-egypt-azerbaijan-indonesia-idUSKBN1CI1ZQ) crackdowns in Indonesia and Azerbaijan, as well as in Egypt. Even in Lebanon, perhaps the most [gay-friendly Arab](https://www.pri.org/stories/2016-08-30/much-middle-east-its-getting-more-dangerous-be-gay) [country](https://www.pri.org/stories/2016-08-30/much-middle-east-its-getting-more-dangerous-be-gay), the police [target the LGBT community](https://76crimes.com/2014/08/15/report-lebanon-targets-gay-men-in-3-raids-45-arrests/). In Iran, Saudi Arabia, and Yemen, homosexual acts are [punishable by death](https://76crimes.com/2014/08/15/report-lebanon-targets-gay-men-in-3-raids-45-arrests/). Meanwhile, Egypt’s laws against debauchery are [similar](http://www.abc.net.au/news/2017-03-04/gay-lesbian-mardi-gras-rights-around-the-world/8126828) to many across the Middle East and other post-colonial countries. However, as Egypt attempts to [tout its diplomatic record](https://theintercept.com/2017/12/06/egypt-gay-lgbt-rights-apco/) and improve its reputation in the international arena, it is important to note that Sisi is repressing a large range of forms of dissent.

args.key_excerpts: Homosexuality is not technically illegal in Egypt. But Egyptian authorities are cracking down on the LGBT community, its supporters, and advocates for social liberalization more broadly., The government immediately arrested over 60 men and women for suspected gay conduct or for waving the flag., Law 10/1961 forbids engaging in, soliciting, or providing facilities for 'debauchery and prostitution.'..., Sisi is demonstrating to the Egyptian populace that though he deposed an Islamist president, his government still upholds conservative religious values., The law allows individuals to refer cases to the state prosecutor if they feel they have been harmed by obscenity.
args.summary:
This Lawfare article by Alyssa Bernstein (published December 28, 2017) examines Egypt's crackdown on the LGBT community using Law 10/1961, which forbids "debauchery and prostitution." Though homosexuality is not technically illegal in Egypt, authorities use this vaguely defined law to prosecute LGBT individuals and their supporters.

Key events include: In September 2017, a Mashrou' Leila concert in Cairo led to over 60 arrests of people waving rainbow flags or suspected of gay conduct. Police performed anal examinations on detainees, and 16 people had been convicted by November 2017. The government also banned media statements supporting homosexuality and intensified entrapment campaigns using fake dating profiles.

Law 10/1961 originated in 1951 and was updated in 1961, carrying up to three years in prison. Under President Mubarak, the first major crackdown was the Queen Boat raid in 2001, where 52 men were arrested. The 2011 revolution temporarily reduced persecution, and President Morsi (Muslim Brotherhood) did not heavily enforce the law. However, President Sisi (who deposed Morsi in 2013) has dramatically expanded arrests, quadrupling prosecutions. The article argues Sisi uses anti-LGBT crackdowns to demonstrate conservative religious values while repressing broader dissent, with over 60,000 political prisoners since August 2013.

The law is also used against media figures, authors, and artists for "violating public morality." Egyptian parliamentarians have proposed new bills to strengthen the law and explicitly criminalize homosexuality. The article notes similar crackdowns in other countries including Indonesia, Azerbaijan, Lebanon, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and Yemen.

## Homosexuality not a crime

Report

[Egypt](en/region/north-africa-middle-east/egypt/)

Whereas, the verdict in the Queen Boat case is expected on 15 March 2003, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) expresses wide concern about repression of homosexuals in Egypt.

Although homosexuality is not referred to in Egyptian legislation, law 10/1961 (articles 9 et 14) relative to " debauchery " and prostitution, which provides for sentences up to 3 years imprisonment, as well as article 98 of the Egyptian Penal Code are used to sue homosexuals. This repression seems to have been intensifies these last months, through Internet in particular.

The FIDH considers that repression on the basis of sexual orientation contradicts dispositions of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, articles 2, 17, 18, 19, et 26 guarantee freedom of conscience and opinion, non-discrimination and right to privacy.

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, to whom the FIDH submitted the Queen Boat case, ruled on June 21, 2002 that their detention was arbitrary. The Working group established that reference to " sex " is to be taken as including sexual orientation.

The FIDH calls on the Egyptian authorities to drop any judicial proceedings on the basis of sexual orientation.

Background  
 On May 11, 2001, 55 Egyptian men, including a 17-year-old boy, were arrested. At the time of the arrest, the vast majority of them were arrested on the Queen Boat, a discotheque popular among the gay community. They were all taken to police stations and to the State Security Intelligence Department. The following day, they appeared before the State Security Prosecutor, who ordered the detention of 54 of them for 15 days. The detainees reported to being beaten and verbally abused by police officers during the first few days of detention. Fifty-two of them were charged and imprisoned until the verdict passed by the Emergency State Security Court for Misdemeanors on November 14, 2001. The State Security Court, established under the emergency law in force since 1981, rules on cases deemed to be of a threat to national security or to national sovereignty and its verdicts cannot be appealed.

The accusation was based on two elements of Egyptian legislation: first, Article 98(f) of the Egyptian Penal Code, targeting "any person who exploits religion in order to promote or advocate extremist ideologies by word of mouth, in writing or in any other manner with a view to stirring up sedition, disparaging or belittling any divinely-revealed religion or its adherents, or prejudicing national unity or social harmony"; and, second, the Anti-Prostitution Act of 1961, which punishes "anyone who habitually engages in debauchery or prostitution."

November 14, 2001, the President of the Emergency State Security Court of Misdemeanors convicted 23 of the accused to sentences ranging from one to three years of imprisonment, and acquitted the other 29 accused. Of the 23 sentenced to prison, 21 were charged with "practice of habitual debauchery", one for "contempt for religion", and one for both charges. The latter two were sentenced to 3 and 5 years of imprisonment, respectively, followed by 3 years of parole. One of the 21 accused, a seventeen-year-old minor, was tried by a juvenile criminal court - whose verdicts of can be appealed - in a trial observed by the FIDH. He was first sentenced to 3 years in prison; upon appeal, on December 19, 2001, his sentence was reduced to 6 months. After spending 6 months in custody, he was sent free. The case took a decisive turn when, on May 23, 2002, President Mubarak, in accordance with the emergency laws in force since 1981, rescinded part of the November 14, 2001 verdict passed by the Emergency State Security Court: he overturned the convictions of 21 of the accused, yet ratified the two harshest sentences, those of two people sentenced to 3 and 5 years of prison, respectively. The President’s reason for overturning the verdict: the charge "habitual debauchery" does not fall within the jurisdiction of the State Security Court. Thus, President Mubarak referred the files of the 50 men to public prosecutors for review. The prosecutors reviewed the case and referred it to a criminal court in Cairo, where, on July 27, 2002, the judge decided to postpone the trial until September 7, 2002. Verdict is due on 15 March.

More so, these examination should not be relied upon as incriminating evidence before the court, as it was obtained through an illegal procedure, specifically a violation of right to bodily integrity, which is protected in the Egyptian Constitution. ٦٢ أ شارع شريف عمارة األيموبيليا - البرج البحري الدور الثاني - شقة ٩٣٢ - القاهرة - مصر 26A Sherif., Emobilia Building - ElBorg El Bashri, 2nd Floor, Flat : 239, Cairo - Egypt تليفون :٧٠٩٦٢٩٣٢ (٢٠٢ ) - فاكس :٤٠٣٢٥٩٣٢ (٢٠٢ Tel. : (0020) 23926907 - Fax. : (0020) 23952304 ( E-mail :info@ug-law.com Web:www.ug-law.com Introduction Most recently, the topic of homosexuality has received much attention in both traditional and social media outlets. It has become a hot topic and sparked much controversy and became a topic of my debate particularly among legal practitioners and others in the public space. The recent attention given to the topic goes back to September 22, 2017, when Mashrou’ Leila (a rock band) held a concert in Cairo. During the concert, some concertgoers waved a rainbow-coloured flag. The rainbow flag was originally designed by Gilbert Baker, who was challenged by Harvey Milk, a gay rights activist to come up with a symbol of pride for the gay community. The flag first appeared in the late 70s after the United States emerged from the Vietnam War. The rainbow flag became a symbol of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender ( LGBTQ) pride, and was used during protests to demand freedom to express sexual orientation in all its forms. In the days that followed, the media mounted a fierce attack on the individuals who raised the flag. This was followed, and according to a story by Reuters1, by sweeping arrests-as many as 33 were arrested. They were charged with committing debauchery, inciting debauchery., and joining an outlawed group that incite deviancy and debauchery. Upon concluding its interrogations, the State Security Prosecution ordered the provisional detention of several those arrested for 15 days pending investigations. More so, BBC reported that based on a report by Amnesty International, the Egyptian authorities will subject six of the men accused in this case to anal examinations by the Forensic Medical Authority.2 United Group noted that there are a number of variant legal opinions on this issue. Some argue that Egyptian laws do not define/recognize a crime related to homosexuality in its two forms--gay and lesbian, and that subjecting those “accused of the crime” to anal examinations constitute sexual violence and a violation of international law. Others argue otherwise. 1 https://ara.reuters.com/article/ME_TOPNEWS_MORE/idARAKCN1C72KB 2 http://www.bbc.com/arabic/live/41459156 ٦٢ أ شارع شريف عمارة األيموبيليا - البرج البحري الدور الثاني - شقة ٩٣٢ - القاهرة - مصر 26A Sherif., Emobilia Building - ElBorg El Bashri, 2nd Floor, Flat : 239, Cairo - Egypt تليفون :٧٠٩٦٢٩٣٢ (٢٠٢ ) - فاكس :٤٠٣٢٥٩٣٢ (٢٠٢ Tel. : (0020) 23926907 - Fax. : (0020) 23952304 ( E-mail :info@ug-law.com Web:www.ug-law.com In this Paper, United Group will attempt to respond to many of the questions raised about this issue, however from a strictly legal point of view. Some of the key questions addressed include: What is the definition of homosexuality? Is homosexuality criminalized in the Egyptian laws, and if yes, what is the prescribed punishment? Does raising the rainbow flag constitute an act of inciting debauchery? Is sex between women criminalized in the law? The paper will also briefly look into the crimes of debauchery and inciting debauchery according to Law No. 10/1961 on Combatting Prostitution. 1- Definition of Homosexuality3 The term ‘Homosexuality” is used to refer to the sexual relationship between two individuals of the same sex (male - male, female - female). The term was coined by a German psychologist Karoly Benkert in 1869. Since then, the term became widely used in all languages, and is now one of the terms used in the natural, psychological, social and legal sciences.4 The term was recently introduced in the Arabic language. The term is a compound of Greek homo, same, and Medieval Latin, sexualis, sexual. It is a generic term that describes a sexual relationship between two individuals of same sex, without specifying whether the sexual relationship is between males or females. Thus the term "Male Homosexuality" is used to signify that the sexual relationship is between two men, and "Female Homosexuality" to signify that the sexual relationship between two women.5 Outside the boundaries of the medical and psychological fields, the term “Al Liwat” is the traditional and commonly used term in the Arabic language for "Male Homosexuality". The term is derived from the name of the Prophet of God Lut ( upon him be peace). Others relevant terms in the Arabic language are also derived from the same origin, such as “Al tat” and “Laat”, all to denote acts similar to the acts committed by the people of Lut. As for Female Homosexuality”, “Sihaq” is the traditional Arabic 3 ElNawaisa, A. M. (2009). Consensual Homosexuality: Its Prohibition and Permissiveness (Vol. 37, Sharia and Law Magazine). UAE: Faculty of Law, UAE University. 4 Charbel, M. (1999), Our Sexual Problems: Reasons and Treatment. 1st ed. Beirut: AlMaaref foundation, p.70. 5 Kamal, A. By the second half of the twentieth century, several countries witnessed revolts against laws that criminalize homosexuality. By time, regulating the issue has gone beyond the notion of criminality or permissibility. In some countries, laws now recognize homosexual unions or marriages, with consideration to all the legal consequences thereof, and prohibit and criminalize discrimination on the grounds on sexual orientation. 2-1 Homosexuality in the Legislation of Arab Countries Some Arab countries explicitly criminalize homosexuality. For example, under Article 534 of the Lebanese Penal Code homosexuality is punishable with up to one year imprisonment for every "intercourse against nature". Article 520 of the Syrian Penal Code also penalizes homosexuality with an imprisonment of up to three years. The term "Intercourse against nature" refers to sodomy and lesbianism, as well as anal intercourse between a man and a woman. Likewise, Article 50 of the Jordanian Military Penal Code criminalizes “whoever performs sex with another person of the same sex with his consent.” The Sudanese law only criminalizes male homosexuality (sodomy), according to Article 148, Paragraph 1:”There shall be deemed to commit sodomy, every man who penetrates his glans, or the equivalent thereof, in the anus of another woman or man, or permits another man to penetrate his glans, or its equivalent, in his anus. “Article 193 of the Kuwaiti Penal Code criminalize "the sexual act between a man and another man with his consent", so does Article 223 of the Omani Penal Code states that criminalizes “whoever performs sensual acts with 6 Ibn Manzur, A. While the federal Penal Code of the United Arab Emirates does not criminalize homosexuality, Article 80 of Abu Dhabi Penal Code criminalizes it. 2-2 Homosexuality in African legislations On the African continent, 34 out of 51 countries criminalize homosexuality-sodomy and lesbianism. Among the countries that criminalize such acts are: Angola, Botswana, Nigeria, Cameroon, Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Gambia, Ghana, Guyana, Liberia, Malawi, Mozambique, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Tanzania and Togo. The Committee unanimously held that the Act violated Articles 2/1 and 26 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. In 1995, the United Nations Committee expressed its concern about the encroachment of private life in some states in the United States of America that criminalizes sexual relations between adult consenting partners of the same sex carried out in private.8 In 1998, the committee expressed its concern regarding some provisions in the Cypriot laws that criminalize performing sex between adult consenting partners.9 8 U.N.doc.ccpR/c/79/Add.50 9 U.N.doc.ccpR/c/79/Add.88 ٦٢ أ شارع شريف عمارة األيموبيليا - البرج البحري الدور الثاني - شقة ٩٣٢ - القاهرة - مصر 26A Sherif., Emobilia Building - ElBorg El Bashri, 2nd Floor, Flat : 239, Cairo - Egypt تليفون :٧٠٩٦٢٩٣٢ (٢٠٢ ) - فاكس :٤٠٣٢٥٩٣٢ (٢٠٢ Tel. : (0020) 23926907 - Fax. : (0020) 23952304 ( E-mail :info@ug-law.com Web:www.ug-law.com Over the years, countries legalized homosexuality after being criminalized. For example, France legalized homosexuality after the French Revolution and its Penal Code of 1791 does not criminalize homosexuality. Poland decriminalized homosexuality in 1932, other countries followed suit. Sweden decriminalized homosexuality in 1944, Greece in 1951, England and Wales 1967, Germany in 1968, Portugal in 1982, Spain in 1979, Russia in 1993, and Japan in 1980. In the United States of America, most states decriminalized homosexual acts between consenting adults, starting with Illinois in 1962. Other states followed: Connecticut in 1971, Colorado and Oregon in 1972, Delaware, South Dakota and Hawaii at 1973 then Ohio at 1974. The seventies witness decriminalizing homosexual acts in a number of states including California, West Virginia, Wyoming, South Dakota, and Vermont. In the eighties, Alaska and Wisconsin decriminalized the act, followed by Maryland, Georgia, Tennessee, Montana, Nevada in the nineties and Arizona and Minnesota in 2001. In 2003, the Supreme Court struck down the sodomy law in Texas, and by extension, the ruling invalidated sodomy laws in the remaining states where it was still on the books. Last, on June 26, 2016, the Supreme Court legalized same sex marriages throughout the United States. A year later, in 2017, the German Parliament passed a law legalizing marriages and full adoption rights for same sex-couples. 3- Crimes against Morality in Egyptian laws This category of crime-crimes against morality-, which are relevant to the subject of this paper, incudes a wide range of crimes prescribed in the Penal Code and others in Law No. 10 of 1961, on the Combatting of Prostitution. The Penal Code enumerates several these crimes including: Crime of scandalous act in public: Article 278 of the Penal Code stipulates that "Whoever commits in public a scandalous act against pudency shall be punished with detention for a period not exceeding one year, or a fine not exceeding three hundred pounds." Perhaps the most lucid definition of this criminal act is the one provided by ٦٢ أ شارع شريف عمارة األيموبيليا - البرج البحري الدور الثاني - شقة ٩٣٢ - القاهرة - مصر 26A Sherif., Emobilia Building - ElBorg El Bashri, 2nd Floor, Flat : 239, Cairo - Egypt تليفون :٧٠٩٦٢٩٣٢ (٢٠٢ ) - فاكس :٤٠٣٢٥٩٣٢ (٢٠٢ Tel. : (0020) 23926907 - Fax. : (0020) 23952304 ( E-mail :info@ug-law.com Web:www.ug-law.com the Court of Cassation in its rulings, which defines it as: “The willful act of impudency that offends the decency of the victim, by words or sight."10 Crime of molesting a female in a manner that offends her modesty: Article 306 bis A of the Penal Code stipulates that: "A penalty of imprisonment for a period not exceeding one year and a fine of not less than two hundred and not more than one thousand pounds, or either penalty, shall be imposed on whoever molests a female in a manner that offends her modesty, by words or deed in a public road or a frequented place. “It is worth noting here that for this type of crime, it is essential that the words or deed Committed be sufficient enough to reveal the nature of the breach of modesty. Such a determination depends on a number of factors including the conditions and circumstances of each case, the established customs and culture standards that might exonerate the offender, and how these acts deeds and acts are widely perceived, in other words, the extent to which they indicate hidden intentions that are different from appearance. Thus, for the act to be considered a crime, it is not necessary that the offence of modesty materialize, it is sufficient that the deed or words be considered as capable of offending such modesty. Besides these two examples, there are other acts that are considered crimes against public morality, including sexual assault, rape and promoting lewdness. While these examples are not directly related to the issue under review, yet, they are highlighted here to note that there are other crimes against morality that are contained in Law No. 10 of 1961. This law includes several terms that are very close to each other, to the extent that some would think that using one of the words would suffice and obviates the need for using the other words. Below are some examples of such words and their meaning: Prostitution: Linguistically speaking, the definition of the word overlaps with that of other words such lewdness, malevolence, debauchery, licentious, adulterer and others. This legal overview document by United Group (an Egyptian law firm) examines the treatment of homosexuality under Egyptian legislation, prompted by the September 22, 2017 arrest of 33 individuals after a Mashrou' Leila concert where attendees waved rainbow flags. The document provides a comprehensive legal analysis of relevant Egyptian laws, court rulings, and constitutional issues.

**Key findings:**
- Egyptian legislation does not contain the term "homosexuality" or define it.
- The Court of Cassation has interpreted "debauchery" (in Law No. 10/1961 on Combatting Prostitution) to mean sex between men.
- Article 9(c) of Law 10/1961 is argued to be unconstitutional because the term "debauchery" is ambiguous and vague, and its definitions do not specifically express male homosexual acts.
- Egyptian law does not criminalize sexual acts between women (lesbianism).
- The crime of "inciting debauchery" cannot be satisfied merely by raising a flag, regardless of its symbolism.
- Forced anal examinations to determine sexual orientation constitute torture, violate constitutional rights to bodily integrity, and evidence obtained through them is inadmissible in court.

**Comparative context:** The document surveys laws in Arab countries (Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Sudan, Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE), African countries (34 of 51 criminalize homosexuality), and European/US jurisdictions (including the landmark Toonen v. Australia UN Human Rights Committee decision).

**Legal elements:** The crime of habitual debauchery requires: (1) practice of debauchery (sex with another man), (2) habituality (repetition on different occasions), and (3) non-selectivity (committing acts with anyone, not in a selective relationship). The crime of incitement to debauchery requires influencing a specific person's will to commit debauchery, with both general and specific criminal intent.

**Constitutional arguments:** The document cites Articles 51, 53, 54, 57, 60, 93, 94, and 95 of the Egyptian Constitution to argue that ambiguous penal provisions violate the rule of law, that bodily integrity is inviolable, and that international treaties (including the UN Convention Against Torture) have force of law in Egypt.

<webpage_content>
![Human Dignity Trust](https://www.humandignitytrust.org/wp-content/themes/hdt-2019/assets/images/logo.png)

## Human Dignity Trust

# Egypt

Egypt criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men. Sentences include a maximum penalty of three years’ imprisonment and a fine. There is evidence of the law being enforced in recent years, and LGBT people are regularly subjected to discrimination and violence.

Last updated: 26 June 2026

## Types of criminalisation

Same-sex sexual activity is prohibited under the Penal Code 1937 and Law 10/1961, which criminalises acts of ‘indecency’, ‘scandalous acts’, and ‘debauchery’. These provisions carry a maximum penalty of three years’ imprisonment and a fine. The local advocacy group Bedayaa [reports](https://rightsafrica.com/2020/03/08/repression-in-egypt-92-lgbtiq-arrests-last-year/) that, in reality, some are convicted to up to six years in prison. Only men are criminalised under this law.

These laws do not explicitly criminalise same-sex sexual activity but have been enforced, to varying degrees, against the LGBT community in recent decades. The provisions are of colonial origin, and their vagueness has allowed them to be applied to same-sex sexual activity over time.

There is substantial evidence of the law being enforced in recent years, with LGBT people being frequently subject to arrest, especially since 2013 following an incident in which a pride flag was raised at a concert (see below). Police use a number of methods to arrest gay men, including using dating apps and social media to entrap them. Although arrests frequently result in conviction, reports suggest a high proportion are acquitted on appeal.

There have been consistent reports of discrimination and violence being committed against LGBT people in Egypt, including abuse, harassment, forced anal examinations, and the forced payment of bribes.

#### **2024**

In January it was [reported](https://cairo52.com/2024/01/24/egypts-economic-courts-homosexuality-is-explicitly-criminalized-under-cybercrime-law/) that the Economic Court in Alexandria explicitly interpreted Article 25 of the Cybercrime law as criminalizing homosexuality. Article 25, which relates to violations of “family principles or values”, had been criticised for being vague and open to abuse. The Economic Court concluded that any charge of “debauchery” under Article 25 transformed into an explicit charge of homosexuality.

#### **2022**

It is [reported](https://www.newarab.com/news/egypt-integrates-sex-education-stop-homosexuality) that in September, the Egyptian Education Ministry issued a directive which included promoting anti-LGBT awareness campaigns in schools to allegedly protect children from “deviant” sexual behaviours. The Supreme Council for Media Regulation also issued a demand in September that Netflix remove “offensive content” and that companies adhere to the country’s “societal values”, largely seen as a demand to remove LGBT+ content from streaming platforms.

#### 2019

According to ILGA World, a draft bill was [introduced](https://ilga.org/downloads/ILGA_State_Sponsored_Homophobia_2019.pdf) to the Parliament’s Legislative and Constitutional Committee to replace Law No. 10/1961 on combating prostitution and debauchery, the law used to criminalise LGBT people in Egypt. Article 14 of the Bill would introduce a penalty of up to seven years in prison for “direct or indirect invitations” to practice debauchery (including same-sex sexual relations) and prostitution on social media and digital spaces.

#### **2017**

Egypt’s Supreme Council for Media Regulation [issued](https://www.egyptindependent.com/egypt-imposes-media-blackout-lgbt-community-members/) an order to ban all forms of promotion or sympathy towards the LGBT community on media outlets, as well as the appearance of LGBT people on media outlets.

#### **2015**

The Supreme Administrative Court [ruled](https://eipr.org/sites/default/files/reports/pdf/the_trap-en.pdf) in favour of the Ministry of Interior in a case filed by a Libyan citizen to overturn the decision barring him from entering the country. This ruling gave the Ministry the power to deport individuals based on their sexual orientation and practices without being required to prove their guilt in court first. The verdict, issued by the Supreme Administrative Court, went against the recommendation issued by the Court’s Commissioners’ Authority.

#### 2023

The US Department of State [reported](https://www.state.gov/reports/2023-country-reports-on-human-rights-practices/egypt/) that authorities charged more than 50 people in at least eight cases under the debauchery law during the year. A case in December involved charges for “incitement to lure males with the intention to commit immoral acts” and “assaulting family principles and values”. This report also alleges police harassment, entrapment through dating apps, forced anal exams, and extortion of bribes and information about other LGBT people to avoid arrest. ILGA World’s [Identities Under Arrest](https://ilga.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Our_Identities_Under_Arrest_2023.pdf) report documented more than 75 examples of de facto enforcement, excluding those targeted in crackdowns and raids. A recent case in January 2023 led to a man jumping off a balcony to his death to avoid arrest.

In February, Human Rights Watch released a [report](https://www.hrw.org/report/2023/02/21/all-terror-because-photo/digital-targeting-and-its-offline-consequences-lgbt) on digital targeting of LGBT people which documented 29 cases of arrest and prosecution of Egypt. Those arrested reported numerous rights violations, including the denial of food and water, family and legal representation, and medical services as well as verbal, physical, and sexual assault. Transgender people are held in jails which don’t conform to their gender identity.

#### 2022

The US Department of State, citing a local rights group, [reported](https://www.state.gov/reports/2022-country-reports-on-human-rights-practices/egypt/) over 250 arrests of LGBT persons since 2013.

A [report](https://www.article19.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Digital-Crime-Scenes-Report-3.pdf) from NGO ARTICLE 19 shows that Egyptian authorities increasingly use technological means to target and prosecute individuals perceived as LGBT, using digital evidence in trials.

#### **2019**

LGBT organisation Bedayaa’s Legal Aid Project [documented](https://rightsafrica.com/2020/03/08/repression-in-egypt-92-lgbtiq-arrests-last-year/) 65 cases of enforcement involving 92 LGBT people in 2019 (76 in 2018) noting that most of these arrests took place “randomly off the street”, though some also came through entrapment on dating apps, and in hotel/house arrests. Fifty cases resulted in convictions at first instance, however 42 resulted in acquittal on appeal.

#### **2018**

Bedayaa [documented](https://rightsafrica.com/2020/03/08/repression-in-egypt-92-lgbtiq-arrests-last-year/) 71 cases of enforcement involving 76 people in 2018.

#### **2017**

The US Department of State Human Rights [report](https://www.state.gov/reports/2017-country-reports-on-human-rights-practices/egypt/) stated that there was an increase in arrests and harassment of LGBT individuals, particularly after a rainbow flag was raised on September 22 at a concert by the rock band Mashrou Leila (see below). [Reports](https://www.hrw.org/news/2018/01/22/more-arrests-egypts-lgbt-crackdown-no-international-outcry) after this incident suggested that more than 85 individuals were arrested in a massive crackdown.

#### **2016**

The Human Rights Watch World [report](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2017/country-chapters/egypt#e81181) stated that a local advocacy group, Solidarity with Egypt LGBTQ+, had recorded 114 criminal investigations involving 274 LGBT individuals launched between the end of 2013 and November 2016, 66 of which involved the authorities’ use of social media.

#### **2014**

One [blog post](https://paper-bird.net/2014/05/18/brutal-gender-crackdown-in-egypt-the-tomorrows-that-never-came/), citing Egyptian activists (Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights) as a source, claimed in May that 77 LGBT individuals had been arrested since October 2013.

In September, an Afghani news source, Khaama Press, [reported](https://www.khaama.com/seven-men-arrested-over-gay-wedding-in-egypt-8612) the arrest of seven Egyptian men after they appeared in a video showing the marriage of two gay men. “Medical tests” were ordered for those individuals arrested. The report also alleges that four men were sentenced to eight years imprisonment for debauchery in April, after being found guilty of attending parties, where “homosexual activity” was alleged to have occurred.

In December, 26 men were [arrested](https://madamasr.com/en/2015/01/12/news/u/defendants-acquitted-in-ramses-bathhouse-case/) in a bathhouse in downtown Cairo’s Ramses area at the behest of television host Mona al-Iraqi, who filmed the ensuing security raid. In January 2015, the Azbakeya Misdemeanors Court acquitted them.

[The actions of homosexuals] are humiliating, regrettable and would anger God.

#### **2013**

In October, 14 suspects were allegedly [detained](https://en.aswatmasriya.com/news/view.aspx?id=b874a7b0-69f8-4128-91e3-e21fbd28d1f2) for investigation into allegations that they had committed “homosexual acts” at an Egyptian medical centre.

#### 2025

Outright International’s [country overview](https://outrightinternational.org/our-work/southwest-asia-and-north-africa/egypt) reports that societal attitudes towards LGBT people are “highly conservative, with widespread public disapproval reinforced by government policies”. Anti-LGBT sentiment is prevalent in educational settings.

#### **2023**

The US Department of State [report](https://www.state.gov/reports/2023-country-reports-on-human-rights-practices/egypt/) found incidents of domestic and street violence against LGBT people, including extortion attempts. Discrimination was reported to be widespread, and there were no attempts by police to tackle it.

#### **2019**

The US Department of State [report](https://www.state.gov/reports/2019-country-reports-on-human-rights-practices/egypt/) for 2019 highlighted that “intimidation and the risk of arrest greatly restricted open reporting [of discrimination and harassment] and contributed to self-censorship”.

#### **2017**

In September, a Lebanese band, Mashrou Leila, [played a concert](https://foreignpolicy.com/2017/12/28/2017-was-a-bad-year-for-egypts-lgbt-community-2018-could-be-even-worse/) to an audience of 30,000 in Cairo, led by openly-gay singer Hamed Sinno. Fans waved rainbow flags in support of LGBT rights, leading to a media outcry against homosexuality and perceived ‘immorality’ and to a mass arrest of LGBT individuals.

In October, Egypt’s Supreme State Security Prosecution [ordered two activists](https://www.hrw.org/news/2017/10/06/egypt-mass-arrests-amid-lgbt-media-blackout), Sarah Hegazy and Ahmed Alaa, to be detained for 15 days pending investigation for allegedly joining a banned group aimed at interfering with the constitution. After three months in pre-trial detention, they were [released](https://madamasr.com/en/2018/01/02/news/u/sara-hegazy-ahmed-alaa-released-on-bail-after-3-months-in-pretrial-detention-in-rainbow-flag-case/) on bail and left the country.

#### **2014**

[Reports](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/africa/egypts-police-using-social-media-and-apps-like-grindr-to-trap-gay-people-9738515.html) suggest that Egyptian police had begun to use social media websites to identify and target gay men. The local LGBT community [issued](https://www.towleroad.com/2014/09/is-egypt-surveilling-social-media-to-hunt-down-gay-people-video/) warnings to avoid using dating apps following rumours that officials were using them to arrest gay men.

## Related Countries

### [Libya](https://www.humandignitytrust.org/country-profile/libya/)

Libya criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. Sentences include a maximum penalty of five years’ imprisonment.

### [Syria](https://www.humandignitytrust.org/country-profile/syria/)

Syria criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. Sentences include a maximum penalty of three years’ imprisonment.

### [Sudan](https://www.humandignitytrust.org/country-profile/sudan/)

Sudan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. Sentences include a maximum penalty of life imprisonment.

We go to great lengths to ensure that, to the best of our knowledge, the information provided on our website is correct and up to date. If you believe that any information on our website is inaccurate, you may bring this to our attention by e-mailing [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#c7a6a3aaaea9aeb4b3b5a6b3a8b587afb2aaa6a9a3aea0a9aeb3beb3b5b2b4b3e9a8b5a0).

--- SOURCE 1: Middle Eastern Films with Trans Themes 2025 : Middle Eastern and North African Films with Transgender Themes ---
URL: http://wikicfp.com/cfp/servlet/event.showcfp?eventid=187726

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Call for Papers (CFP) posted on WikiCFP, seeking chapter proposals for "The Handbook of Trans Cinema," edited by Douglas Vakoch. The handbook aims to provide an encyclopedic overview of international trans cinema, organized into three parts: Film Genres (Part I), National Overviews of Trans Cinema (Part II), and Core Concepts (Part III). 

Specifically, the CFP is seeking chapters on Middle Eastern and North African films with transgender themes for Part II (National Overviews), including chapters on Trans Cinema from Algeria, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, Morocco, Palestine, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, UAE, and others. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Lesley Bauer (Juris Doctorate Candidate, Mitchell Hamline School of Law, May 2024) provides a comprehensive analysis of the treatment of transgender individuals in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. Key findings include:

**Legal Framework:** Despite international human rights law advancements (UDHR, UN Resolutions, Yogyakarta Principles), transgender individuals in MENA face systemic discrimination. Most MENA states inherited colonial-era laws criminalizing homosexuality, now used to target transgender individuals through vague provisions against "indecent," "immoral," or "unnatural" behavior.

**Legal Obstacles:** Almost no MENA states have standardized legal gender recognition processes. Where processes exist, they require surgical/hormonal interventions, expensive forensic medical exams, and can take 3-10 years. Sunni Islamic authorities distinguish between permitted "sex correction" (for intersex individuals) and prohibited "sex change" (for transgender individuals), with states like Egypt, UAE, Jordan, Oman, and Morocco instituting restrictions on gender-affirming surgery.

**Specific Country Examples:** Kuwait (2007) criminalizes "imitating the opposite sex"; UAE penalizes men appearing in women's clothing; Tunisia's Article 226 criminalizes "indecency" against transgender people. Courts in Bahrain, UAE, Egypt, and Kuwait have rejected legal gender recognition applications based on sharia distinctions.

**Discrimination:** Transgender individuals face pervasive discrimination in healthcare (unsafe underground clinics), employment, housing, and street violence. They experience police brutality, torture, sexual assault, and are often placed in men's cells when detained. Security forces use social media and dating apps to entrap transgender individuals.

**Progress:** Post-Arab Spring (2011), LGBTQ+ civil society movements have grown. Organizations work on decriminalization, legal aid, HIV prevention, media training, and alliance-building. Notable progress includes: Iraq accepting UPR recommendations on SOGI rights (2010, 2014); a 2017 Lebanese appeals court allowing legal gender recognition without surgery; and a 2018 Tunisian higher court recognizing gender affirming care based on medical necessity. However, most organizations operate underground due to registration restrictions.

The MENA Trans Archives, hosted by Cairo52, is the first open-access database dedicated to transgender rights in the Middle East and North Africa region. It provides resources on case law, legal gender recognition, criminalization laws, healthcare policies, Islamic religious edicts (Fatwas), and country profiles for 19 countries.

**Key Terminology:** Terms like "gender" and "transgender" are not officially recognized. Instead, terms such as "Sex Identity Disorder" (reflecting emphasis on biological sex), "Sex Change/Transition" (implying impermissibility under Islamic Sharia), "Sex Correction" (for intersex individuals, allowed as medical necessity), "Transsexual," "Mukhannath" (effeminate men), "Mustrijla" (masculine women), and "Khuntha" (intersex) are used.

**Gender-Affirming Healthcare:** Six countries (Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, UAE, Jordan) ban gender-affirming healthcare for transgender individuals, permitting it only for intersex individuals as "sex correction." Iraq is the only exception with a 2002 policy recognizing "transsexualism" as valid, though implementation is unclear. Access is largely limited to DIY hormone therapy.

**Legal Gender Recognition:** There is a legislative vacuum across the region. Most countries lack specific laws for transgender people, forcing them through lengthy judicial processes. Of 19 identified cases, 73.67% (14 cases) resulted in unfavorable outcomes. Only Morocco and Saudi Arabia have clear provisions for intersex legal recognition.

**Islamic Fiqh:** Prevailing Islamic jurisprudence distinguishes between transgender (viewed as having a mental illness) and intersex (viewed as having a biological condition). While altering Allah's creation is prohibited, intersex surgeries are permitted as "necessities." The majority of Fatwas (15 of 17) follow this logic, with only two (including Iran's Khomeini) recognizing Gender Identity Disorder as valid.

**Criminalization:** No country explicitly criminalizes being transgender, but laws against crossdressing, sodomy, public order, and morality are applied to de facto criminalize transgender individuals. Countries like Sudan, Oman, UAE, Kuwait, and Lebanon have explicit laws targeting crossdressing. In 2023, Iraq and Kuwait proposed laws explicitly criminalizing transgender identity.

**Country Summaries:** The database covers Egypt (most knowledgeable but restrictive, with 2006 landmark Supreme Court ruling), Iraq (explicit criminalization passed in 2023), Morocco (de facto criminalization under Article 498), UAE (explicit criminalization, medical liability law bans gender-affirming care), Syria (no legal recognition, war hinders healthcare), Occupied Palestinian Territories (complex jurisdictions, pinkwashing concerns), Qatar (strict criminalization), Tunisia (de facto criminalization, inconsistent court rulings), Lebanon (mixed progress, 2015 legal recognition milestone), Oman (explicit criminalization under 2018 Penal Code and 2019 Royal Decree), Saudi Arabia (Sharia law criminalizes non-conformity, only intersex healthcare allowed), Sudan (Article 152 criminalizes non-conformity, ongoing conflict), Jordan (rising targeting, new laws restricting LGBTQ+ rights), Algeria (de facto criminalization, no legal framework), Mauritania (de facto criminalization, no healthcare or recognition), Libya (de facto criminalization, recent rulings calling "gender" Haram), Yemen (erosion of rule of law, militia attacks), Kuwait (Article 198 criminalizes non-compliance, healthcare illegal), and Bahrain (denied researcher access, evidence of discriminatory violence).

SUMMARY:

"Be Like Others" (also known as "Transsexual in Iran") is a 2008 documentary film written and directed by Iranian-American filmmaker Tanaz Eshaghian. It explores the lives of transgender women in Iran, focusing on patients at Dr. Bahram Mir-Jalali's Mirdamad Surgical Centre, a sex-reassignment clinic in Tehran. The film highlights the paradox that while homosexual relationships are illegal and punishable by death in Iran, sex reassignment surgery is permitted following a 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini allowing such operations for "diagnosed transsexuals."

The documentary follows two main subjects: Ali Askar, a 24-year-old man who doesn't want to become a woman but sees no other option in Iranian society due to his feminine appearance, and Anoosh, another young man ostracized for his femininity. Ali undergoes surgery (becoming Negar) but is disowned by his family, experiences depression, and turns to prostitution. Anoosh becomes Anahita and is initially happy and engaged, though her boyfriend becomes distant after the surgery.

Eshaghian's film suggests that many Iranians pursue sex reassignment not because they identify as transgender, but because it allows them to escape persecution for homosexuality. The film won three Teddy Awards at the Berlin International Film Festival, was nominated for the Grand Jury Prize at Sundance, and was nominated for a GLAAD Media Award for Outstanding Documentary. It is a co-production between Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States, and France.

--- SOURCE 11: Queer Representation in Arab and Middle Eastern Films: A Case Study ... ---
URL: https://www.alphavillejournal.com/Issue20/HTML/ArticleKarim.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic article by Maria Abdel Karim, published in Alphaville: Journal of Film and Screen Media (2020), examines queer representation—specifically lesbianism—in three transnational Middle Eastern women's films: Caramel (2007, Lebanon) by Nadine Labaki, Circumstance (2011, Iran) by Maryam Keshavarz, and In Between (2016, Israel/Palestine) by Maysaloun Hamoud. The article analyzes how each director navigates censorship, social stigma, and cultural constraints to represent queer Arab women, who face dual marginalization for being both women and queer in patriarchal societies.

Key themes across the three films:

- **Caramel** (Labaki): Uses covert, coded representation of lesbianism through a tomboyish character (Rima) and suggestive scenes like a shampooing sequence. The film avoids explicit "coming out" and uses darkness as a motif for hidden queer desire. Labaki deliberately chose subtlety, stating "I do not think you can get anywhere by shocking people." The film was widely accepted in Lebanon and became the most financially successful Lebanese film ever.

- **Circumstance** (Keshavarz): A bolder, overt portrayal of lesbian romance between two Iranian teenage girls, set in a country where homosexuality is punishable by death. The film was banned in Iran and the Middle East. Keshavarz received death threats and had to film in Lebanon using a fake script. The controversial love-making scene uses the Islamic prayer call (adhan) as background music. The film won the Audience Award at Sundance Film Festival (2011).

- **In Between** (Hamoud): Follows three Palestinian women sharing an apartment in Tel Aviv, with an openly lesbian character (Salma). The film depicts lesbian intimacy in broad daylight, challenging the stereotype that queer relationships should be hidden. Hamoud received death threats and a fatwa (the first from Palestine in nearly 70 years). The film was banned in Umm al-Fahm but won awards at San Sebastian and Toronto film festivals.

Common conclusions: None of the films offer a happy ending for queer characters. Emigration (to Dubai, Berlin, or the West) is presented as a common but costly escape route. The article argues that while covert representation (Labaki's approach) avoids censorship, overt representation (Keshavarz and Hamoud) is more impactful for social change. The rise of online streaming platforms and virtual film festivals offers new opportunities for queer Arab cinema to circumvent censorship and reach audiences.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: I'm a Transgender Scientist and I See Myself in "Frankenstein" - Electric Literature ---
URL: https://electricliterature.com/im-a-transgender-scientist-and-i-see-myself-in-frankenstein

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a personal essay published in Electric Literature (May 2023) by a transgender graduate researcher in developmental biology at Caltech. The author draws parallels between their experience as a trans scientist and Mary Shelley's "Frankenstein," exploring the tension between being both the scientist (doctor) and the subject of scientific inquiry (monster).

The essay traces the author's journey: initially feeling empowered by the "pliability of the living body" and seeing transition through the lens of scientific possibility, they later confront the reality that science is not a neutral space of liberation but one of control. The author discusses the historical invention of the "modest witness" by 17th-century scientist Robert Boyle — an ideal of the neutral, unmarked scientific observer whose objectivity is predicated on invisibility and self-effacement.

A key incident involves a professor at the author's graduate school who posted views about binary biological sex, including the question: "Question for scientists who do not believe that humans have two distinct binary sexes: How many legs does a dog have?" When the author and peers raised concerns about discrimination, a senior professor compared trans identity to "open carry" gun laws, leading the author to exclaim "I am not a gun." The complaint yielded little action, and the author subsequently removed mentions of transness from public platforms, deleted pronouns from email signatures, and postponed medical transition.

The essay draws on historian Susan Stryker's 1994 work "My Words to Victor Frankenstein" and philosopher Donna Haraway's concept of the "modest witness." The author concludes by reframing their perspective: recognizing that the institutional power they feared is fragile, and that monstrosity — the visible, constructed, and self-aware — is ultimately a source of power rather than shame. The piece ends with the author finding humor in a professor who added "XY" chromosomes to their bio as a rebuttal to pronouns, realizing they'd been afraid of this "chromosome-wielder" for too long.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Like the monster, I am too often perceived as less than fully human due to the means of my embodiment; like the monster's as well, my exclusion from human community fuels a deep and abiding rage in me that I, like the monster, direct against the conditions in which I must struggle to exist." — Susan Stryker, "The laboratory is not a site of liberatory transformation. It is a site of control.", "If my first mistake was failing to live in such an unmarked body, my second was actively calling attention to it.", "I am not a gun.", "I call upon you to investigate your nature as I have been compelled to confront mine. I challenge you to risk abjection and flourish as well as have I. Heed my words, and you may well discover the seams and sutures in yourself." — Susan Stryker

URL: https://medicalhealthhumanities.com/2023/11/27/prescription-rage-on-teaching-susan-stryker-frankenstein-and-affect-in-medical-discourse

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an academic blog post by Heather Glenny, a Postdoctoral Fellow at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, published on the health humanities journal SYNAPSIS on November 27, 2023. The article explores the role of affect (particularly rage) in medical discourse, drawing on a class she taught called "Medicine in British Popular Culture" while on a Study Abroad in London with 13 students.

The central argument is that Western medical discourse has historically demanded emotional detachment and affective restraint, rooted in Enlightenment ideals. This creates an "infrastructure of feeling" where only tamed affects like calculated empathy and active detachment are sanctioned, while intense emotions like rage are treated as aberrations to be erased or concealed.

Glenny discusses teaching Susan Stryker's 1994 performance piece "My Words to Victor Frankenstein Above the Village of Chamounix: Performing Transgender Rage" alongside Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. Stryker's work allegorizes transness with the creature's medicalized constructedness and rage, reclaiming both as trans values. Key questions explored include: Can rage spatialize medical discourse? How does Stryker's refusal to entirely externalize medicine (while still feeling rage against it) open up richer affective possibilities? Stryker's body is presented as a site where medicine and extreme affect fuse together.

The article also considers whiteness as an enabling privilege for rage, noting that Stryker's whiteness provides certain affective allowances and buffers from retaliation not equally available to people of color.

In a coda, Glenny draws a tangential comparison to Mark Cuban's angry outbursts on Shark Tank, particularly regarding medical products, noting how his privilege (wealth, whiteness, maleness) allows his anger to disrupt medical and health discourse, while raising questions about what this makes possible for affective horizons in medicine.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In Western medical discourse, which affective modes are sanctioned, which are monitored, which are erased? For whom? By whom? And how does affect influence how we perceive medical authority?", "the [medical] men who made [her] body" also defined it with the performative proclamation, 'it's a boy!' at birth and catalog transness 'as an emotional disorder'", "Rage, alongside and *as* medicine, (re)anatomizes. Her body is a site for fusing medicine with extreme affect, holding both together at once.", "In considering rage as a viable affect in medical discourse, it's necessary to consider whiteness as an enabling privilege. Fueled by tropes assigning violent anger to people of color, and people who are Black in particular, there's an unequal degree of safety socially sanctioned by whiteness that allows for rage to disrupt medicine's affective ecologies."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Utah Public Radio article from April 19, 2023, profiles queer theorist and trans historian Susan Stryker, reflecting on her 30-year career. Stryker is the first executive director of the GLBT Historical Society, won the Monette-Horowitz Prize for LGBTQ activism, and authored the foundational text 'Transgender History.' She discussed her work with UPR before a talk at Utah State University. Stryker taught herself filmmaking to co-create the Emmy-winning documentary 'Screaming Queens: The Riot at Compton's Cafeteria,' which tells the story of a 1966 militant resistance by trans women at a San Francisco cafeteria — three years before Stonewall. Her most famous essay, 'My Words to Victor Frankenstein Above the Village of Chamonix' (turning 30 in 2023), uses the Frankenstein metaphor to explore the relationship between transsexuality and medical authority, reclaiming the word 'monster.' It remains the most-read essay in the queer journal GLQ. Stryker is currently working on 'Changing Gender,' a book about the evolution of gender in the U.S. from colonization to the present, and hopes to create an art film about Christine Jorgensen. She expressed a strong sense of responsibility to speak out on trans history amid current culture wars.

He is a professor in the Department of English and Comparative Literature and the Institute for Research on Women, Gender, and Sexuality at Columbia University (since 2017), previously at USC and UC San Diego. "The Empire Strikes Back: A Posttranssexual Manifesto" is a 1987 essay by Sandy Stone, widely considered the founding text of transgender studies in academia. The essay was written primarily in response to Janice Raymond's 1979 book "The Transsexual Empire: The Making of the She-Male" and the harassment Stone faced as a transgender woman working at Olivia Records.

The essay critiques how the Western medical establishment has historically studied and treated transgender individuals, arguing that medical literature, autobiographies, and diagnostic criteria (such as Harry Benjamin's) have reinforced a strict gender binary. Stone examines how transsexual individuals were pressured to conform to diagnostic criteria to access surgery, creating a feedback loop, and how the institution of "passing" required self-erasure with negative psychic and political consequences.

Stone criticizes trans-exclusionary radical feminists, particularly Raymond's claim that "all transsexuals rape women's bodies," calling it inexcusable bigotry. Rather than seeking shared discourse with feminism, Stone proposes constituting transsexuals as a "genre"—a set of embodied texts capable of disrupting binary understandings of gender. She calls for transsexuals to forego passing and speak as transsexual subjects, becoming "posttranssexual" by reading themselves aloud and writing themselves into the discourses that have written them.

The essay was completed while Stone was a doctoral student at UC Santa Cruz under Donna Haraway, and it was first presented in 1988. It was published in 1991 in the anthology "Body Guards" and later in "The Transgender Studies Reader" (2006). The work draws on Haraway's "A Cyborg Manifesto," Gloria Anzaldúa's "mestiza consciousness," and the theories of Jacques Derrida and Michel Foucault.

2. **Passing and its harms**: Stone critiques the imperative to pass, arguing it forces transsexuals to lie about their histories and sever ties with their prior selves. The group notes that the essay does not say "don't try to pass" but rather calls for trans people to come forward with their full experiences.

3. **Transsexual vs. transgender terminology**: The group discusses how "transsexual" is a medical term tied to the medical-industrial complex and diagnostic criteria, while "transgender" emerged as a broader umbrella term.
