From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Hunter_Schafer-64977.jpg/250px-Hunter_Schafer-64977.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hunter_Schafer-64977.jpg)

[Hunter Schafer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter_Schafer "Hunter Schafer")'s role as transgender teen [Jules Vaughn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jules_Vaughn "Jules Vaughn") in *[Euphoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphoria_(American_TV_series) "Euphoria (American TV series)")* (2019–present) garnered critical acclaim.

Portrayals of [transgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender "Transgender") people in [mass media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_media "Mass media") reflect societal attitudes about transgender identity, and have varied and evolved with public perception and understanding. Media representation, [culture industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_industry "Culture industry"), and [social marginalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_exclusion "Social exclusion") all hint at popular culture standards and the applicability and significance to mass culture, even though media depictions represent only a minuscule spectrum of the transgender group,[[1]](#cite_note-1) which essentially conveys that those that are shown are the only interpretations and ideas society has of them. However, in 2014, the United States reached a "[transgender tipping point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender_tipping_point "Transgender tipping point")", according to [*Time*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)").[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) At this time, the media visibility of transgender people reached a level higher than seen before. Since then, the number of transgender portrayals across TV platforms has stayed elevated.[[4]](#cite_note-4) Research has found that viewing multiple transgender TV characters and stories improves viewers' attitudes toward transgender people and related policies.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

## Historically

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Media_portrayals_of_transgender_people&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Historically")]

Transgender identity was discussed in the mass media as long ago as the 1930s. *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_magazine "Time magazine")* magazine in 1936 devoted an article to what it called "[hermaphrodites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermaphrodite "Hermaphrodite")", treating the subject with sensitivity and not [sensationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensationalism "Sensationalism"). It described the call by [Avery Brundage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avery_Brundage "Avery Brundage"), who led the American team to the [1936 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics "1936 Summer Olympics") in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), that a system be established to examine female athletes for "sex ambiguities"; two athletes changed sex after the Games.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

[Christine Jorgensen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christine_Jorgensen "Christine Jorgensen") was a transgender woman who received considerable attention in American mass media in the 1950s. Jorgensen was a former [G.I.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G.I._(military) "G.I. (military)") that went to Denmark to receive sex reassignment surgery. Her story appeared in publications including [*Time*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)") and *[Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek "Newsweek")*. Other representations of transgender women appeared in mainstream media in the 1950s and 1960s, such as [Delisa Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delisa_Newton "Delisa Newton"), [Charlotte Frances McLeod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Frances_McLeod "Charlotte Frances McLeod"), Tamara Rees, and Marta Olmos Ramiro, but Jorgensen received the most attention. Her story was sensationalized, but received positively. In comparison, news articles about Newton, McLeod, Rees, and Ramiro had negative implications.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

## Literature

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Media_portrayals_of_transgender_people&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Literature")]

See also: [List of fictional trans characters § Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fictional_trans_characters#Literature "List of fictional trans characters")

In February 2016, John Hansen of *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")* noted that for the past few years, "YA and middle grade books with trans main characters remain sorely lacking", and as such Hansen pointed to ten transgender authors who have trans characters in their novels.[[8]](#cite_note-Hansen-8) Even so, Dahlia Adler of [Barnes & Noble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnes_&_Noble "Barnes & Noble") noted that literature with transgender protagonists is quickly evolving with more "trans authors in the spotlight".[[9]](#cite_note-adldah-9) Christina Orlando of *[Book Riot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_Riot "Book Riot")* wrote that one of the biggest caps in the publishing industry is "transgender fiction about the trans experience", further stating that "trans stories always seem to be a second thought", pushed aside so that other "palatable narratives" can take its place.[[10]](#cite_note-bookriot-10) Additionally, Hannah Weiss of *[Insider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insider_Inc. "Insider Inc.")* wrote, in 2020, that readers can find a "find a vast variety of fantasy and sci-fi stories" which star non-binary and trans characters, most of which are written by trans people.[[11]](#cite_note-insider2020-11)

Reviewers for *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")*, *[Barnes & Noble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnes_&_Noble "Barnes & Noble")*, *[Insider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insider_Inc. "Insider Inc.")*, and *Book Riot* highlight some of the same books with transgender characters. These include Everett Maroon's *The Unintentional Time Traveler* (2014), Pat Schmatz's *Lizard Radio* (2015), [Meredith Russo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meredith_Russo "Meredith Russo")'s *If I Was Your Girl* (2016), April Daniels' *Dreadnought* (2017), [Anna-Marie McLemore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna-Marie_McLemore "Anna-Marie McLemore")'s *When the Moon Was Ours* (2016), [C. B. Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._B._Lee "C. B. Lee")'s *Not Your Villain* (2017).[[8]](#cite_note-Hansen-8)[[9]](#cite_note-adldah-9)[[10]](#cite_note-bookriot-10)[[11]](#cite_note-insider2020-11) Barnes & Noble further points to Matthew J. Metzger's *Spy Stuff* (2016)[[9]](#cite_note-adldah-9) while *Insider* highlights [Akwaeke Emezi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akwaeke_Emezi "Akwaeke Emezi")'s *[Pet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pet_(novel) "Pet (novel)")* (2019), Rich Larson's *Annex* (2018), Amy Rose Capetta's *The Brilliant Death* (2018), and a collection of stories titled *All Out: The No-Longer-Secret Stories of Queer Teens throughout the Ages* (2018) which are edited by Saundra Mitchell.[[11]](#cite_note-insider2020-11) *Book Riot* and *The Guardian* listed 12 other books with transgender characters and themes.[[a]](#cite_note-12)

## Painting

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Media_portrayals_of_transgender_people&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Painting")]

The portrayal of [transgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender "Transgender") people in painting is difficult to identify because painting is a [visual art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_arts "Visual arts") in which the viewer is only able know what the eye can see, especially in earlier times due to the lack of openness and terminology in society. It is hard to determine a transgender individual in a painting because the genitals, the fundamental feature that doctors use to assign [biological sex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_sex "Biological sex"), are oftentimes not depicted.[[12]](#cite_note-13) Before the 20th century, visual representations of cross-dressing were extremely rare and scarce information is known about individuals who broke gender norms in earlier eras;[[13]](#cite_note-14) the [LGBTQ movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ_movements "LGBTQ movements") had not happened and LGBTQ+ individuals were not as widely accepted in Western culture. Portrayals of non-conforming in visual art forms have been around forever, and these art forms are increasingly becoming more accepted and visible in society.

According to David Getsy, an art history professor at the School of the [Art Institute of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Institute_of_Chicago "Art Institute of Chicago"), "The historical record has so little in it around evidence of transgender lives – or what we would now call transgender lives – and the evidence we do have is couched in oppression and negativity". He also considers the one story narrative of history that erases evidence of oppressed identities and how the limited evidence that we do have of such works is just a piece of a greater archival records that have been lost.[[14]](#cite_note-Lang-15)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Il_femminiello.jpg/250px-Il_femminiello.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Il_femminiello.jpg)

"II Femminiello" by Giuseppe Bonito, 1740-1760, oil on canvas, 77.1 by 63.2 cm

The oil on canvas "Alonso Díaz de Guzmán" c. 1626, attributed to [Juan van der Hamen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_van_der_Hamen "Juan van der Hamen") could be considered one of the first "trans" portraits in the history of [Baroque art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_painting "Baroque painting").[[15]](#cite_note-16) The painting was a depiction of Alonso Díaz de Guzmán, born as a girl with the name [Catalina de Erauso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalina_de_Erauso "Catalina de Erauso"). Erauso wrote an autobiography, telling the story of his lived experience as a young girl, dressed as a man, who ran away from his convent, ultimately how Erauso was given the nickname "Lieutenant Nun".[[16]](#cite_note-17) Art collective Cabello/Carceller has attempted to accumulate different visual media with the goal of challenging the heteronormative representations in visual culture since 1992 and created a "new" portrait of Erauso. The exhibition, an analogue-digital portrait gallery, featuring the painting by Cabello/Carceller as well as the historical portraits dating back to 1625, was on view in [Akuna Zentro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azkuna_Zentroa "Azkuna Zentroa") in 2022.[[17]](#cite_note-18)

Displayed in the [Portland Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_Art_Museum "Portland Art Museum") and seen as one of the earliest paintings of gender fluidity painted sometime between 1740–1760, [Giuseppe Bonito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Bonito "Giuseppe Bonito")'s "II Femminiello" is a medium oil on canvas measuring 77.1 by 63.2 centimeters.[[18]](#cite_note-19) "[Femminielli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femminiello "Femminiello")" was directly translated to "little female-men" to refer to cross-dressers in 18th century Italian society. The term was associated with the "third sex" and was accepted by society, even used with endearment toward these cross-dressers, mostly coming from poverty stricken neighborhoods that were seen to bring good luck, combining the strength of both males and females.[[19]](#cite_note-20) The term "femminiello" is not to be directly compared to the term transgender but as a separate somewhat parallel term used in Italian culture. Known to work in the genre "pittora ridicula" (ridiculous paintings), Bonito's intentions of his depiction of the "femminiello" is unclear. According to [Sotheby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sotheby's_Institute_of_Art "Sotheby's Institute of Art"), "in these pictures, artists chose subjects from the lower classes and depicted them in mildly amusing ways or situation, and often with moralizing overtones".[[14]](#cite_note-Lang-15)

Early portrayals of non-conforming in paintings not only appeared in Western paintings but also from all other places. [Hosoda Eisui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eishi "Eishi")'s "Wakashu with a Shoulder-Drum" (1769–1770) is a notable piece that has only recently received recognition. "[Wakashu"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wakashū "Wakashū") were recognized as their own gender, determined by sex, age, physical appearance, and the role they played in the sexual hierarchy that was present in the Edo Period.[[20]](#cite_note-21) In art, they were portrayed as indeterminable gendered people, but in real life, they were seen as desirable to both men and women. The term described males who had not completed the "[genpuku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genpuku "Genpuku")", the Japanese coming-of-age traditional ritual who were oftentimes identified by their hairstyle, "a slightly shaven crown flanked by side locks", which differed from a man who would have no crown, only featuring side locks. During the [Edo period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo_period "Edo period") (1603–1868), gender was not binary in Japan, and gender dynamics were also influenced by age and appearance, not just sex.[[21]](#cite_note-22) However, since the making of this painting and the 1700s, gender relationships have changed in Japan due to Western colonization during the late 19th century. At the [Royal Ontario Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Ontario_Museum "Royal Ontario Museum"), "Wakashu with a Shoulder-Drum" was displayed from May 27 to November 27, 2016[[22]](#cite_note-23) in "A Third Gender: Beautiful Youths in Japanese Edo-Period Prints and Paintings", the first exhibition in North America to highlight gender dynamics, featuring the Wakashu, in the Edo Period of Japan.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Thomas_Stewart_%E2%80%93_Chevalier_d%27Eon.jpg/250px-Thomas_Stewart_%E2%80%93_Chevalier_d%27Eon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Thomas_Stewart_–_Chevalier_d'Eon.jpg)

"Chevalier d' Eon" by Thomas Stewart, after Jean Laurent Mosnier 1792

"Chevalier d'Eon" originally painted by French artist [Jean-Laurent Mosnier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Laurent_Mosnier "Jean-Laurent Mosnier") (1743–1808) and presented at the [Royal Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Academy_of_Arts "Royal Academy of Arts") in 1791,[[23]](#cite_note-24) was recreated by Thomas Stuart. The painting portrayed [Chevalier d'Eon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevalier_d'Éon "Chevalier d'Éon"), born as Charles Geneviève Louis Auguste André Timothée d'Éon de Beaumont. Despite conservative gender norms in the 18th century, she was accepted as a woman into society, serving the King and playing a key role in negotiating peace that ended the [Seven Years War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War").[[24]](#cite_note-25)

[Ria Brodell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ria_Brodell "Ria Brodell")'s 2016 piece "Captain Wright" c. 1834, gouache on paper at 11 by 17 inches is featured in the collection at the [Davis Museum at Wellesley College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davis_Museum_at_Wellesley_College "Davis Museum at Wellesley College").[[25]](#cite_note-26) Mr. Wright and his wife lived at Kennington Lane with a respectable reputation, known for his jovial personality, love for rabbits, and frequent presence at the nearby pubs. On Sunday, December 14, 1834, an extraordinary discovery was published in the London newspaper, The Bell's New Weekly Messenger; Mr. Wright's body, examined after his death, had possessed woman genitalia, marking his biological sex as female. Mr. Wright was referred to as a "creature" in the article, and people speculated the motivation behind his identity. Ria Brodell created a series of paintings called "Butch Heroes", attempting to reveal names in our history "who were assigned female at birth but whose gender presentation was more masculine than feminine". Brodell highlights, "[t]hough some could be identified today with the terms '[lesbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesbian "Lesbian"),' '[transgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender "Transgender"),' '[nonbinary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-binary "Non-binary"),' '[genderqueer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genderqueer "Genderqueer"),' etc., these myriad LGBTQIA terms were not available to them during their lifetimes. Since it is impossible to know exactly how each person would self-identify using today's terminology, I view this project as an ongoing effort to document a shared history within the [LGBTQIA community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ_community "LGBTQ community")".[[26]](#cite_note-27)

## Comics and manga

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Media_portrayals_of_transgender_people&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Comics and manga")]

See also: [List of fictional trans characters § Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fictional_trans_characters#Comics "List of fictional trans characters")

According to a study by Erik Melander in 2005, at least 25% of webcomic creators were female. This percentage was significantly larger than the number of successful women creating print comics at the time, and the number may have been even higher, as a certain percentage of contributors were unknown.[[27]](#cite_note-28) In 2015, 63% of the top 30 comic creators on webcomic conglomerate [Tapas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapas_(website) "Tapas (website)") were female.[[28]](#cite_note-29) In 2016, 42% of the webcomic creators on [Webtoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webtoon_(platform) "Webtoon (platform)") were female, as was 50% of its 6 million active daily readers.[[29]](#cite_note-30)[[30]](#cite_note-31) *[Girls with Slingshots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girls_With_Slingshots "Girls With Slingshots")* creator Danielle Corsetto stated that webcomics are probably a female-dominated field because there is no need to go through an established publisher. [ND Stevenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ND_Stevenson "ND Stevenson"), creator of *[Nimona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nimona "Nimona")* and *[Lumberjanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumberjanes "Lumberjanes")*, noticed that webcomics predominantly feature female protagonists, possibly to "balance out" the content of mainstream media. Corsetto noted that she has never encountered [sexism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexism "Sexism") during her career, though Stevenson described some negative experiences with [Reddit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit "Reddit") and [4chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4chan "4chan"), websites outside of their usual channels.[[31]](#cite_note-Interview-32) However, there exist a large amount of openly gay and lesbian comic creators that self-publish their work on the internet. These include amateur works, as well as more "mainstream" works, such as *[Kyle's Bed & Breakfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyle's_Bed_&_Breakfast "Kyle's Bed & Breakfast")*.[[32]](#cite_note-AfterElton-33) According to Andrew Wheeler from *[ComicsAlliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ComicsAlliance "ComicsAlliance")*, webcomics "provide a platform to so many queer voices that might otherwise go undiscovered",[[33]](#cite_note-ComicsAlliance-34) and Tash Wolfe of *[The Mary Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mary_Sue "The Mary Sue")* has a similar outlook on transgender artists and themes.[[34]](#cite_note-MarySue-35)

Within *[The Transformers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Transformers_(IDW_Publishing) "The Transformers (IDW Publishing)")* comic book series by [IDW Publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IDW_Publishing "IDW Publishing"), the Transformer [Arcee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcee "Arcee") is a transgender lesbian.[[35]](#cite_note-36) Initially introduced as being the result of unnatural experimentation, later storylines had the character embrace her identity as a transgender Transformer and portray her identity in a more positive light.[[36]](#cite_note-37) [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics") introduced Alysia Yeoh as the first major transgender character written in a contemporary context in a mainstream comic book.[[37]](#cite_note-38) She is a fictional character created by writer [Gail Simone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gail_Simone "Gail Simone") for the *[Batgirl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batgirl "Batgirl")* ongoing series, and is [Barbara Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Gordon "Barbara Gordon")'s best friend, and a [transgender woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans_woman "Trans woman"). They went on to premiere the first ever transgender wedding in *Batgirl #45*.[[38]](#cite_note-39) [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics") has followed suit, with writer [Al Ewing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Ewing "Al Ewing") adapting popular character [Loki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loki_(Marvel_Comics) "Loki (Marvel Comics)") to have a fluid gender identity.[[39]](#cite_note-40)

Transgender themes are also found in manga. One notable example is *[Wandering Son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wandering_Son "Wandering Son")*, which deals with issues such as being transgender, gender identity, and the beginning of puberty. [Gary Groth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Groth "Gary Groth") of Fantagraphics Books said in an interview he licensed *Wandering Son* because "it's not a typical choice for a manga title published in the U.S. and it's not typical subject matter for comics in general",[[40]](#cite_note-Groth-41) saying that the subject is "perfectly legitimate ... for literature—or comics".[[40]](#cite_note-Groth-41) Web comics have also included trans characters, with award-winning[[41]](#cite_note-wcca-42) series *[Questionable Content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Questionable_Content "Questionable Content")* adding trans woman Claire Augustus in comic 2203.[[42]](#cite_note-qc2203-43) In the manga *[Fire Punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_Punch "Fire Punch")* by [Tatsuki Fujimoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatsuki_Fujimoto "Tatsuki Fujimoto"), the character Togata has received praise for being an accurate portrayal of a transgender character with his [gender dysphoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender_dysphoria "Gender dysphoria") being a defining part of his characterization.[[43]](#cite_note-44)

## Film

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Media_portrayals_of_transgender_people&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Film")]

Main article: [List of transgender characters in film and television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_transgender_characters_in_film_and_television "List of transgender characters in film and television")

Further information: [Portrayal of transgender people in horror films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrayal_of_transgender_people_in_horror_films "Portrayal of transgender people in horror films")

### Asia

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Media_portrayals_of_transgender_people&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Asia")]

[Bao Hongwei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bao_Hongwei "Bao Hongwei"), Media Studies professor at the [University of Nottingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nottingham "University of Nottingham"), identified the 1990s as a formative decade for transgender representation in mainland Chinese film. During this time, the rise of independent film allowed for a “[coming out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_out "Coming out")” of queer and transgender characters in film.[[44]](#cite_note-45) Bao states that independent filmmakers during [the Sixth Generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_China#The_sixth_generation "Cinema of China") and with the New Documentary Movement encountered [cross-dressing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-dressing "Cross-dressing") performers working in urban Chinese bars, inspiring filmmakers to create films centered around gender-nonconforming people.[[45]](#cite_note-46)

[BAFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_of_Film_and_Television_Arts "British Academy of Film and Television Arts") nominated film producer, Elhum Shakerifar, has examined how transgender identities are portrayed in Iranian film. Shakerifar argues that sex reassignment is often depicted as a “loophole” for queer representations within Iranian media.[[46]](#cite_note-47) Shakerifar further elaborates that Western media has developed a fascination with Iran’s depictions of sex changes and often rely on the “shock” of a conservative Islamic state permitting such operations. They continue by stating that some Iranian filmmakers deliberately shape representations either to appeal to Western audiences or promote specific political agendas.[[47]](#cite_note-48) Films such as *Nature’s Humour* (2006) sought to open the eyes of parliament members on transgender issues in Iran. Shakerifar critiques how films have privileged medical transitions rather than giving transgender individuals moments to express their voice.[[48]](#cite_note-49)

Mohamed Rashid VP, Sourav V & Bangalore Morarji, scholars at [University of Hyderabad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hyderabad "University of Hyderabad") and [Vellore Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vellore_Institute_of_Technology "Vellore Institute of Technology"), analyze how transgender representation in [Malayalam cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam_cinema "Malayalam cinema") has evolved from comedic stereotypes towards more nuanced and empathetic portrayals. They argue that films like *[Randu Penkuttikal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randu_Penkuttikal "Randu Penkuttikal")* (1978) used comedic stereotypes, while films like *[Soothradharan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soothradharan "Soothradharan")* (2001) depicted a transgender character in a “double life”, which reinforces transgender people as deceitful and inauthentic.[[49]](#cite_note-50) They noted that over time, representation shifted, such as the film *[Aalorukkam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aalorukkam "Aalorukkam")* (2018), which centers on Priyanka, a transgender woman, who deals with exile and family reconciliation in a more realistic portrayal.[[50]](#cite_note-51) Using [Stuart Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Hall_(cultural_theorist) "Stuart Hall (cultural theorist)")’s representation theory, the authors argue that early portrayals were heavily stereotyped and hypersexualized, but more recent films use discourse from local media and legal reforms to present transgender characters with empathy and realism.[[51]](#cite_note-52) Additionally, they draw attention to how criminalization of transgender lives in Indian law influenced film narratives and how legislative changes have created a space for more respectful storytelling.[[52]](#cite_note-53)

### North America

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Media_portrayals_of_transgender_people&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: North America")]

Early representation of transgender and gender variant characters were often dictated by social codes and acceptance of their time. In the United States, portrayals from the 1960s and 70s depicted transgender women as deceptive, dangerous, or tragic figures.[[53]](#cite_note-54) In 2017, Nikki Reitz of [Grand Valley State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Valley_State_University "Grand Valley State University") notes that films in the 2010s have served to center transgender characters within [cisgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisgender "Cisgender") character’s life stories, or been portrayed by cisgender actors.[[54]](#cite_note-55) Professor Traci B. Abbott argues that the apparent progress of the 2010s has produced racialized and normative hierarchies rather than attempting to dismantle them.[[55]](#cite_note-56) Long Tran, Media Studies scholar at the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington"), situated these depictions within a larger queer film history, stating that Hollywood’s portrayal of transgender characters provides needed moments of visibility, but often has centered moments of tragedy.[[56]](#cite_note-57)

Traci B. Abbott, professor in English and Media Studies at [Bentley College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bentley_University "Bentley University"), situates an initial study of transgender representations in the 1960s. Abbott notes that characters during 1965 to 1980s were solely played by white [cisgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisgender "Cisgender") male actors, and were only played by non-white actors when hypersexualizing [sex workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_worker "Sex worker") such as in the film *[Riot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riot_(1969_film) "Riot (1969 film)")* (1969).[[57]](#cite_note-58) Abbott states that mainstream American cinema connected gender variance with criminality and psychological instability.[[58]](#cite_note-59) Films such as *[Psycho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psycho_(1960_film) "Psycho (1960 film)")* (1960) and *[Dressed to Kill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dressed_to_Kill_(1980_film) "Dressed to Kill (1980 film)")* (1980) reinforced what Abbott identifies as the “trans killer” stereotype, implying that [transgender feminine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transfem "Transfem") figures are threats to the social order.[[59]](#cite_note-60) Abbott argues that these portrayals, often centered for cisgender audiences, conflate transgender identity as a spectacle and affirm a rigid [gender binary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender_binary "Gender binary").[[60]](#cite_note-61) Abbott states that this created a pattern of representation that persisted into the following decades.[[61]](#cite_note-62) In the 1980s, writer, filmmaker, and actor [Jake Graf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jake_Graf "Jake Graf") said that he couldn't "find himself in any of the TV or film characters he saw" and called the worst manifestation of this was in the film *[Boys Don't Cry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boys_Don't_Cry_(1999_film) "Boys Don't Cry (1999 film)")* (1999).[[62]](#cite_note-63)

[*Southern Comfort*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Comfort_(2001_film) "Southern Comfort (2001 film)") (2001) is a documentary film, directed by Kate Davis,[[63]](#cite_note-:0-64) that goes over the life of a transgender man, [Robert Eads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Eads "Robert Eads"). As a transgender man, Robert was denied health care for his ovarian cancer because doctors were afraid their reputation would be negatively affected.[[63]](#cite_note-:0-64) The film being a documentary accentuates the factuality of the discrimination transgender people go through. The film took the audience through the life of Robert Eads– it showed his family, "chosen" family and his battle with ovarian cancer. His chosen family were his friends that he considered to be family.  Due to the denial of attention to his ovarian cancer, Robert Eads died.[[64]](#cite_note-:1-65) By walking through Robert's life the audience is introduced to the various struggles that transgender people may face. This documentary film mainly focused on the struggles transgender people face in the healthcare system. The recognition of these issues advocated for change by displaying the prejudice and discrimination faced by transgender people in the healthcare system.[[64]](#cite_note-:1-65)

In February 2006, [Logo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logo_(TV_channel) "Logo (TV channel)") aired *Beautiful Daughters*, a documentary film about the first all-trans cast of *[The Vagina Monologues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Vagina_Monologues "The Vagina Monologues")* (1996), which included Addams, [Lynn Conway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynn_Conway "Lynn Conway"), [Andrea James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_James "Andrea James"), and Leslie Townseand directed by Josh Aronson and Ariel Orr Jordan.[[65]](#cite_note-66) Also in 2006, [Lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifetime_(TV_channel) "Lifetime (TV channel)") aired a movie biography on the [murder of Gwen Araujo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Gwen_Araujo "Murder of Gwen Araujo") called *[A Girl Like Me: The Gwen Araujo Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Girl_Like_Me:_The_Gwen_Araujo_Story "A Girl Like Me: The Gwen Araujo Story")*.[[66]](#cite_note-67)

Additionally, in 2017 [Jake Graf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jake_Graf "Jake Graf"), a trans filmmaker released a short film called *Dusk*,[[67]](#cite_note-68) which tells the story of a transgender man from his childhood through adulthood. The film highlights the struggles trans men go through with transitioning and the lack of resources and acceptance in society available to them. Chris, in the film, meets a dream woman named Julie, but struggles with self-identity and how life could be different. One of the struggles depicted is how gender roles are critiqued and expected in a closed society. Ultimately, the film ends with Chris being old with Julie and still in their romantic relationship, which helps Chris understand that some questions in life have no answers or right ones which make us who we are.

In 2013, [GLAAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLAAD "GLAAD") noted a number of films which they felt had positive transgender representation. The organization specifically listed *[The World According to Garp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_World_According_to_Garp_(film) "The World According to Garp (film)")* (1982), *[Second Serve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Serve "Second Serve")* (1986), *[The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Adventures_of_Priscilla,_Queen_of_the_Desert "The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert")* (1994), *[My Life in Pink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Life_in_Pink_(film) "My Life in Pink (film)")* (*Ma Vie en Rose*) (1997), *[Southern Comfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Comfort_(2001_film) "Southern Comfort (2001 film)")* (2001), *[Normal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_(2003_film) "Normal (2003 film)")* (2003), and *[Transamerica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transamerica_(film) "Transamerica (film)")* (2005).[[68]](#cite_note-GLAAD2013-69) *[Bustle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bustle_(magazine) "Bustle (magazine)")* also argued that *TransAmerica* had positive depiction of transgender people.[[69]](#cite_note-bustletison-70)

Nikki Reitz further examined transgender representation in film and television in an article in the journal, *Cinesthesia*. Reitz details that often trans women are cast as villains in film and television, citing examples of bad representation in the films *[Sleepaway Camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepaway_Camp "Sleepaway Camp")* (1983) and *[Silence of the Lambs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Silence_of_the_Lambs_(film) "The Silence of the Lambs (film)")* (1991), and further criticizing TV shows such as *[Law & Order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_&_Order "Law & Order")* (1990–2010), *[CSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSI:_Crime_Scene_Investigation "CSI: Crime Scene Investigation")* (2000–2015), *[NCIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCIS_(TV_series) "NCIS (TV series)")* (2003–Present), and *[The Closer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Closer "The Closer")* (2005–2012) as doing the same thing. Reitz further criticized the practice of "casting cisgender men in the roles of trans women", in films such as *[The Danish Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Danish_Girl_(film) "The Danish Girl (film)")* (2015) and *[Dallas Buyers Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Buyers_Club "Dallas Buyers Club")* (2013), while saying that often lauded characters in *[Orange Is the New Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Is_the_New_Black "Orange Is the New Black")* (2013–2019) and *[Tangerine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangerine_(film) "Tangerine (film)")* (2015) fall into existing tropes, though the film *[Boy Meets Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_Meets_Girl_(2014_film) "Boy Meets Girl (2014 film)")* (2014) does not, for the most part. Reitz concluded that casting trans actors and actresses to portray transgender characters will "slow the perpetuation of negative stereotypes of trans people" and will cause public opinion of trans women to improve, along with the "quality of life" for such individuals.[[70]](#cite_note-71)

In 2012, PhD student Jeremy Russell Miller argued in his dissertation, *Crossdressing cinema: an analysis of transgender representation in film*,[[71]](#cite_note-:12-72) that there should also be an emphasis on the recurring issue of the use of Transgender characters in comedic films. There has been a constant theme or trend of utilizing male characters dressed as women for comedic effect.  In award-winning films such as *[Victor/Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor/Victoria "Victor/Victoria")* (1982), *[Some Like It Hot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Some_Like_It_Hot "Some Like It Hot")* (1952), and *[Big Momma's House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Momma's_House "Big Momma's House")* (2000), there is an implication of having male-identifying actors become and act as female characters to bring a focus of laughter.[[71]](#cite_note-:12-72) Each film grossed over $20 million and won an Oscar over ten other nominated films.[[71]](#cite_note-:12-72) Miller's argument highlights the fact that profit is made from the humiliation of the display of transgender people.[[71]](#cite_note-:12-72) They are often used as the butt of the joke and made into objects to ridicule. While comedies should be taken lightly and not seriously, they should still be called out for how damaging it can be to associate transgender people as subjects of laughter. Further, films such as *[Mrs. Doubtfire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mrs._Doubtfire "Mrs. Doubtfire")* (1993) and *[100 Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/100_Girls "100 Girls")* (2000) invalidate the process of transitioning that display heteronormative privileges that cisgender men have over transgender people. As these movies cut from a character being one gender to another, it allows for each character to keep their heteronormative identities. This helps preserve their privilege of being heteronormative.[[71]](#cite_note-:12-72)

Yolanda Mercader Martinez, professor at the [Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana Xochimilco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UAM_Xochimilco "UAM Xochimilco"), states within Mexican film in the early 2000s, stories began to shift away from stereotypical and comedic portrayals of transgender individuals. Mercader Martinez states that independent filmmakers began centering [trans\*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans* "Trans*") and [travesti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travesti_(gender_identity) "Travesti (gender identity)") characters, primarily during the years 2005-2016.[[72]](#cite_note-73) Films such as [*Muxes*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mute_(2005_film) "Mute (2005 film)") (2005), *Morir de pie* (2011), *Quebranto* (2013), and *[Carmin Tropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmin_Tropical "Carmin Tropical")* (2014) were influential in portraying transgender lead character fighting against discrimination, precarious labor, and developing their own gender expressions, often based in Mexican regional and indigenous practices.[[73]](#cite_note-74) Mercader Martinez argues that these films have shifted away from earlier uses of cross-dressing as comic relief and instead highlight the authentic life experiences of transgender and gender nonconforming individuals throughout Mexico.[[74]](#cite_note-75)

During the four-year period of 2017–2020, [GLAAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLAAD "GLAAD")'s annual Studio Responsibility Index found that major studios had produced no films with transgender or non-binary characters.[[75]](#cite_note-76) However, in March 2021, [Patti Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patti_Harrison "Patti Harrison") became the "first known trans actor to voice a character in a Disney animated movie", specifically *[Raya and the Last Dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raya_and_the_Last_Dragon "Raya and the Last Dragon")*.[[76]](#cite_note-77)

In March 2022, Professor Cáel M. Keegan argued against the idea that more favorable media portrayals of transgender people could greatly change how they were treated within society.[[77]](#cite_note-:02-78) In his article for *[Film Quarterly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_Quarterly "Film Quarterly")*, he discussed how popular portrayals end up overshadowing more nuanced or unconventional depictions, thus becoming more "assimilative" than revolutionary.[[77]](#cite_note-:02-78) In light of this issue, Keegan suggested that portrayals commonly considered to be aversive (or "'bad' trans object[s]") might actually be better equipped to produce thought-provoking depictions because they "cannot fit within the aesthetic system" at all.[[77]](#cite_note-:02-78) While examining the films *[Tootsie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tootsie "Tootsie")* (1982), *[It's Pat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Pat "It's Pat")* (1994), and *[The Assignment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Assignment_(2016_film) "The Assignment (2016 film)")* (2016), Keegan also attempted to vindicate their controversial portrayals of transgender people by claiming that their uncomfortable natures "point to...broader vision[s] for trans politics" overall.[[77]](#cite_note-:02-78)

### South America

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Media_portrayals_of_transgender_people&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: South America")]

Professor Angela Mooney of [Texas Woman’s University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Woman's_University "Texas Woman's University") states that films from the 2010s in Brazil have provided joyful representations of transgender life.[[78]](#cite_note-79) Mooney highlights films like *[Alice Junior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Júnior "Alice Júnior")* (2019) and *Valentina* (2020) as shifting narratives away from just coming out stories and instead providing comprehensive views on the lives of transgender people.[[79]](#cite_note-80) These contemporary films have been able to stray away from using [trans\*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans* "Trans*") and [travesti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travesti_(gender_identity) "Travesti (gender identity)") characters as comedic element that was prevalent in the 1970s and 1980s.[[80]](#cite_note-81)

In their 2018 PhD dissertation at the [University of Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ottawa "University of Ottawa"), Javier Enrique Garcia Leon argues that Venezuelan transgender cinema is a site where transgender identities are positioned in relation to politics, race, and social precarity. Garcia Leon states that such as [*Pelo Malo*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Hair_(2013_film) "Bad Hair (2013 film)") (2013) and *Cheila, una casa pa maita* (2010) within state-sponsored and independent productions that narrate the lives of transfeminine figures under the Bolivarian government.[[81]](#cite_note-82) Garcia Leon states that these films frequently showcase the effects of racialization and poverty.[[82]](#cite_note-83) Documentaries like *[Yo, indocumentada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yo,_indocumentada "Yo, indocumentada")* (2011), which follow transgender women seeking legal recognition and portray violence and exclusion as central issues.[[83]](#cite_note-84) Garcia Leon argues that recent Venezuelan cinema moves between exposing the social pressures faced by transgender people and documenting their efforts to gain rights and recognition.[[84]](#cite_note-85)

Garcia Leon additionally covers how Colombian films approach transgender representation by focusing on everyday life rather than spectacle. He highlights Ana Cristina Monroy’s documentary *[Esta pueblo necesita un muerto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esta_pueblo_necesita_un_muerto?action=edit&redlink=1 "Esta pueblo necesita un muerto (page does not exist)")* (2008), which uses interviews and close-up shots to portray the life of a Black transgender woman in the [Choco Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chocó_Department "Chocó Department").[[85]](#cite_note-86) According to Garcia Leon, the film addresses themes such as violence, mourning, and social abandonment, but does so in a way that gives the protagonist dignity and presence, instead of treating her as a sensational figure.[[86]](#cite_note-87) He argues that this film and similar Colombian films offer a more grounded and community-centered representation of transgender lives, emphasizing personal experience and local realities.[[87]](#cite_note-88)

args.summary:
This Wikipedia article examines the portrayal of transgender people across various media forms, reflecting societal attitudes and evolving alongside public perception. It notes that the United States reached a "transgender tipping point" in 2014, with media visibility of transgender people reaching unprecedented levels, and research shows that viewing multiple transgender TV characters improves attitudes toward transgender people and related policies.

**Historically:** Transgender identity was discussed in mass media as early as the 1930s, with Time magazine covering "hermaphrodites" sensitively in 1936. Christine Jorgensen received significant attention in the 1950s, with her story sensationalized but received positively.

**Literature:** YA and middle-grade books with trans main characters remain lacking, though literature with transgender protagonists is evolving. Notable works include Meredith Russo's *If I Was Your Girl* (2016), April Daniels' *Dreadnought* (2017), and Anna-Marie McLemore's *When the Moon Was Ours* (2016).

**Painting:** Identifying transgender individuals in historical paintings is difficult due to the visual nature of art and lack of historical terminology. Notable works include Giuseppe Bonito's "II Femminiello" (1740-1760), depicting "femminielli" in Italian society, and Hosoda Eisui's "Wakashu with a Shoulder-Drum" (1769-1770), featuring the "wakashu" as a recognized third gender in Edo-period Japan. Ria Brodell's "Butch Heroes" series documents historical figures assigned female at birth with masculine gender presentation.

**Comics and Manga:** Webcomics provide a platform for queer voices. DC Comics introduced Alysia Yeoh as the first major transgender character in a mainstream comic. Marvel adapted Loki to have fluid gender identity. Manga like *Wandering Son* and *Fire Punch* address transgender themes.

**Film:** 
- **Asia:** Chinese independent film in the 1990s began featuring gender-nonconforming performers. Iranian film often depicts sex reassignment as a "loophole" for queer representation. Malayalam cinema evolved from comedic stereotypes to more nuanced portrayals.
- **North America:** Early depictions (1960s-70s) portrayed transgender women as deceptive, dangerous, or tragic. Films like *Psycho* (1960) and *Dressed to Kill* (1980) reinforced the "trans killer" stereotype. The documentary *Southern Comfort* (2001) highlighted healthcare discrimination. GLAAD noted positive representation in films like *The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert* (1994), *Transamerica* (2005), and others. From 2017-2020, major studios produced no films with transgender or non-binary characters. Patti Harrison became the first known trans actor to voice a character in a Disney animated movie (*Raya and the Last Dragon*, 2021).
- **South America:** Brazilian films from the 2010s like *Alice Junior* (2019) and *Valentina* (2020) provide joyful representations of transgender life. Venezuelan and Colombian cinema address themes of violence, exclusion, and legal recognition.

**Live-action Television:** GLAAD's 2012 review of scripted television found 54% of episodes containing transgender characters had negative representations.
