Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer ([LGBTQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ "LGBTQ")) people in [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") face repression and discrimination.[[3]](#cite_note-PinkNews-3) Both male and female same-sex behavior is punishable by death within the country.[[4]](#cite_note-ilga_2020-4): 135–136 Therefore, there are no protections for LGBTQ people in Saudi Arabia.

The law of Saudi Arabia is uncodified; a [Wahhabist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wahhabist "Wahhabist") interpretation of [sharia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharia "Sharia"), derived from the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran") and the [Sunnah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunnah "Sunnah"), is the basis of the law and justice system.[[5]](#cite_note-IDuA-5): 205 In particular, the Quranic account of the [prophet Lut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lot_in_Islam "Lot in Islam") and certain teachings of [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") in the Sunnah, inform the legal treatment of same-sex sexual activity and nonconforming-gender presentation. [Homosexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexuality "Homosexuality") and [transgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender "Transgender") status or gender non-conformity are widely seen as immoral and indecent, and the law allows penalties for acts of homosexuality of [capital punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment "Capital punishment"),[[4]](#cite_note-ilga_2020-4): 69–74[[1]](#cite_note-wp_ten_2016-1)[[6]](#cite_note-pink_apr_2019-6) prison sentences of indeterminate length[[a]](#cite_note-7)[[2]](#cite_note-irb_Canada-2) (the maximum term is unknown),[[7]](#cite_note-ilga_frameworks-8) fines, [flogging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flogging "Flogging"), and deportation for foreigners.[[8]](#cite_note-bbc_2015_flog-9) During investigations and detentions, mistreatment of suspects and detainees, including beatings and torture, have occurred.[[5]](#cite_note-IDuA-5): 208–209 Community violence against LGBTQ persons occurs.[[9]](#cite_note-toys-10)[[10]](#cite_note-times_2016_wikileaks-11)

In May 2023, the [Saudi Tourism Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Tourism_Authority "Saudi Tourism Authority") website updated its FAQ page stating that all visitors, including LGBTQ visitors, were welcome to visit the country.[[11]](#cite_note-12) Though homosexuality remains illegal, enforcement of the laws is not universal.[[12]](#cite_note-13) The move follows a series of social and economic changes, including the abandonment of the enforcement of wearing the [hijab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijab "Hijab") in public,[[13]](#cite_note-14)[[14]](#cite_note-15) and the opening of the first public beach in Saudi Arabia where women can wear bikinis.[[15]](#cite_note-16) The decision to host the [2034 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2034_FIFA_World_Cup "2034 FIFA World Cup") within Saudi Arabia received strong criticism from the LGBTQ community.[[3]](#cite_note-PinkNews-3)[[16]](#cite_note-17)

## Legality

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Legality")]

### Criminal laws

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Criminal laws")]

See also: [Legal system of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_system_of_Saudi_Arabia "Legal system of Saudi Arabia") and [LGBT in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_in_Islam "LGBT in Islam")

Saudi Arabia has no [criminal code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_code "Criminal code"). The primary source of law in Saudi Arabia is the [Sharia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharia "Sharia") (Islamic law), which is derived from the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran"). Specifically, prohibition of same-sex sexual acts is based on the Quranic story of the prophet [Lut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lot_in_Islam "Lot in Islam") and traditions of the teachings of [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") contained in the [Sunnah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunnah "Sunnah").[[17]](#cite_note-Campbell-18) *[Ijma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ijma "Ijma")*, or scholarly consensus on the meaning of the Quran and the Sunnah, developed after Muhammad's death. *[Qiyas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiyas "Qiyas")*, or analogical reasoning applied to the principles of the Quran, Sunnah and *ijma* is used:[[18]](#cite_note-19) Judges apply their personal interpretation of sharia to any particular case (*[ijtihad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ijtihad "Ijtihad")*) and are not bound by any previous decisions, sometimes resulting in divergent judgements even in apparently identical cases.[[19]](#cite_note-Otto161/2-20) In addition, royal decrees and government regulations have been issued. Reformers have often called for codified laws to be instituted, and there appears to be a trend in the country to codify, publish and even translate some Saudi criminal and civil laws.[[20]](#cite_note-21) However, the traditional interpretation of Sharia is that it prohibits homosexual acts (as *[zina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zina "Zina")* or unlawful sexual intercourse) and, specifically, *[liwat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liwat "Liwat")* or [sodomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodomy "Sodomy"), though there is a difference of opinion on the punishment ranging from none at all ([Hanafi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanafi "Hanafi")) to the death penalty.[[21]](#cite_note-22)[[22]](#cite_note-23)[[23]](#cite_note-peters-24)

In 1928, the Saudi judicial board advised Islamic judges to look for guidance in two books by the Hanbalite jurist [Marʿī ibn Yūsuf al-Karmī al-Maqdisī](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar'i_al-Karmi "Mar'i al-Karmi") (died 1033/1624). *Liwat* (sodomy) is to be:

> ...treated like [fornication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fornication "Fornication"), and must be punished in the same manner. If *muḥṣan* [commonly translated as "adulterer" but technically meaning someone who has had legal intercourse, but who may or may not currently be married] and free [not a slave], one must be stoned to death, while a free bachelor must be punished with 100 lashes and banished for a year.

Sodomy is proven either by the perpetrator confessing four times or by the testimony of four trustworthy Muslim men, who were eyewitnesses to the act. If there are fewer than four witnesses, or if one is not upstanding, then they are all to be chastised with 80 lashes for slander.[[24]](#cite_note-25) These safeguards contained in Sharia for capital crimes are not complied with, according to the ILGA. It considers that Saudi Arabia has[[4]](#cite_note-ilga_2020-4): 73–74

> ... failed to incorporate the procedural protections and safeguards that Sharia law has traditionally associated with the death penalty. ... factors such as the religion, citizenship, and social status of the accused can be a strong determinant of the conviction and severity of punishments, with working-class migrant workers usually being judged and treated more harshly than upper-class Saudi citizens.

— ILGA (2020). "Death Penalty: Saudi Arabia – Enforcement". *State-sponsored Homophobia* report.

In the 1980s, Saudi King Khaled issued numerous royal decrees designed to secure support among religious fundamentalists in the aftermath of an uprising of religious extremists in 1979, known as the [Grand Mosque seizure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Mosque_seizure "Grand Mosque seizure").

The "Rules of Apprehension, Temporary Custody & Precautionary Detention Regulation" codified the criminal code on homosexuality by listing it among the crimes that warranted arrest and detention. In addition to law enforcement, a second royal decree formally established the [Committee for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Committee_for_the_Promotion_of_Virtue_and_the_Prevention_of_Vice_(Saudi_Arabia) "Committee for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice (Saudi Arabia)") (CPVPV) and gave this committee the power to arrest and detain people who violate the traditional teachings of Islam, including acts of homosexuality and cross-dressing.

Combating homosexuality remains one of the major goals of the CPVPV, along with its campaign against the consumption of alcohol and the practice of magic.[[25]](#cite_note-2010_sg-26)

In September 2013, it was announced that all [Gulf Cooperative Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Cooperation_Council "Gulf Cooperation Council") had agreed to discuss a proposal to establish some form of, yet unknown, testing in order to ban gay foreigners from entering any of the countries.[[26]](#cite_note-27)[[27]](#cite_note-28) However, it has been suggested that concern regarding the hosting of the [2022 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_FIFA_World_Cup "2022 FIFA World Cup") by [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar"), and fears for the inevitable worldwide controversy if it is decided that football fans will have to be screened for homosexuality, made officials backtrack the plans and insist that it was a mere proposal.[[28]](#cite_note-29)

According to a transcript published by Saudi [state media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_media "State media") in March 2022, [Crown Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Prince_of_Saudi_Arabia "Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia") [Mohammed bin Salman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_bin_Salman "Mohammed bin Salman"), the *de facto* ruler of Saudi Arabia, stated in an interview with *[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic")* magazine that the death penalty has been abolished in the country, except for instances of murder or when an individual poses a threat to many people.[[29]](#cite_note-30)

In 2019, to coincide with the introduction of tourist visas to the country, the Saudi government decreed a code to regulate the behavior of Saudi citizens and foreigners in public places. The [new Public Decency Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Decency_Law_in_Saudi_Arabia "Public Decency Law in Saudi Arabia") contains nineteen regulations, violations of which are subject to fines. Proscribed practices include public displays of affection, wearing immodest clothing, using profanity, and displaying immoral advertising. Some behaviors unrelated to sexual or gender expression are also covered; for example, littering, taking photographs and videos of people without permission, and queue jumping. The authority of the religious police to intervene in such matters has been reduced, with the general police force being the "sole authority responsible for monitoring offenses and imposing fines".[[30]](#cite_note-31)[[31]](#cite_note-32)

### Enforcement cases

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Enforcement cases")]

|  |

In 2000, the [Saudi Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Saudi_Arabia "Politics of Saudi Arabia") reported that it had sentenced nine Saudi men to extensive prison terms with lashing for engaging in [cross-dressing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-dressing "Cross-dressing") and homosexual relations.[[32]](#cite_note-33)

In 2001, Saudi teacher and playwright Muhammad Al-Suhaimi was charged with promoting homosexuality and after a trial was sentenced to prison. In 2006, he was given a pardon and allowed to resume teaching.[[33]](#cite_note-34)

In May 2005, the government arrested 92 men for homosexuality, who were given sentences ranging from fines to prison sentences of several months and lashings. Likewise, on 7 November 2005 [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh") police raided what the Saudi press called a "beauty contest for gay men" at [Al-Qatif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qatif "Al-Qatif"). What became of the five men arrested for organizing the event is not known.[[34]](#cite_note-35)

Persons caught living in the kingdom illegally are often accused of other crimes, involving illegal drugs, pornography, prostitution and homosexuality. Several such police crackdowns were reported in 2004–2005.[[35]](#cite_note-36) A similar raid in 2008 netted [Filipino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipino_people "Filipino people") workers arrested on charges of alcohol and gay prostitution.[[36]](#cite_note-arabnews1-37) The *[Arab News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_News "Arab News")* newspaper article on the arrests stated, "Gay rights are not recognized in the Middle East countries and the publication of any material promoting them is banned".[[36]](#cite_note-arabnews1-37)

International protests from human rights organizations prompted some Saudi officials within the Saudi Arabian embassy in Washington, D.C., to imply that their kingdom will only use the death penalty when someone has been convicted of child molestation, rape, sexual assault, murder or engaging in anything deemed to be a form of political advocacy.[[37]](#cite_note-38)

In 2010, Prince [Saud bin Abdulaziz bin Nasir al Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saud_bin_Abdulaziz_bin_Nasser_Al_Saud "Saud bin Abdulaziz bin Nasser Al Saud") was found guilty at the [Old Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Bailey "Old Bailey") in London of [murdering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder "Murder") his servant Bandar Abdulaziz in their suite at the [Landmark Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Landmark_London "The Landmark London") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London").[[38]](#cite_note-BBC_News-39) During the trial, it was alleged that the prince had received a "sexual massage" before the murder, and that he and Abdulaziz had been in a sexual relationship. According to the prosecutor, the Prince sexually and physically abused his servant as well as paid other men for sexual services.[[39]](#cite_note-40)[[40]](#cite_note-41) He was sentenced to life imprisonment. In March 2013, he was allowed to return to Saudi Arabia to serve the remainder of his term in a Saudi prison. According to the agreement between the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") and Saudi Arabia, he must serve at least 20 years before he can be released.[[41]](#cite_note-42)

In 2011–2012, the Saudi newspaper *[Okaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okaz "Okaz")* announced that the government had arrested over 260 people for the crime of homosexuality over a one-year period. According to the official report, the men were caught cross-dressing, wearing ladies' makeup and trying to pick up other men.[[42]](#cite_note-Stewart_2012-43)

A gay Saudi diplomat named Ali Ahmad Asseri applied for asylum in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") after he claimed the Saudi government discovered his sexuality and also because of dissent.[[43]](#cite_note-44)

In 2014, a 24-year-old Saudi Arabian man was sentenced to three years' detention and 450 lashes after a [Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina "Medina") court found him guilty of "promoting the vice and practice of homosexuality", after he was caught using [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") to arrange dates with other men.[[44]](#cite_note-twitter-45)

In February 2017, 35 [Pakistani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistanis "Pakistanis") transgender women were arrested at a party in [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh").[[45]](#cite_note-46) Two were allegedly forced into sacks and beaten to death with sticks by Saudi authorities.[[46]](#cite_note-:0-47) State media reported that 35 men who were dressed as women and wearing make-up were arrested, but did not report that anyone from the event was executed, nor that any of the attendees were transgender.[[46]](#cite_note-:0-47) Reports of the deaths had circulated in Pakistani media by March, but the [Saudi Interior Ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Interior_(Saudi_Arabia) "Ministry of Interior (Saudi Arabia)") denied that anyone was executed and claimed that the reports were false.[[47]](#cite_note-:1-48) The ministry later said that a 61-year-old Pakistani from the event died while in custody after suffering from a [heart attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_attack "Heart attack").[[47]](#cite_note-:1-48)

In April 2019, 37 Saudi men were [beheaded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decapitation "Decapitation") on after confessing to terrorism and [spying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espionage "Espionage") [on the country for Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran–Saudi_Arabia_proxy_conflict "Iran–Saudi Arabia proxy conflict").[[48]](#cite_note-49) One of those executed, admitted to having sexual relationships with four of the other accused men and organizing during a trial held in 2016. He also admitted to organizing violent anti-government protests. His motive was that he [opposed to the Sunni Sect of Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunniphobic "Sunniphobic") due to his hatred of the state and the Saudi people.[[49]](#cite_note-50)

On 13 October 2019, Saudi authorities arrested a 23-year-old national, Suhail al-Jameel, for posting a picture of himself wearing short shorts at the beach. He is a [gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay "Gay") social media personality in Saudi Arabia, who openly documented his sexuality on [Snapchat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat "Snapchat") and Twitter. Al-Jameel wrote on Snapchat that he was arrested on the charges of sharing nudity online. Soon after fans started using a #freesuhail hashtag on Twitter.[[50]](#cite_note-51) He was released from prison in October 2022.[[51]](#cite_note-52)

In July 2022, Tala Safwan, a female Egyptian [influencer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influencer "Influencer") living in [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh"), posted a video chatting with a female Saudi friend. Safwan invited her friend to her house, saying that “everyone will be asleep” and that “no one will hear her scream.” Many in the country interpreted this as sexual innuendo, and Safwan was subsequently arrested.[[52]](#cite_note-53)[[53]](#cite_note-54)

## Same-sex relationships

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Same-sex relationships")]

Saudi Arabia bans [same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage "Same-sex marriage"), [domestic partnerships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_partnership "Domestic partnership"), and [civil unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_union "Civil union"). The country neither recognizes nor performs these types of same-sex actions. The maximum punishment for same-sex behavior in Saudi Arabia is [death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_for_homosexuality "Capital punishment for homosexuality").

## Censorship

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Censorship")]

Main article: [Censorship in Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_Saudi_Arabia "Censorship in Saudi Arabia")

The Saudi government censors the media. Fines, imprisonment and, for foreigners, deportation are imposed on any person possessing, importing, distributing or producing media without governmental approval. Media content, including advertising, cannot be seen as insulting [the royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Saud "House of Saud") or conflicting with Islamic teachings and values.[[54]](#cite_note-55) Anything perceived to condone homosexuality or as support for LGBTQ rights can result in prosecution.[[55]](#cite_note-hrw.org-56)

Homosexuality and cross-dressing are dealt with in print news through news coverage of criminal matters, the [HIV/AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS") pandemic or allusions to perceived Western [decadence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decadence "Decadence").[[56]](#cite_note-57)

Radio and TV programs are similarly banned from expressing support for LGBTQ rights, but homosexuality and cross-dressing can be discussed as long as the negative attitudes and biases are reinforced.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] For example, a call-in TV show may feature a discussion about the immorality or "illness" of homosexuality, or, as in the 2011 case of [Mirel Radoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirel_Radoi "Mirel Radoi"), a Romanian-born footballer playing in Saudi, coverage may focus on a celebrity expressing disapproving views. In the Radoi case, the footballer implied, as an insult, that an opponent he was complaining about was gay. (Radoi was fined and suspended from play for two matches by the Saudi football disciplinary committee for these remarks.)[[57]](#cite_note-58)

The government has allowed public movie theaters since 2018, but the films are censored, as are the DVDs purchased in many retail stores. LGBTQ themes are generally one of the themes edited out of movies. Customs agents keep a list of films or TV shows that are not allowed to be brought into the kingdom.[[58]](#cite_note-59) Foreign films that include small acknowledgments of a character's LGBTQ identity are often banned in the kingdom, even if the content or depiction is not sexually explicit.[[59]](#cite_note-60)

Government regulation of the Internet generally falls under the Royal Decrees on Anti-Cyber Crime (2007). Article 6 prohibits creating, distributing or accessing online content or webpages that the government deems to be [pornographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pornographic "Pornographic") or in violation of religious values or public morals or is a threat to public health, safety or order.[[60]](#cite_note-WIPO_2007-61)

The Saudi government has frequently blocked Internet users in the kingdom from accessing web pages or other online content that express support for LGBTQ rights.[[61]](#cite_note-62) The restrictions on the Internet extend to blogs, social media and video upload webpages.[[62]](#cite_note-63)

In 2010, a 27-year-old Saudi man was charged with [homosexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexuality "Homosexuality") and impersonating a police officer when he posted a comical video of himself online, where he discusses popular culture, shows off his chest hair and flirts with the camera man. He was sentenced to a year in prison, with 1,000 lashes, and ordered to pay a fine of 5,000 rials (US$1,333).[[63]](#cite_note-64)

In a crackdown across stores in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, according to the Saudi state-run TV channel [al-Ekhbariya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Ekhbariya "Al-Ekhbariya"), government officials seized rainbow-colored clothing, products, toys, etc. The officials claimed that the June 2022 move was aimed at curbing the direct and indirect promotion of homosexuality in the country. An unnamed official from the [Ministry of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Commerce_(Saudi_Arabia) "Ministry of Commerce (Saudi Arabia)") claimed that they were looking out for "slogans that violate the rules of Islam and public morals like promoting homosexuality colors, targeting the young generation." The items seized in the crackdown included hair accessories for children, backpacks, pencil cases, and rainbow stripes featured on crayon packs. When asked for comments from the Saudi authorities, none were received.[[64]](#cite_note-65) In December 2022, authorities in neighboring [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar") carried out a similar purge.[[65]](#cite_note-66)

## Gender identity

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Gender identity")]

According to [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch"), Saudi Arabia has no laws against transgender people. Arrests and prosecutions of individuals wearing clothing not considered appropriate to their sex (cross-dressing), men wearing makeup, or "feminine" accessories, occur. Penalties include prison sentences and floggings.[[66]](#cite_note-67)[[67]](#cite_note-Reuters-68)[[5]](#cite_note-IDuA-5): 207

Over the past 36 years, more than 2,000 individuals in Saudi Arabia have undergone [sex reassignment surgeries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender-affirming_surgery "Gender-affirming surgery") (also known as "sex-correction surgeries" in Saudi Arabia) due to [gender dysphoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender_dysphoria "Gender dysphoria"). However, the [Ministry of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Health_(Saudi_Arabia) "Ministry of Health (Saudi Arabia)") does not permit sex change operations, by which a person with a clear gender identity and matching physical features seeks to change sex.[[68]](#cite_note-69)

In 2017, two [transgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender "Transgender") Pakistanis were allegedly "packed in sacks, thrashed with sticks and tortured to death" by Saudi police.[[69]](#cite_note-ind_2017-70) A statement from the [Saudi Interior Ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Interior_(Saudi_Arabia) "Ministry of Interior (Saudi Arabia)"), however, said the reports were "totally wrong and nobody was tortured".[[70]](#cite_note-71)[[71]](#cite_note-72)

People with a transsexual or transgender identity cards are not allowed to make the [pilgrimage to Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj").[[72]](#cite_note-73) However, in February 2018 it was reported that a group of transgender individuals from [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan") were allowed to be sent to Saudi Arabia for [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj").[[73]](#cite_note-74)[[67]](#cite_note-Reuters-68)

In March 2023, a 23-year old Saudi transgender woman, named [Eden Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide_of_Eden_Knight "Suicide of Eden Knight"), died by [suicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide "Suicide") after being [forced to detransition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detransition#Forced_detransition "Detransition") by her family in Saudi Arabia.[[74]](#cite_note-75)[[75]](#cite_note-76)

### Intersex rights

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Intersex rights")]

There are no [bodily protections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodily_integrity "Bodily integrity") for intersex individuals in Saudi Arabia. Many intersex infants born with ambiguous genitalia suffer from [infanticide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infanticide "Infanticide"). The killing of intersex infants is primarily motivated by fears of the social [shame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shame "Shame") of having an intersex child.[[76]](#cite_note-77)[[77]](#cite_note-78)[[78]](#cite_note-79) [Intersex genital surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersex_genital_surgery "Intersex genital surgery") on newborns for cosmetic purposes is fully legal and encouraged.[[79]](#cite_note-80)

## Living conditions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Living conditions")]

### Cultural norms

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Cultural norms")]

Unmarried women and families are generally kept separate from single men as much as possible, and dating is generally seen as being [taboo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taboo "Taboo") and immoral. Opposite sex couples may be harassed if they demonstrate affection in public; however it is not uncommon to see [heterosexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterosexual "Heterosexual") men seemingly expressing affection toward each other in public (e.g., kissing on the cheeks or holding hands.) The practice of men holding hands or kissing on the cheeks in public, is a social custom in parts of the Middle East and Asia; it is a symbol of friendship and not homosexuality.[[80]](#cite_note-81) Bars and nightclubs are illegal. While the CPVPV views combating homosexuality as one of its major objectives, the targets of its interventions against improper socialising are more likely to be the mixed-sex, than the single-sex gathering.[[25]](#cite_note-2010_sg-26)

### Discrimination and harassment

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Discrimination and harassment")]

Saudi Arabia has laws against discrimination on the basis of gender[[81]](#cite_note-82) but not [sexual orientation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_orientation "Sexual orientation"). Harassment or violence against LGBTQ people is not addressed in any bias-motivated or [hate crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate_crime "Hate crime") law. Advocacy for LGBTQ rights is illegal within the kingdom. The required exit and entry visa paperwork does not ask people about their sexual orientation, as it does their [nationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationality "Nationality"), [sex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_sex "Biological sex"), religion and [marital status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marital_status "Marital status"). In 2011, [Mirel Radoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirel_Radoi "Mirel Radoi"), a Romanian football player who plays for the Saudi Alhilal Club, was fined 20,000 Saudi Riyals and suspended for two matches after calling a Saudi Arabian football player, [Hussein Abdul Ghani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussein_Abdul_Ghani "Hussein Abdul Ghani"), who plays for Nasr Club, gay. The public comment, intended as an insult, was highly controversial and generated quite a bit of coverage in the Saudi press, including the refusal of Hussein Abdul Ghani to shake hands with Mirel Radoi after a later game.[[82]](#cite_note-83)

The climate of discrimination and fear among the LGBTQ community in Saudi Arabia means that only Saudis who have sought asylum abroad, such as [Abdulrahman Alkhiary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdulrahman_Alkhiary "Abdulrahman Alkhiary") (also known as Wajeeh Lion), are able to publicly identify as gay. Alkhairy states that he is the first openly gay Saudi man.[[83]](#cite_note-84)

### Education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Education")]

Public education in Saudi Arabia is required to teach basic Islamic values based on the interpretation of the Quran, which includes a strong condemnation of homosexuality. In addition, Islam condemns cross-dressing. The [Ministry of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Education_(Saudi_Arabia) "Ministry of Education (Saudi Arabia)") approved textbooks that reflect the country's Islamic and cultural view against homosexual acts by stating that "homosexuality is one of the most disgusting sins and greatest crimes", and that the proper punishment for the intentional act of homosexual intercourse in public is capital punishment.[[84]](#cite_note-85) However, in 2020 the Ministry of Education was found to have removed the condemnation of homosexuality as something punishable by death from textbooks.[[85]](#cite_note-86)

In 2012, the Saudi government asked the CPVPV to assist in the expulsion of students who were judged, by their mannerisms and taste in fashion, to be gay or lesbian.[[86]](#cite_note-HuffPost_2012-87)

Private schools exist in Saudi Arabia, mainly to serve the needs of expatriates with children, and they are generally allowed more discretion in setting up their own school curriculum and policies. Unless a majority of the expatriate families are Muslim, the private school is likely to only teach the basic beliefs of Islam, through lessons about the culture, language and history of Saudi Arabia. Textbook content or policies regarding homosexuality or cross-dressing tends to be influenced by the prevailing attitudes of the expatriates and their country of origin.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

### Clubs and associations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Clubs and associations")]

Appearing to support or endorse homosexuality or LGBTQ rights can result in prosecution.[[55]](#cite_note-hrw.org-56) This applies to individuals as well as clubs or associations operating the kingdom.

In MDLBeast Soundstorm, an annual multi-day music festival in Riyadh, observers have reported that it included the public display of LGBTQI+ culture.[[87]](#cite_note-88)[[88]](#cite_note-89)

The clandestine Green Party of Saudi Arabia, formed in 2001, expressed support for LGBTQ rights as part of its larger human rights platform. It is unclear if the party still exists, as reports are that its members were subjected to a government crackdown. [*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] A Facebook group for the party seems to still exist, as of 2024.

## HIV/AIDS

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: HIV/AIDS")]

Officially, [men who have sex with men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men_who_have_sex_with_men "Men who have sex with men") account for a low number of [HIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV "HIV") cases in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and little in the way of preventative educational materials exist for [men who have sex with men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men_who_have_sex_with_men "Men who have sex with men"), although a 2024 report from the Saudi AIDS National Program does make some mention of [men who have sex with men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men_who_have_sex_with_men "Men who have sex with men").[[89]](#cite_note-90)

Legally, Saudi citizens who are living with HIV/AIDS are classified as being disabled and thus are entitled to free medical care, which may include access [PrEP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-exposure_prophylaxis_for_HIV_prevention "Pre-exposure prophylaxis for HIV prevention"), protection of their privacy (as to how they became infected), housing, and employment.

The government has produced or allowed [NGOs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NGOs "NGOs") to produce, educational material on how the disease has spread since the 1980s. Abdullah al-Hokail, a Saudi doctor who specializes in the pandemic, has been allowed to air public service announcements on television about the disease and how it is spread.[[90]](#cite_note-arabnews2006-91) Yet, ignorance, fear and prejudice are often directed at people living with the disease. While the government has designated several hospitals to treat those people infected with AIDS or HIV, other hospitals often refuse to care for such people or fail to treat them in a compassionate and humane manner.[[91]](#cite_note-92) Hospitals and schools are often reluctant to distribute government information about the disease because of strong taboos and the stigma attached to how the virus can be spread.[[92]](#cite_note-93) For example, [condoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condom "Condom") are legal, but until recently, they were rarely available anywhere other than certain hospitals or medical supply stores.

### 1990s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 1990s")]

In the late 1990s, the Saudi government began to step up a public education campaign about AIDS-HIV slowly. It started to recognize [World AIDS Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_AIDS_Day "World AIDS Day"), and the Arabic and English daily newspapers were permitted to run articles and opinions expressing the need for more education about the disease and more compassion for those infected.

### 2003

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: 2003")]

In 2003, the government announced that it knew of 6,787 cases, and in 2004 the official number rose to 7,808. The government statistics claim that most of the registered cases are foreign males who contracted the disease through "forbidden" sexual relations.[[93]](#cite_note-94)

### 2006

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: 2006")]

In June 2006, the Ministry of Health publicly admitted that more than 10,000 Saudi citizens were either infected with HIV or had AIDS.[[94]](#cite_note-nytimes2006-95) In December 2006, the *[Arab News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_News "Arab News")* ran an editorial that called for greater public awareness of how the virus is spread and more compassion for those people infected.[[95]](#cite_note-96) In the same year, a Saudi citizen named Rami al-Harithi revealed that he had become infected with HIV while having surgery and has become an official proponent of education and showing compassion to those people infected.[[94]](#cite_note-nytimes2006-95) Saudi Princess Alia bint Abdullah has been involved in the Saudi AIDS Society, which was permitted in December 2006 to hold a public charity art auction followed by a discussion on how the disease was impacting the kingdom; the event included participation by two Saudis living with HIV. It was organized with the help of the director-general of the AIDS Program at the Saudi Ministry of Health, Dr. Sana Filimban.[[96]](#cite_note-97)

### 2007

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: 2007")]

In January 2007, a Saudi economics professor at [King Abdul Aziz University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_University "King Abdulaziz University") was permitted to conduct of survey of a handful of Saudi University students on their level of education about the pandemic.[[97]](#cite_note-98) While much of the work on AIDS-HIV education has been supported by members of the Saudi royal family or medical doctors, there is an attempt to gain permission to create some independent AIDS societies, one of which is called Al-Husna Society, that would work on helping people infected with the disease find employment, education families and work to fight the prejudice that faces people infected.[[98]](#cite_note-99) In 2007, a government-funded[[99]](#cite_note-USStateD_2002licence-100) organization, the [National Society for Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Society_for_Human_Rights "National Society for Human Rights"), published a document suggesting ways to improve the treatment of people living with the disease. The proposed *"Bill of Rights"* document was criticized by [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch") for allegedly undermining human rights and global efforts to fight the pandemic.[[100]](#cite_note-101)

### 2011

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: 2011")]

According to a Gulf Cooperation Council report on HIV/AIDS, "Stigma and discrimination towards people living with HIV, weak surveillance system, travel restrictions and mandatory HIV testing along with gender inequalities were identified as critical issues that are hindering an effective AIDS response in the region."[[101]](#cite_note-102)

### Foreigners and HIV/AIDS

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=LGBTQ_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Foreigners and HIV/AIDS")]

Foreigners who are applying for a work visa are required to demonstrate that they are not infected with the virus before they can enter the country, and are required to get a test upon arrival at a government accredited lab. To be issued their first work permit, they are also required to perform the test again before the renewal of a residency or work permit. Any foreigner that is discovered to be infected will be deported to the country of origin as soon as they are deemed fit to travel.[[102]](#cite_note-103)

args.summary:
This Wikipedia article covers the legal and social status of LGBTQ people in Saudi Arabia. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is illegal and punishable by death. The legal system is based on Wahhabist Sharia law, with no codified criminal code. Penalties can include capital punishment, indeterminate prison sentences, flogging, fines, and deportation for foreigners. There are no legal protections against discrimination, no recognition of same-sex relationships, and no legal gender identity recognition.

Key points include:
- The Quranic story of Prophet Lut and teachings of Muhammad inform the legal treatment of same-sex activity and gender non-conformity.
- Saudi Arabia has no criminal code; judges apply personal interpretation of Sharia (ijtihad).
- In 1928, the Saudi judicial board advised that liwat (sodomy) should be punished like fornication—death by stoning for muhsan (married/adulters), and 100 lashes plus one year banishment for unmarried free men.
- In May 2023, the Saudi Tourism Authority stated LGBTQ visitors are welcome, though homosexuality remains illegal.
- The 2034 FIFA World Cup hosting decision drew strong criticism from LGBTQ communities.
- The Committee for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice (CPVPV) has powers to arrest for homosexuality and cross-dressing.
- In 2022, rainbow-colored items were seized in Riyadh stores to curb "promotion of homosexuality."
- Over 2,000 sex reassignment surgeries have been performed, but the Ministry of Health does not permit sex change operations.
- Transgender individuals are not allowed to make the Hajj pilgrimage.
- In March 2023, Saudi transgender woman Eden Knight died by suicide after being forced to detransition by her family.
- Intersex infants face infanticide and non-consensual genital surgeries.
- Public education teaches that homosexuality is a "disgusting sin" punishable by death, though in 2020 this specific death penalty language was removed from textbooks.
- HIV/AIDS education exists but is limited by stigma; foreigners with HIV are deported.
