**Melting Away** ([Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language"): נמס בגשם, *Names Ba-Geshem*) is a 2012 Israeli drama film written by Billy Ben-Moshe and directed by Doron Eran, starring [Hen Yanni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hen_Yanni "Hen Yanni") in the lead role. This is the first Israeli feature film deals with parents coping with their [transgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender "Transgender") child. [[1]](#cite_note-1)

## Production

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Melting_Away&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Production")]

The idea for the movie was conceived after the [2009 Tel Aviv gay centre shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Tel_Aviv_gay_centre_shooting "2009 Tel Aviv gay centre shooting"). Doron Eran and Billy Ben-Moshe watched TV and heard that parents refused to visit their injured kids at the hospital because they were afraid that their friends and relatives would know that their son is [homosexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexual "Homosexual") or their daughter is [lesbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesbian "Lesbian"). The director Doron Eran made [auditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audition "Audition") for 120 actors until he found Hen Yanni, the actress he chooses for the lead role.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

## Plot

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Melting_Away&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Plot")]

Shlomo Shapira discovers one day that his teenage son Asaf likes to [wear women's clothes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-dressing "Cross-dressing"). With the silent consent of his wife Galia, he decides to teach his son a lesson. On a rainy night Asaf returns to his parents' home after a party but they refuse to open the door, even though he cries. Shlomo tell Galia that after Asaf discovers the hard world outside he will come back home and will forget all of this nonsense, but he was wrong. Four years later, Shlomo is dying from cancer and Galia turns to Eytan, a [private investigator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_investigator "Private investigator") to find her son and tell him about his father. Eytan finds Asaf in a Tel-Aviv gay night club. It turns out that Asaf [transitioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitioning_(transgender) "Transitioning (transgender)") and has become a beautiful singer named Anna. On the next day a woman named Anna came to the hospital where Shlomo is hospitalized, saying she is a private nurse sent from the [insurance company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurance_company "Insurance company"). Anna visits her father day after day and they gradually get to know each other. She succeeds in conquering Shlomo's heart with her charming personality. At the same time, Galia visits her daughter Anna a few times and gradually accepts her.

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Melting_Away&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Prizes")]

* Special award for breakthrough performance to [Hen Yanni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hen_Yanni "Hen Yanni") for her role in "Melting Away"- Tel Aviv International LGBT Film Festival

* Audience Award for Best Narrative Feature at the ImageOut: Rochester LGBT Film and Video Festival, October 2012

* Festival Award at the Au fil(m) du temps- IMAJ Israeli Film Festival, Belgium 2011 [[3]](#cite_note-3)
* Hen Yanni was nominated to [Ophir Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ophir_Award "Ophir Award") for best actress [[4]](#cite_note-4)

args.key_excerpts: This is the first Israeli feature film deals with parents coping with their transgender child., The idea for the movie was conceived after the 2009 Tel Aviv gay centre shooting., Special award for breakthrough performance to Hen Yanni for her role in 'Melting Away'- Tel Aviv International LGBT Film Festival, Hen Yanni was nominated to Ophir Award for best actress
args.summary:
**Melting Away** (Hebrew: נמס בגשם, *Names Ba-Geshem*) is a 2012 Israeli drama film directed by Doron Eran and written by Billy Ben-Moshe, starring Hen Yanni in the lead role. It is the first Israeli feature film to deal with parents coping with their transgender child.

**Production:** The idea was conceived after the 2009 Tel Aviv gay centre shooting, when the filmmakers saw parents refusing to visit their injured children at the hospital due to fear of others learning their child was LGBTQ+. The director auditioned 120 actors before casting Hen Yanni.

**Plot:** Shlomo Shapira discovers his teenage son Asaf likes to wear women's clothing. With his wife Galia's silent consent, he refuses to let Asaf into the house on a rainy night, hoping the lesson will force him to change. Four years later, Shlomo is dying from cancer. Galia hires a private investigator who finds Asaf, who has transitioned and become a female singer named Anna. Anna visits her father in the hospital disguised as a private nurse, slowly winning his heart, while Galia also gradually accepts her daughter.

**Cast:** Hen Yanni plays Asaf Shapira / Anna; Ami Weinberg plays Shlomo; Limor Goldstein plays Galia; supporting cast includes Oded Leopold, Eyal Rozales, Yonatan Barak, Shay Kadimi, Hannan Suissa, Shosha Goren, and Arnon Zadok.

**Prizes:**
- Special award for breakthrough performance to Hen Yanni – Tel Aviv International LGBT Film Festival
- Audience Award at Boston Jewish Film Festival (2012)
- Audience Award for Best Narrative Feature at ImageOut: Rochester LGBT Film and Video Festival (2012)
- Audience Award at Shalom Europa IFF, France (2012)
- Festival Award at Au fil(m) du temps- IMAJ Israeli Film Festival, Belgium (2011)
- Hen Yanni was nominated for the Ophir Award for Best Actress

**Details:** 86 minutes, Hebrew language, released January 12, 2012.

# Israeli film embraces transgender teen, stunned parents

![Image 4](https://jweekly.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/12/fox-michael.jpg)by[Michael Fox](https://jweekly.com/author/michael-fox/)June 21, 2013 December 29, 2016

Doron Eran’s empathetic and touching drama “Melting Away” may be the first Israeli feature film about parents coming to terms with a transgendered child. It begins with a poignant confession.

“No one tells you what it means to be a good mother — if it’s being the mother my son wants me to be, or the mother I think he needs,” a 40-something woman sadly confides to us, before we realize that she is speaking to, of all people, a private detective.

Between their conversation and a succinct, effective flashback, we learn that Galya and her self-made, my-way-or-the-highway husband, Shlomo, locked their teenage son Assaf out of the house four years ago when they discovered his stash of women’s clothing.

![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.jweekly.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/5_artpic-150x150.jpg?w=150&crop=0%2C0px%2C100%2C150px&ssl=1)

Hen Yanni in “Melting Away”

They expected he would return in a few days, start seeing a therapist, and his gender issues would disappear. In fact, Assaf disappeared without a word.

Now Shlomo’s been diagnosed with terminal cancer and Galya wants the private eye to find Assaf. That mission is accomplished with ease, but with a twist: Assaf is now Anna, and her night job is singing in a drag club.

Once upon a time in movies, this would have comprised the climax. The film would have been about an outsider making his/her own way, and finding the new identity to be a mixed but positive blessing. Somewhat surprisingly, Anna’s secret is revealed to the audience — though not to Galya, thanks to the private eye’s tactfulness and his compliance with Anna’s wishes — in the first 15 minutes, setting the stage for a less sensationalistic story of gradual rapprochement between child and parents.

Call it the new normal.

“Melting Away,” which played this year’s East Bay International Jewish Film Festival and others across the U.S. and internationally, has its San Francisco premiere Sunday, June 23 at the Roxie, as part of Frameline37, the San Francisco International Lesbian Gay Bisexual Transgender Film Festival.

The filmmaker and his partner and screenwriter, Billy Ben-Moshe, reportedly were inspired by the aftermath of the 2009 shooting attack at the Israel Gay Youth Organization in Tel Aviv that left two dead. Some parents, presumably shocked to learn that their children weren’t straight, declined to visit them in the hospital.

As part of its contribution toward tolerance and acceptance, “Melting Away” has no interest in providing a forum for hate speech. When Anna’s family discovers the truth, they are understandably stunned but don’t spew homophobic insults.

The 2011 film operates from the perspective that it’s not Anna’s problem that Galya and Shlomo need to adjust to having a daughter in lieu of a son. It’s their issue, and they have to work through it themselves.

There are moments where “Melting Away” feels like a TV movie, thanks to a limp score and a couple of weak fades to black. Likewise, the film’s emphasis on the positive, although a welcome change of pace from the bitterness and bile that’s often deemed necessary in a story like this, robs it of a degree of narrative tension and slam-bang ending.

That said, “Melting Away” is a satisfying, uplifting movie that succeeds on the basis of consistently solid acting that builds and honors our emotional investment in the characters’ destinies.

Hen Yanni conveys Anna’s toughness and sensitivity with-out evoking stereotypes, al-though we’re puzzled why she’s so quick to forgive her father. Limor Goldstein infuses the dying Shlomo with gravitas, vulnerability and love.

The title refers to a song Anna performs near the end of the film, but also alludes to the difficult and often painful process of dissolving the prejudices, expectations and resentments that stand between parents and children.

Frameline37, which runs through June 30, also presents Michael Mayer’s Israeli-Palestinian love story, “Out in the Dark,” at 9:30 p.m. June 28 at the Castro.

Local Jewish filmmakers Rob Epstein and Jeffrey Friedman’s documentary featurette, “The Battle of amfAR,” which screens at 4:30 p.m. Wednesday, June 26 at the Castro, traces the efforts of Elizabeth Taylor and Dr. Mathilde Krim, a scientist and Jew by choice, to halt AIDS.

**“Melting Away”** screens at 7 p.m. June 23 at the Roxie Theater, 3117 16th St., S.F. In Hebrew with English subtitles. (Not rated, 86 minutes) www.frameline.org

args.key_excerpts: "No one tells you what it means to be a good mother — if it's being the mother my son wants me to be, or the mother I think he needs," a 40-something woman sadly confides to us, before we realize that she is speaking to, of all people, a private detective., "Melting Away" is a satisfying, uplifting movie that succeeds on the basis of consistently solid acting that builds and honors our emotional investment in the characters' destinies., The title refers to a song Anna performs near the end of the film, but also alludes to the difficult and often painful process of dissolving the prejudices, expectations and resentments that stand between parents and children., The filmmaker and his partner and screenwriter, Billy Ben-Moshe, reportedly were inspired by the aftermath of the 2009 shooting attack at the Israel Gay Youth Organization in Tel Aviv that left two dead.
args.summary: This is a film review article from J. The Jewish News of Northern California, published June 21, 2013, by Michael Fox. The article reviews the Israeli feature film "Melting Away" (2011) by director Doron Eran, described as the first Israeli feature film about parents coming to terms with a transgender child. The film follows Galya and Shlomo, who locked their teenage son Assaf out of the house four years ago after discovering his women's clothing. When Shlomo is diagnosed with terminal cancer, Galya hires a private detective to find Assaf, who now lives as Anna, a woman who sings at a drag club. The film focuses on the gradual rapprochement between parents and child, emphasizing that the parents' adjustment is their own issue to work through. The filmmaker and screenwriter Billy Ben-Moshe were reportedly inspired by the aftermath of the 2009 shooting attack at the Israel Gay Youth Organization in Tel Aviv. The review notes the film features solid acting from Hen Yanni (Anna) and Limor Goldstein (Shlomo), and the title refers to the process of dissolving prejudices and resentments between parents and children. The film had its San Francisco premiere on June 23, 2013 at the Roxie Theater as part of Frameline37, the San Francisco International LGBTQ Film Festival. The article also mentions other related films screening at the festival, including "Out in the Dark" and the documentary featurette "The Battle of amfAR" by local Jewish filmmakers Rob Epstein and Jeffrey Friedman.

# Warming up to Melting Away: Israeli Film Festival to screen LGBT title

![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/b3f2962bc333a715fca01ddc8e1a2e936e9b24470c4089b2bf01340f012403dc?s=96&d=https%3A%2F%2Fi0.wp.com%2Fepgn.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2020%2F03%2FPGNfavicon.png%3Fresize%3D150%252C150%26ssl%3D1&r=g)by [Larry Nichols](https://epgn.com/author/larry/)

### Share this:

* [Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook](https://epgn.com/2012/03/29/18042961-warming-up-to-melting-away-israeli-film-festival-to-screen-lgbt-title/?share=facebook&nb=1)
* [Share on X (Opens in new window) X](https://epgn.com/2012/03/29/18042961-warming-up-to-melting-away-israeli-film-festival-to-screen-lgbt-title/?share=x&nb=1)

![](https://i0.wp.com/epgn.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/03/18034365.jpg?fit=399%2C266&ssl=1) 

The 16th annual Israeli Film Festival is hosting a screening of the first feature film in Israeli cinema dealing with the subject of parents with a gender-questioning child.

“Melting Away” follows the story of a teenager who is kicked out of his family’s house because his homophobic father is in shock when he discovers his son’s cross-dressing and gender-questioning. Years later, the mother hires a private investigator to find her son and tell him his father is dying of cancer and that she would like to reconnect.

But the former son — now living as a woman (played by Chen Yani) and performing at a gay cabaret — is unwilling to even speak to her parents, holding a deep resentment toward them for throwing her out when she was a teenage boy. However, curiosity gets the better of her and she decides to dress up as a nurse and visit her father daily.

Israeli director and producer Doron Eran said that while he has been trying to get this script made into a film for a long time, it took a real-life tragedy to inspire him to finally get the story onto the screen.

“My wife wrote the script about four years ago and we planned to shoot it in Toronto,” he said. “It’s inspired by a true story of a family that I knew in my neighborhood about 17 years ago. I went to Toronto and I tried to create the production there and the economic downturn destroyed the company in Toronto, so I came back to Israel. I put the script aside and I carried on in other projects. In 2009, a guy came into a workshop of young gays and lesbians [in Tel Aviv] and he shot them. He killed two of them and 15 of them were wounded. It was all over Israeli TV and we sat at home, me and my wife, watching it. It was on all three channels and the country was in shock.

But after that the channels went to the hospital and around one in the morning the guy in the television set said that some of the parents don’t want to come and visit their children because they don’t want their neighbors to see on the TV that their kids are homosexuals and lesbians. That was the idea and motivation behind picking up this script again.”

Eran said that while he believes the attack was an anomaly in Tel Aviv, which is Israel’s most liberal city, further research found that antigay sentiment outside the city are far more common.

“Even though my motivation was because of this crazy guy who shot these kids, we believed there was no problem with the leaders in Israel. On television, we have ‘Israeli Idol’ and one of the jurors there, she’s transgender. Everybody told me that there is no problem in Israel because every kid in Israel sees her in prime time. But slowly, when I came and did the research, I found that outside of Tel Aviv, it’s so totally different. Just like New York in America is quite different from the South in the United States. Slowly I found very sad stories. One of the saddest stories I found through my research was in the north of Israel. The youngest kid in the family, the father found out that he liked women’s clothes so he tied him to the bed and, for three months, he gave him shots of hormones to make him a man. I thought it was one of the most horrible stories I’ve heard in my life.”

Eran added that in those areas, the film often struggles to impart its message even to those willing to understand it.

“People ask me if the people in Israel are ready for this kind of movie. And I said yes, of course,” Eran said. “I don’t see any problem. But even now, when I distributed the film in Israel, in Tel Aviv everybody came to see the film. But when I screened it in the north and south of Israel, very few people came. It was hard for them to get this story. Even at the premiere, when the television came and interviewed the audience, people said, ‘It’s a very good movie. We love the movie. We believed it happened. But until it comes to our family, to our house … ’ So in the center of Israel, I don’t see any problem with these kinds of stories but outside of Tel Aviv, I believe people still don’t get this and they don’t want to understand this.”

But Eran said he wasn’t frustrated by the lack of empathy some audiences had after viewing the film.

“It is because of that I made this movie,” he said. “I have three children and I think that a parent, when you decide to make a kid, you must understand that you must love them with no conditions. That is what the film is about. If one parent would see this movie and they had a problem like that in their home and if this movie changed their way of thinking, I did it. I believe movies can change ways of thinking and I hope I did it here.

“Two days ago, I got a call from a guy late at night and he said, ‘I saw your film with my mother and we cried through the screening. We stayed for about 20 minutes after everyone left the theater. And I wanted to tell you thanks very much for giving me this gift of this movie.’ And I said, ‘Thank God you called me because a filmmaker needs that sometimes.’”

Besides earning praise from individual viewers, “Melting Away” has been screened at and won acclaim from film festivals all over Europe and North America, including the Tel Aviv International LGBT Film Festival. Eran, who has participated in Q&A sessions for the film, said he is often asked why a straight director and screenwriter would write and champion a film about LGBT subject matter.

“People ask me why I made this film because it’s not my world,” Eran said. “I said that I made this movie for parents. I knew this family 17 years ago. It is a very good story because it’s a very dramatic situation. I made this film for parents, not especially for kids and gays and lesbians. North of Tel Aviv, if two guys are walking holding hands, in about half an hour someone will hit them. There are not one or two days that pass without something like that happening. So it’s a very good idea to make a film on this kind of subject, because I believe that this film can change people’s ways of thinking. And if we can save some kids that cannot get the support from their parents, we made it.

One of the questions in the movie I wanted fathers to ask themselves is, when his own boy decides to change his [gender] and be a woman, what does it mean about him and what he thinks about himself and his sexuality? Sometimes we want to control a kid’s life so much and so hard that we forget that when we make a child and we give them life, it’s his life. It’s not our life. So we have to respect that.” n

The 16th annual Israeli Film Festival runs through April 1. “Melting Away” is screened 8:45 p.m. March 31 at Mitchell Auditorium, 3128 Market St., followed by a reception with a guest appearance by lead actor Chen Yani. args.summary:
This is a detailed analysis video from the YouTube channel "POSITIF" (پوزیتیف) about the 1997 Iranian film "Adam Barfi" (آدم برفی / Snowman), directed by Davoud Mirbagheri. The film is one of the most controversial in Iranian cinema history due to its plot involving cross-dressing by star actor Akbar Abdi.

**Key Historical Context:**
- The film was made in 1994 (1373) by Davoud Mirbagheri, with the same cast as his TV series "Imam Ali." Produced by the Howzeh Honari (Art Bureau), it was banned for 3 years.
- A harsh article in Kayhan newspaper by editor Mehdi Nassiri targeted the film for Akbar Abdi's cross-dressing. The film was banned by Ezzatollah Zarqami just before the Fajr Film Festival.
- Mohammad Ali Zaman (director of the Howzeh Honari) lobbied for the film's release, eventually getting it shown to President Hashemi Rafsanjani and Ayatollah Khamenei, who deemed it unproblematic.
- Released in 1997 (1376), it became the year's highest-grossing film, but faced violent attacks from Ansar-e Hezbollah groups (led by Masoud Dehnamaaki and Allah Karam) who physically assaulted cinemas and audiences, including a pregnant woman who suffered a miscarriage.
- The film ran in rotation for 2 years until 1999.

**Plot Summary:**
The story follows Abbas (played by Akbar Abdi), an Iranian man desperately trying to get a visa to the United States. Stranded in Turkey, he meets Iranian acquaintances who suggest his only way to America is to become a woman and marry an American. Abbas transforms into "Dorna" (a female character).

**Analysis Framework:**
The video analyzes the film through multiple lenses:
1. **Sheikh San'an allegory** – The classical Persian story from Attar's Mantiq al-Tayr about a pious sheikh who falls in love with a Christian girl, mirroring Abbas's journey and the fear of Western cultural influence.
2. **Judith Butler's gender theory** – The film is examined through Butler's concept of gender performativity (that gender is a social role performed daily), and the idea of "hacking" gender through signs and repetition.
3. **Ta'ziyeh (Shabih-khani) tradition** – The Iranian passion play tradition where men play women's roles, maintaining a clear distance between performer and role (as opposed to Western mimesis/realistic imitation).
4. **Film Farsi (pre-revolutionary Iranian cinema)** – The film's nostalgic references to the "tipe" (stock characters) of pre-revolution Iranian cinema, particularly through the characters played by Parviz Parastui and Dariush Arjmand.

**Theoretical Conclusions:**
- The film creates a "border zone" identity (liminal space) across three axes: Iran→America (migration), male→female (gender), and old→new Iranian cinema (temporal).
- Turkey serves as the "purgatory" point where all three axes converge.
- The ending requires Dorna (the female persona) to die so Abbas can return to Iran, suggesting that in-between states cannot survive in the film's ultimately binary worldview.
- The film paradoxically operates within Iran's propagandistic framework (the "cultural invasion" discourse) while simultaneously exposing the instability of the very concepts it seeks to defend.

The video was recorded in Mordad 1405 (July-August 2026) and is presented by armia Heydari and Javad Ebrahimi Nejad.

## Abstract

This article traces the historical becoming of the contemporary supersaturation of images of queer and transgendered Iran through the narrative and tropic devices introduced by filmmakers in the past twenty years. I argue that the censorship code enforced by the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance is partly responsible for the formation of what has come to be a ubiquitous figure in the New Iranian cinema: the “cross-dressing” or “passing” figure. By performing close readings of Baran and Dokhtaraneh Khorshid—two films that are exemplary of a subgenre organized around the “cross-dressing” or “passing” figure—I identify a “transgender move”: a temporary space of political and agential potential that many spectators—both domestic and diasporic—seek in the post 1990s New Iranian cinema.

# Art And Culture

One of the most important contributions of studying abroad to students is that it provides opportunities to open the door to a new world in the field of art and culture.

Türkiye Scholarships offers many cultural and artistic opportunities for international students to increase their cultural knowledge and gain an artistic perspective. As Türkiye Scholarships, we care about our students discovering the deep-rooted heritage that Türkiye offers in all areas of culture and art, from literature to history, painting to theater, music to cinema. Here are some of the cultural and art activities that you can participate in in Türkiye…

[![Türkiye Scholarships](https://tbbsweb.azureedge.net/tbbsweb/Page/Discover/ArtAndCulture/1sinema.jpg)](#Cinema)

[### Cinema](#Cinema)

# Cinema

The first public cinema in Türkiye opened in 1910. Since then, cinema has become one of the most popular branches of art in Türkiye. Turkish cinema attracts international attention with its many world-famous directors and award-winning films.

  

Many film festivals are held all over Türkiye every year at various times. Antalya Golden Orange Film Festival, İstanbul Film Festival, Adana Golden Boll Film Festival, Ankara Film Festival, Bosphorus Film Festival, Mobile Film Festival and Malatya International Film Festival are among the most well-known. Films are screened in their original language and often have both Turkish and English subtitles.

![Türkiye Scholarships](https://tbbsweb.azureedge.net/tbbsweb/Page/Discover/ArtAndCulture/sinema_1192797694.jpg)

Türkiye offers cinema entertainment in all its cities with a total of 2,698 movie theaters. While some cinemas are independently located in city centres, the majority are insive large shopping malls. Movie theatres screening alternative films to boxoffice fillms also attract great attention.

Don't forget to take advantage of the student discount when buying your movie ticket.

# Theatre

Theaters in Türkiye can be divided into three as state theatres, municipal theaters and private theatres. You can enjoy the works of both Turkish and international playwrites, while the language of the plays is generally Turkish. Unlike the cinema, it is helpful to plan ahead as theater tickets sell out rapidly.

  

You can buy tickets to the plays in your city and follow the tours and festivals organized on the General Directorate of State Theaters [website](http://www.devtiyatro.gov.tr/). Don't forget to take advantage of the student discount when buying your theatre ticket..

![Türkiye Scholarships](https://tbbsweb.azureedge.net/tbbsweb/Page/Discover/ArtAndCulture/tiyatro_1081029959.jpg)

If you wish to participate rather than just be a spectator, you can join drama courses organized either privately or by municipalities, or join your university’s theatre club.

# Music

Turkish music has a very wide repertoire, which is enriched by the fusion of Western music and Middle Eastern melodies. From pop music to classical Turkish music, from Turkish folk music to hip-hop, a varied musical experience awaits you in Türkiye. If you enjoy music, then you will be pleased to know that music festivals are widespread in Türkiye. You will also find many venues where you can attend concerts of local bands in your city or artists popular throughout Türkiye.

  
 ![Türkiye Scholarships](https://tbbsweb.azureedge.net/tbbsweb/Page/Discover/ArtAndCulture/muzik.png)

The main music festivals you should follow:

İstanbul Music Festival, International Ankara Music Festival, İzmir European Jazz Festival, International Mersin Music Festival, International Gümüşlük Music Festival, Aspendos International Opera and Ballet Festival

# Sports

he most popular sports in Türkiye are football, basketball and volleyball. National league matches are very popular.

  
 ![Türkiye Scholarships](https://tbbsweb.azureedge.net/tbbsweb/Page/Discover/ArtAndCulture/spor.jpg)

If you are not only a spectator but also an athlete, you can take advantage of the sports facilities at your campus and join school teams

If you are interested in traditional Turkish sports, you can take courses in areas such as archery, oil wrestling and horse riding. In addition, sports enthusiasts who feel up to it can follow sports festivals and competitions that can only be experienced in Türkiye, such as the Intercontinental Swimming Race and the Ethnosport Culture Festival.

# Turkish Handicrafts

Türkiye's artistic wealth has been shaped by a wide geography extending to Anatolia, the Balkans, Central Asia and the Middle East. In this aspect, Türkiye is a unique country where there are numerous alternatives for art lovers.

  
 ![Türkiye Scholarships](https://tbbsweb.azureedge.net/tbbsweb/Page/Discover/ArtAndCulture/el_1143057317.jpg)

. In Türkiye, where both traditional handicrafts and modern art are popular, you can enjoy the arts such as miniature, carpet making, rug making, tile making, ceramic-pottery making, embroidery, needle lace, leather work, copper making and felt making. You can master more common crafts such as calligraphy, marbling and cross-stitch by attending workshops at your university or in your city.

# Gastronomy

When you first come to Türkiye, you may have difficulty getting used to the food. We are sure that in a very short time this rich cuisine will become an indispensable part of your life and will be what you will miss most when you return to your country.

![Türkiye Scholarships](https://tbbsweb.azureedge.net/tbbsweb/Page/Discover/ArtAndCulture/gastronomi1.jpg)

When you first come to Türkiye, you may have difficulty getting used to the food. We are sure that in a very short time this rich cuisine will become an indispensable part of your life and will be what you will miss most when you return to your country.

![Türkiye Scholarships](https://tbbsweb.azureedge.net/tbbsweb/Page/Discover/ArtAndCulture/gastronomi2.jpg)

Turkish cuisine is one of the cuisines with the richest food culture in the world. Every city in Türkiye has its own unique cuisine and a special recipe that it is famous for. In addition to tasting different flavors every period of the year according to the changes of the seasons, don’t forget to try our traditional dishes prepared for special days such as Ramadan.

![Türkiye Scholarships](https://tbbsweb.azureedge.net/tbbsweb/Page/Discover/ArtAndCulture/gastonomi3.jpg)

If you are interested in gastronomy and the culinary arts, you can [click here](https://www.kulturportali.gov.tr/turkiye/genel/neyenir) to learn more about our regional dishes that form the basis of traditional Turkish cuisine, from Eskişehir çiğbörek to Gaziantep baklava, from Oltu Cağ kebab to Kayseri mantı. You can also attend courses to learn how to make your favorite Turkish dishes.

This is a Facebook post from the Close Up Cinematic Initiative (dated February 13, 2026) featuring filmmaker Bircan Birol in their "Filmmaker in Focus" series. Birol was born in Istanbul into a Turkish and Kurdish household, raised by "strong and loud women" in a multicultural 'gecekondu' (squatter) neighborhood, which shaped her filmmaking as a tool for social impact.

Her Close Up project titled "Your Honor" follows Efruz, a trans law student in Turkey who lives under constant threat. The film documents Efruz over the years as her dream of becoming a human rights lawyer is challenged, and the two friends find hope in friendship and resistance. The post includes a link to the full interview and hashtags related to documentary filmmaking and women filmmakers.

# Emirati Filmmaker Pushes Boundaries, Exposes Hidden Lives

The filmmaker behind "Only Men Go to the Grave" unravels a story about a traditional Arab family grappling with issues of sexuality and gender identity.

In this Aug. 18, 2017 photo, Emirati filmmaker Abdulla Al Kaabi speaks to The Associated Press in Dubai after screening his film "Only Men Go To The Grave."Razan Alzayani / AP

[Add NBC News to Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=nbcnews.com)

By Associated Press

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — An Emirati filmmaker is pushing boundaries and bypassing state censors by delicately unraveling a story about a traditional Arab family grappling with issues of same-sex love, gender identity, sectarianism and women's rights.

The movie focuses on a conservative Iraqi family who begin seeing and unearthing one another's secrets after the family matriarch goes blind and dies.

What makes the film "Only Men Go to the Grave" particularly avant-garde is that the LGBTQ characters are not simply supporting characters or portrayed as Westernized or globalized elites, like past characters in other famous Arabic films. Rather, the film's stars are same-sex lovers who are also traditional Arab mothers, wives and caretakers.

The movie, by filmmaker Abdallah Al Kaabi, also reveals its central male character to be struggling with his masculinity and gender. In possibly the movie's boldest scene, the character dresses in full makeup, a wig, jewelry and a dress.

**Related: [9 Must-See LGBTQ Art Shows Around the World](https://www.nbcnews.com/feature/nbc-out/9-must-see-lgbtq-art-shows-fall-n795171)**

Al Kaabi says he believes the film's handling of homosexuality and gender identity helped propel it to the big screen.

"A movie in the end is a story and people don't really have a problem with what you talk about in the story, but they have a problem with how you expose it," he told The Associated Press after a screening of the film. "I think you need to show good taste when you talk about controversial and taboo issues," he said.

The lovers in his film are never shown being physically intimate.

Egyptian cinema — the oldest and most revered film industry in the Arab world — has tackled homosexuality in film since the 1950s, though often portraying it as something that exists among a progressive minority. Gay characters have also been portrayed in some films as psychologically ill or are punished in some way.

Tunisian cinema has also depicted gay characters in movies since the 1970s, while a genre of so-called queer cinema is currently surfacing among Lebanese filmmakers.

Egyptian film critic Joseph Fahim said Al Kaabi's film appears to be the first made by an Arab Gulf filmmaker to tackle the issue of homosexuality in such a candid manner.

"My pastime was to travel and dream through movies so I was watching a lot of Hollywood movies, Egyptian movies and Bollywood movies," he said.

Across the Gulf, there are varying degrees of censorship and support for independent filmmakers like Al Kaabi.

Despite there being no theaters in Saudi Arabia, a handful of films have been shot there in recent years. In Kuwait, which once held the mantle for Gulf theatrical productions, censors pulled Disney's new "Beauty and the Beast" from theaters this year after the public's reaction to what Disney called its first "gay moment" for a character.

Last year, the UAE approved a law that would allow gender reassignment surgery for those who psychologically identify as the opposite sex.

The scene of the male character dressed in women's clothing, shocking for its raw and rare portrayal of a person struggling with gender identity, left one young Emirati college student perplexed.

"There are things I really didn't understand in the movie, like the man. Why was he wearing these kinds of clothes like woman clothes?," Mahra Al-Nuaimi said after watching the movie.

Her cousin, Moza Al-Hamrani, appeared less confused by the filmmaker's motives. As a student of film, she said she hoped to one day have the chance to produce similarly groundbreaking work.

"The issues to do with gender identity and sexuality — I thought like 'Whoa, did he really do that?'" But I was also proud that someone finally spoke out about it, because these issues exist but everybody turns a blind eye," she said.

# ‘West Side Story’ Banned in Saudi Arabia, Other Gulf Nations

Just a month after 'Eternals' suffered the same fate, Steven Spielberg's musical adaptation has fallen foul of regional censors, this time supposedly over the inclusion of a transgender character.

By
[Alex Ritman](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/author/alex-ritman/)

### [Alex Ritman](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/author/alex-ritman/)

U.K. Correspondent

### More Stories by Alex

![Ariana DeBose as Anita in 20th Century Studios’ WEST SIDE STORY.](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/DF-20702_R_CROP-H-2021.jpg?w=1296&h=730&crop=1)

The Sharks and the Jets won’t be facing off in the Gulf.

[Steven Spielberg](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/t/steven-spielberg/)‘s Oscar-hopeful [*[West Side Story](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/t/west-side-story/)*](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-reviews/west-side-story-steven-spielberg-1235056068/) adaptation will not screen in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman or Kuwait, *The Hollywood Reporter* has confirmed.

In Saudi Arabia and Kuwait — considered the strictest in terms of censorship — the film wasn’t granted a release certificate. In the remaining countries, censors requested cuts that Disney refused to make. The film had been due for release on Dec. 9 and was on all major cinema websites.

While the reasoning is unconfirmed, regional sources tell *The Hollywood Reporter* that the decision was due to the character Anybodys, written as transgender in the new adaptation and played by nonbinary actress Iris Menas. With homosexuality officially illegal across the Gulf, films that feature any LGBTQ references or issues often fall foul of the censors.

*West Side Story* follows hot on the heels of Disney’s *Eternals*, [which was yanked from release across](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/eternals-banned-saudi-arabia-qatar-kuwait-1235042241/) the region last month over the inclusion of the MCU’s first gay superhero, Phastos (played by Brian Tyree Henry), in particular a scene in which he shares a kiss with his onscreen husband, Ben (Haaz Sleiman).

Like *West Side Story*, censors made cut requests that Disney refused. The film did eventually land in cinemas in the UAE with Disney having removed all intimate scenes.

args.key_excerpts: In Saudi Arabia and Kuwait — considered the strictest in terms of censorship — the film wasn't granted a release certificate., Regional sources tell The Hollywood Reporter that the decision was due to the character Anybodys, written as transgender in the new adaptation and played by nonbinary actress Iris Menas., West Side Story follows hot on the heels of Disney's Eternals, which was yanked from release across the region last month over the inclusion of the MCU's first gay superhero.
args.summary: Steven Spielberg's 'West Side Story' adaptation has been banned from screening in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman, and Kuwait. In Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, the film was not granted a release certificate. In the other countries, censors requested cuts that Disney refused to make. The film was due for release on December 9. Regional sources indicate the decision was due to the character Anybodys, who is written as transgender in the new adaptation and played by nonbinary actress Iris Menas. Homosexuality is officially illegal across the Gulf, and films with LGBTQ references often face censorship. This follows Disney's 'Eternals,' which was pulled from the region last month over the inclusion of a gay superhero and a same-sex kiss. In that case, the film eventually screened in the UAE with Disney having removed all intimate scenes.

## Abstract

This article traces the diaspora of transgender and gender-nonconforming Palestinians in two documentary films made twenty years apart, Cinema Fouad (dir. Soueid, 1993) and Sultana’s Reign (dir. Moussally, 2023). Using queer/trans and post/decolonial theorists including Judith Butler, Hamid Naficy, and Walter Mignolo, the author takes a historical approach to queer Arab identity, navigating white Western assumptions bred from colonialism. Identifying nuance and authenticity as key to representations of diasporic non-Western queerness, this article engages with issues of language and assimilation and calls for a more expansive definition of queer.

# Masculinities to Trans-femininities: Evidence through the “Girl” Film

## Authors

* Anas Ahmadi   Universitas Negeri Surabaya     [https://orcid.org/0000-0003-2583-2703 (unauthenticated)](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-2583-2703)

## DOI:

 <https://doi.org/10.17583/mcs.11837>

## Keywords:

 Masculinities, transfeminist, film, sex, LGBT

## Abstract

This study aims to explore the life journey of a man who wants to become a transfeminist woman through the perspective of masculinity studies. This study uses a qualitative method. The results of this study are as follows.  First, Lara as a transfeminist made psychological changes by making herself a graceful figure, changing her love desires by loving men, and having aspirations of becoming a ballerina so that she is like a natural woman. Second, Lara as a transfeminist made physical changes to become a normal woman by wearing earrings and women's clothes, cooking, doing feminizing hormone therapy to grow breasts, and planning to do a sex reassignment surgery to have a vagina. Third, from the aspect of attitude, Lara's family that supports Lara's transformation from male to female has become a controversy. However, in society, Lara, who is a transfeminist, is still controversial and not everyone accepts the presence of transfeminism/LGBT. This can be seen in how society bullies and sexually harasses her. In the end, Lara, who was assigned as a male, actually turned into a female.

args.summary: This webpage presents an academic article titled "Masculinities to Trans-femininities: Evidence through the 'Girl' Film" by Anas Ahmadi (Universitas Negeri Surabaya), published in the journal *Masculinities & Social Change*, Vol. 13 No. 1 (February 2024). The study uses qualitative methods to explore the life journey of a man who wants to become a transfeminist woman, analyzed through the lens of masculinity studies, using the film "Girl" (2018, directed by Lukas Dhont) as evidence. Key findings: (1) Psychological changes — Lara (the protagonist) transforms herself into a graceful figure, shifts her love desires toward men, and aspires to become a ballerina to embody a natural woman. (2) Physical changes — Lara wears earrings and women's clothing, cooks, undergoes feminizing hormone therapy to grow breasts, and plans sex reassignment surgery. (3) Social/attitudinal aspects — Lara's supportive family is controversial, and society largely remains unaccepting of transfeminism/LGBT, as shown through bullying and sexual harassment. The article is published under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License, with the author retaining copyright. A comprehensive reference list of approximately 150 sources is provided, covering masculinity studies, transfeminism, film studies, psychology, and LGBT issues.

## Abstract

Cinema provides ‘privileged access’ ([Zubrycki 2011](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b50)) into trans lives, recording and revealing private life experiences and moments that might never be seen, nor heard and after the time had passed, only present in memory and body for the individuals involved. Film, a temporal medium, creates theoretical issues, both in the presentation and representation of the trans body and for audiences in viewing the images. Specific narrative, stylistic and editing techniques including temporal disjunctions, may also give audiences a distorted view of trans bodily narratives that encompass a lifetime. Twenty first century cinema is simultaneously creating and erasing the somatechnical potentialities of trans. This article will explore temporal techniques in relation to recent trans cinema, comparing how three different filmmakers handle trans narratives. Drawing upon recent films including the Trans New Wave ([Ford 2014](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b15), [2016a](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b16), [2016b](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b17)), such as the experimental animated autoethnographic short film _Change Over Time_ (Ewan Duarte, United States, 2013), in tandem with the feature film _52 Tuesdays_ (Sophia Hyde, Australia, 2013), I will analyse the films as texts which show how filmmakers utilise temporality as a narrative and stylistic technique in cinematic trans narratives. These are texts where cinematic technologies converge with trans embodiment in ways that are constitutive of participants and audiences' understanding of trans lives. This analysis will be contrasted with the use of temporal displacement as a cinematic trope of negative affect, disembodiment and societal disjunction in the feature film _Predestination_ (The Spierig Brothers, Australia, 2014), providing a further basis for scholarly critique of cinematic somatechnics in relation to the trans body.

## Introduction

Through cinema, trans filmmakers are engaged in a project which presents a uniquely trans vision of life on screen. To draw from André Bazin: ‘the creation of an ideal world in the likeness of the real, with its own temporal destiny’ ([Bazin 1960](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b7): 6), illustrates the temporality of cinematic experience, including the duration of the film in exhibition and connects audiences in time to narratives, events, places, characters and bodies that exist within and outside the screen. To connect onscreen and spectator bodies, cinema utilises compressions and distortions of time, through screenwriting, editing and visual techniques where long narrative sequences are compressed through flashbacks, reminisces, uses of memory and mnemonics. The duration of character participation in a film may follow characters (in fiction) and interview/participants (in documentaries) over weeks, months and years of life, subsequently compressed into seconds and minutes of screen time. Cinematic temporality extends beyond the human physical life span. The disjunction in time between film production and public exhibition, further disjuncts time, as screening is frequently separated in time by months or years from the date of final post-production to the date a film is released. Through exegesis of cinematic narratives, the temporal compression of story arcs into cinematic time are revealed. Compression of time presents unique temporal issues. This includes the minimisation of life narratives into short temporal stories, where for example, five minutes of documentary time may be utilised to show experiences that required months and years to traverse, or may be the story of an entire life. Such temporal disjunctions between lived experience and cinematic representations may convey a distorted view of trans bodily narratives to audiences.

This article will explore temporal techniques in relation to recent trans cinema, comparing how three different filmmakers handle trans narratives drawing upon recent independent films, including exemplar texts of the Trans New Wave ([Ford 2014](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b15), [2016a](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b16), [2016b](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b17)). The Trans New Wave is a new genre in cinema emerging in the twentyfirst century that utilises ‘autobiographical and biographical materials in the construction of their film stories, as a means of understanding, tracing and constructing identity’ ([Ford 2016b](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b17): 222). These films are initially identified by [Tristan Taormino (2008)](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b48) as emerging from transporn and centralised sexuality in trans experience. Filmmakers identified by Taormino (such as Buck Angel) are part of a New Wave era of trans cinematic production, in which the socio-cultural significance of all aspects of a trans life are represented across styles and forms. Like the American and French new wave films emerging in the middle of the twentieth century, Trans New Wave texts emphasise the personal dimensions of authorial experience as influencing the mediation of reality ([Ford 2016b](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b17): 222). Importantly for the purposes of this article, Trans New Wave affirms the importance of trans authorship and production of cinema as more reflective of the diversity of trans lives. Since 2008, there has been an identifiable increase in exhibition and production of films by independent trans filmmakers and films with trans themes, characters and narratives across styles and genres ([Ford 2016b](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b17)).

The discussion is positioned within the emerging international field of trans cinema studies and transqueer methodologies ([Leung 2014](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b30); [Siebler 2012](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b43)), utilising theoretical and reflective approaches of cultural studies and textual exegesis. Where feminist temporality theories have considered monumental and cyclical time (Kristeva 1979, [1981](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b29); [Cixous 1994](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b8)) and gay, lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex, and queer temporality theories have deconstructed progressive linear time geographically and ethnographically ([Halberstam 2005](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b22); [Rooke 2010](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b37)), this article offers to show how cinematic time simultaneously creates and distorts trans bodily narratives, perpetuating and complicating audience understandings of gender diverse lives. This occurs, in part, due to the inability of mainstream linear cinematic time to effectively convey the polytemporality of gender diverse experiences and lives, central to understanding our lives. ‘Mainstream films’ can be defined as films produced and distributed by major studios (see Motion Picture Association of America [MPAA] 2014) with high production costs ([Ford 2016b](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b17): 35). In order to secure the largest possible heterogeneous audience, these films rely on linear narratives for economy of storytelling. Trans New Wave films utilise polytemporality and therefore better illustrate the gender diversity of trans lives. Polytemporality, coined in this article, denotes where multiple time periods overlap and are embraced by the individual as central to trans and genderqueer experiences.

Experimental animated autoethnographic short film _Change Over Time_ (Ewan Duarte, USA, 2013) will be examined in tandem with the feature film _52 Tuesdays_ (Sophia Hyde, Australia, 2013) as texts which show how filmmakers utilise temporality as a narrative and stylistic technique in cinematic trans narratives. These are films where cinematic technologies converge with trans embodiment in ways that are constitutive of participants and audiences' understandings of trans lives. This offers the opportunity to engage a transliterate theoretical approach innovatively, building upon established uses and meanings of transliteracy ([Thomas et al. 2007](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b49); [Sukovic 2016](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b46)), to translating narratives and imagery in transgender films to a wider audience, embedded within understandings of trans issues, gender and sexualities within the communities producing the films – to be _trans_ literate (Ford 2014b, [2016a](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b16)).

The term trans is used throughout this discussion as an inclusive, non-essentialist term, encompassing gender diversity, always mindful that trans as a Western concept, does not encompass the range of gender expressions and experiences throughout time within non-Western, Indigenous and First Nations' cultures. Trans* with the asterisk is not used in this article, as it has not been adopted by all scholars and is viewed by some as redundant, elite and as a Western colonising of trans potentiality. This approach is in tandem with respect for Indigenous cultures that have traditionally used a wide range of terms to express gender and sexual diversities throughout time, in terms that do not even exist in Western languages ([Epple 1998](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b13); [Estrada 2011](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b14); [Ford 2016b](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b17)).

Transliteracy enables understanding of the critical nexus between socio-cultural circumstances and how minoritised communities creatively respond. A transliterate reading of contemporary trans cinema involves an understanding that such films are often actively utilised by gender-diverse communities in cultural formation. These are texts which reflect contemporary trans lives and may be used in different settings, including as educational tools. The use of temporality within films of the Trans New Wave will be contrasted with the use of temporal displacement as a cinematic trope of negative affect, disembodiment and societal disjunction in the feature film _Predestination_ (The Spierig Brothers, Australia, 2014), providing a further basis for scholarly critique of cinematic somatechnics in relation to the trans body.

The films within this discussion centralise transmasculine cinematic narratives, utilising a range of temporal strategies in the representations. Films _Change Over Time_ and _52 Tuesdays_ employ the temporal strategy of one year to structure the narratives, strategically highlighting the centrality of temporal concerns within the title of each film: literally referring to ‘time’ (Duarte) and ‘52’ (Hyde) – the number of weeks in a chronological year. Trans New Wave filmmaker Ewan Duarte (United States) focuses his attention on the ontological meaning of the technicities that lead to his physical transitional changes and which can only take place ‘over time’. This is contrasted to the use of the chronological time-span of one linear year to structure screen production in Sophie Hyde's (Australia) first independent feature film. Each of these films presents a particular insight into what Jay Prosser called ‘the specificity of transsexual experience’ ([Prosser 2006](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b34): 279).

Each film navigates how time is interconnected in the successes or perceived failures of the transgender body within the structures of hegemonic society. In the case of feature film _Predestination_, through the use of bodily temporal dislocation, a devastating rupture of the trans body is created. This text presents extremely disturbing views that gender may be involuntarily assigned at a surgeon's whim and that a trans person is a sociopath who will destroy the world. This last text is cited within this article as an example of an independent film with mainstream distribution and screen industry funding support ([Groves 2012](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b21)) that has caused considerable concern regarding trans representation in cinema.

The films selected are also texts that are temporally constrained internally and externally, being produced within the same year of 2013–2014 and of different temporal durations, from short to feature length productions: _Change Over Time_ is seven minutes, _52 Tuesdays_ is one hour and fifty-four minutes and _Predestination_ is one hour and hour thirty-seven minutes. The starting point for a comparison of these films is that they were produced within a compressed cinematic space and socio-cultural time period of 2013–2014 when transgender lives were becoming increasingly visible in screen media. As films which compress trans narratives into specific cinematic timecodes, exploration of what the durational concepts utilised within these films may convey to audiences about trans experiences is examined.

Awareness of how temporal issues frame trans experiences is intensified through my extended period of fieldwork over the past ten years with independent film and filmmakers within the gay, lesbian, bisexual, transgender, and queer communities as well as with filmmakers such as Ewan Duarte cited within this article, in tandem with my prior training as a film editor and work as a Festival Director. Duarte's earlier short documentary _Spiral Transition_ (Duarte, United States, 2010), alludes to the temporality of trans experiences through the use of physical movement, with the central character walking slowly and reflectively to the centre of a spiral that has been created in the landscape using earth and stones.[1](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#fn1) Films such as these are texts where cinematic technologies converge with trans embodiment in ways that are constitutive of participants and audiences' understanding of trans lives, being produced from within the gender-diverse community. In a film such as _52 Tuesdays_ whilst temporality may be used in ways that intelligently reflect the durational aspects of transitional processes (literally over the course of one year), for audiences who view this narrative compressed in under two hours of cinematic time, the effect may be to simultaneously undermine the authenticity of the trans journey.

Through widening discussion of the temporal strategies utilised within recent transmasculine representations in cinema to include exegesis of the Australian feature films _52 Tuesdays_ and _Predestination_, cinematic temporality is foregrounded as both an innovative production strategy for an independent (lower budget) feature in _52 Tuesdays_ and as a transphobic narrative technique in _Predestination_. The term ‘independent film’ is used within this article as established through fieldwork with filmmakers and current screen industry definitions ([Screen Australia 2012](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b39); [Directors Guild of America [DGA] 2011](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b11)) as outside the Studios and with lower (and no) budget productions ([Ford 2016b](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b17): 29). The production budget is the central criteria in defining what makes an independent film, along with independence from the major studio system of production and distribution. It is noted that specific independent filmmakers move into the mainstream screen industry and vice versa and that there may be significant reciprocal influences between independent and mainstream film. _52 Tuesdays_ presents a significant narrative development in representational strategies in contemporary trans cinema, presenting parallel and intertwined narratives of a parent during gender transition relating to an adolescent daughter who is not only learning to relate to their parent as a father but simultaneously awakening to her own sexuality.

The interconnection between time, embodiment and technologies suggested by these films highlights the somatechnical possibilities of cinematic trans. The established definitions of ‘somatechnics’ and ‘somatechnical’ following [Nikki Sullivan (2014)](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b47), remains a cogent point of convergence for considerations of twenty first century trans cinema. As Sullivan explained:
> _technés_ are the dynamic means in and through which corporealities are crafted: that is, continuously engendered in relation to others and to a world … Given this, the primary aim of somatechnics as a critical orientation is – at least as I understand it – to queer orderability by bringing to light the operations of power, the soma-techno-logic, that constitute(s) (un)becoming-with in situated ways. ([Sullivan 2014](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b47))

Such ‘situated ways’ include cinematic depictions of trans in cultural spaces where ‘the operations of power’ may seem invisible, backgrounded to the cultural creations onscreen and yet may be understood as based in the ‘business’ aspect of show business: a highly financed established screen industry. The power to produce (or not produce) specific screen content illustrates how ‘operations of power’ are made visible within hegemonic society via cinema, at times to devastating affect and effect. When somatechnics is addressed in temporal terms, this critique of cinematic power becomes synonymous with the queering of normative notions of time and life suggested by scholars such as [Jack Halberstam (2005)](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b22) and [Alison Rooke (2010)](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b37). Such a queering, or ‘transqueering’ ([Leung 2014](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b30)) leads to embodiments that ultimately also hold power, in this case, to challenge hegemonic notions of time ‘chrononormativity’ ([Freeman 2010](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b20)).

## Cinematic Temporality

Although cinema records and presents temporal moving images, films also become static representations frozen in both cinematic and linear time, recording particular sequences of moments in the fictional screen text, or the factual individual life narrative. This movement of time, both in the onscreen world of the text and in the life of the screen characters and documentary participants, continues in the experience of viewing and writing about these texts. While audiences may view the images of an individual's gender transition, or a transerotic sexual encounter that took place in 2010 in a documentary short such as _Trans Boys_ (Ali Russell and Monique Schafter, Australia, 2012), the texts give a sense of immediacy, engagement and what documentary scholars call ‘privileged access’ ([Zubrycki 2011](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b50)) into what would otherwise be private life experiences and moments, never seen, nor heard and after the time had passed, only present in memory and body for the individuals involved. The ability of cinema to extend the temporal duration of life narratives is highlighted by Mary Doane who speaks of cinema ‘and its technological promise to capture time: immortality, the denial of the radical finitude of the human body, access to other temporalities, and the issue of the archivability of time’ (2002: 2).

In reflecting upon the nature of time in relation to these texts, scholars such as [Jack Halberstam (2005)](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b22) have been kept in mind that it is the normative notion of time and life that the queer life challenges, as we traverse a unique path that has its own temporal trajectory, a specifically queer ‘time and place’. In fieldwork with trans filmmakers and community, ‘Acknowledging this temporality is to queer an otherwise normative rational version of ethnographic time’ ([Rooke 2010](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b37)). The non-hegemonic temporal trajectory that Halberstam so rightly pointed to has become a central narrative within trans films to convey the somatechnical possibilities inherent within transitional journeys. This includes temporal narratives where gender transition takes place at a time when trans ‘adolescence’ may converge with what hegemonic society would consider as linear middle age and brings with it a renewed polytemporal trajectory that is embraced and celebrated by gender-diverse communities but is frequently beyond the scope of hegemonic societal structures to understand.

### Change Over Time[2](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#fn2)

_Change Over Time_ is an animated experimental personal documentary that focuses upon ‘the inner life of experiences and transformation’ during the filmmaker's first year on ‘T’ (testosterone), conveyed through using ‘an impressionistic and poetic approach’ to sharing the filmmaker's ‘emotional and soul experiences’ (Duarte 2013) of transitioning.[3](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#fn3) Ewan's work is embedded within the trans and queer communities of San Francisco and he self-identifies as a Trans New Wave filmmaker. To convey the poetic way in which Duarte utilises cinematic technologies to convey his journey (stop-motion digital animations, image fades and overlays, live-action time-lapse photography, and altered temporal durations), a number of frame enlargements ([Figures 2](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#f2), [3](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#f3)) have been created from his film, a technique of film scholarship that renders the moving cinematic image into a single static frame more akin to photography and different than publicity stills, because the image is produced directly from the film ([Ford 2016b](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b17)) and so contains the unique essence of the cinematic moving image. Using frame enlargements is quite appropriate to this discussion exploring temporalities in recent trans cinema and cinematic time.

Like the feature film _52 Tuesdays_, Duarte uses a temporal strategy directly connected to the chronological movement of time. This is achieved through the use of his voice counting days, weeks and months, following dates of significance in his first year of ‘T’ in his personal diary, with changes in vocal intonation being an audible record of his ‘change over time’. The dates and diary pages are overlaid with images that poetically visually convey the affective dimensions of transitioning ([Figures 1](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#f1), [2](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#f2)). This makes this short film quite unique amongst the representations that are being produced about trans lives.

Open in Viewer![Image 2](https://www.euppublishing.com/cms/10.3366/soma.2019.0265/asset/images/soma9_0058_1.jpg)

Figure 1. _Change Over Time_ publicity still (Source: ©Ewan Duarte Productions 2013). Reproduced courtesy of Ewan Duarte.

Open in Viewer![Image 3](https://www.euppublishing.com/cms/10.3366/soma.2019.0265/asset/images/soma9_0058_2.jpg)

Figure 2. _Change Over Time_ frame enlargement. (Source: _Change Over Time_ ©Ewan Duarte Productions 2013). Reproduced Courtesy Ewan Duarte.

Duarte represents the movement in time, his ‘change over time’ as an ongoing journey along a path that becomes illuminated with rainbow colored rungs, like on a skywalk bridge, and in the background, he is shown walking forwards, embracing his future that is becoming ([Figure 3](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#f3)). This temporal journey is a deeply personal account, an ontological trans cinematic experience. Duarte grieves ‘the loss of (his) queer visibility’ and speaks of ‘the death of his pre-T self’ (Duarte 2013) choosing to focus upon his emotional journey, diarising the changes through poetic writing and art, asking ‘What kind of man will I become? … What will I pass into?’. The filmmaker speaks of ‘integration’ and of a ‘liminal space’ and ‘that there is no transition finish line’.[4](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#fn4)

Open in Viewer![Image 4](https://www.euppublishing.com/cms/10.3366/soma.2019.0265/asset/images/soma9_0058_3.jpg)

Figure 3. _Change Over Time_ frame enlargement. (Source: _Change Over Time_ ©Ewan Duarte Productions 2013). Reproduced Courtesy Ewan Duarte.

Significantly, the filmmaker chose not to show himself engaged in specific technicities of embodiment during stages of medical/surgical transition, such as using ‘T’ in the film. He talks about his experiences of these technicities, such as using ‘T’. Necessary aspects of this journey (including medical artifacts such as syringes, sterile swabs, and bandaids) are seen obscured in several scenes, forming a wallpaper-like background, merging into images of nature such as branches of a tree growing and a stream of flowing water, images of movement and integration. There is an emphasis on the fluvial processes of temporality rather than focussing upon a single action in isolation from external events. Integrating these images, with images of nature is also suggestive of healing and new growth and holds ‘reparative’ ([Sedgewick 2003](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b41)) value as a cinematic strategy, as the sterile swabs and bandaids become motifs of healing and regeneration, rather than images of wounding.[5](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#fn5) Such reparative uses of medical technologies (including cinematic narratives of gender confirmation surgeries and subsequent bandaging) are used recurrently in recent trans cinema, including _52 Tuesdays_. In each image, what Sedgewick called the ‘reparative’ (2003) value of the technicity is emphasised. These are the techniques by which trans embodiment is realised. Duarte speaks of himself gently: ‘this beautiful boy is becoming a beautiful man’, noting the use of the liminal ‘boy’ adolescent form, becoming the ontologically constitutive ‘man’ of his presenting-future.

Throughout the film Duarte utilises temporality stylistically and symbolically. Recognisable temporal markers include the image of a sun rising – symbolically and literally the starting point of time for each new day – behind a page on which a chronological date of June 14 is shown, with subtler shifts indicated through the use of increased motion writing. Duarte uses actual dates to mark time, moving through the pages of his diary to denote change, which can be audibly traced during the film as his voice changes. Throughout, the filmmaker uses changing backgrounds to depict external temporal markers, seasonal changes, a forest with light and shadow alternating amongst the trunks of tall trees, a city, a stream flowing. The audience hears Ewan speaking autoethnographically and self-reflexively: ‘I give birth to a change over time’ (Duarte 2013). The temporal markers of four months of meeting a new love interest and of six months falling in love provide affective responses to the cycles of internal and external motion. Duarte chooses his words with elegance and meaning, using ‘liminality’ and ‘becoming’ repeatedly during the film. As the pages of his diary are shown with dates, he speaks of shifting from ‘moon cycles’ to ‘cycles of the sun’, referencing the ongoing cycles of nature reflected in his internal and external changes. Duarte's use of an experimental filmic style, alternating animations, imagery and self-reflexive writing brings the audience into an ontological connection with the filmmaker's personal experiences. Through autoethnographic diarising and through mimetic writing, Duarte writes his body into being. In this, Duarte stands out amongst the Trans New Wave filmmakers for writing, directing and producing texts which convey glimpses of the ontological meaning of transitioning. As in his previous film _Spiral Transition_ (Duarte, USA, 2010), the calendrical cycle of one year becomes symbolic, with limitless movement towards the centre of being.

### 52 Tuesdays

As a counterpoint film to the textual example of _Change Over Time_ from the Trans New Wave, _52 Tuesdays_ presents the experiences of gender dysphoria and transitioning through an innovative temporal production strategy and temporally constrained narrative of one linear year, literally 52 weeks, with the added production constraints that the film was shot within compressed timeframes of only once a week, every Tuesday until midnight, over the course of one consecutive year (Figures [4](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#f4), [5](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#f5) and [6](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#f6)). The inciting incident of the narrative is James' (Del Herbert-Jane) announcement of his transition to his adolescent daughter Billie (Tilda Cobham-Hervey). The narrative then follows the story of James over the course of one year as he transitions physically, emotionally and socially as a man and into his new role as a father in relation to his daughter. Throughout the film, the transition is largely experienced from the point of view of Billie, as a parallel narrative within her coming of age story.

Open in Viewer![Image 5](https://www.euppublishing.com/cms/10.3366/soma.2019.0265/asset/images/soma9_0058_4.jpg)

Figure 4. _52 Tuesdays_, Publicity Poster ©Closer Productions 2013 (Source: viewed 24 January 2017, [http-/www.imdb.com/title/tt3100636/mediaviewer/rm1207094784](https://http-/www.imdb.com/title/tt3100636/mediaviewer/rm1207094784); International Movie Database [IMDB] 2013) Reproduced under Fair dealing provisions.

Open in Viewer![Image 6](https://www.euppublishing.com/cms/10.3366/soma.2019.0265/asset/images/soma9_0058_5.jpg)

Figure 5. _52 Tuesdays_, DVD Cover, ©Closer Productions 2013 (Source: Peccadillo Pictures gallery, viewed 24 January 2017, [https://www.peccapics.com/product/52tuesdays/#ad-image-0](https://www.peccapics.com/product/52tuesdays/#ad-image-0)). Reproduced under Fair dealing provisions.

Open in Viewer![Image 7](https://www.euppublishing.com/cms/10.3366/soma.2019.0265/asset/images/soma9_0058_6.jpg)

Figure 6. _52 Tuesdays_, North American Theatrical Release Poster, ©Closer Productions 2013 (Source: viewed 24 January 2017, [http://www.movieposterdb.com/Poster/0585328c](http://www.movieposterdb.com/Poster/0585328c)). Reproduced under Fair dealing provisions.

_52 Tuesdays_ had its world premiere at Sundance in 2014 and subsequently won Best Director (in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition), then went on to European Premiere in the Berlinale film festival, winning the Crystal Bear for Best Film in the Generations 14+ category ([Closer Productions 2014](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b9)).

These awards and honor nominations are noted as significant as this directly impacts the distribution and theatrical release of a film, increasing screening opportunities. Awarded films become canonical cinematic representations and may become influential in the development of subsequent cinematic images. Such films may also have influence on audience reception of cinematic narratives and on how people view the subject matter portrayed ([Ford 2016a](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b16)).

The DVD cover, which may be the first contact point of a film with the audience outside theatrical release, suggests an issue that emerges within the text of the cinematic narrative, namely that this story does not unfold from a transgender point of view – something that will be returned to in the conclusion ([Figure 5](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#f5)). The cover utilises an almost sensational 1950s B Grade cinema voice and tabloid-style marketing line announcing: ‘As Jane become James, he will always be Billie's Mother’. This type of misgendering and incorrect use of gender pronouns within contemporary cinema is an issue that I have raised in previous journal articles in an exegesis of _Dallas Buyers Club_ (Jean-Marc Vallee, United States, 2013) ([Ford 2016c](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b18), [2017](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#core-collateral-b19)). It is disappointing to recognise that a similar use of misgendering language is also an issue in _52 Tuesdays_ in relation to the central character James and by other characters in addressing James ‘she’, ‘her’ and ‘mum’ explicitly throughout the film. Whilst this could be interpreted as a way of reflecting the difficulties of Billie (James' daughter) and Harry (James' brother) in accepting James' transition, the use of incorrect pronouns throughout the film (from the DVD cover on) is devastating, as this projects a ‘failure’ upon the trans person to be recognised in their own terms. In considering production strategies, the decision to promote the DVD with this misgendered marketing logline becomes difficult to understand, given that the official website for the film contains a downloadable media guide on the correct use of ‘Transgender Terms & Pronouns’ (_52 Tuesdays_ n.d.); which the DVD cover ([Figure 7](https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/soma.2019.0265#f7)) strategically seems to have ignored in favor of a sensational marketing logline.

Open in Viewer![Image 8](https://www.euppublishing.com/cms/10.3366/soma.2019.0265/asset/images/soma9_0058_7.jpg)

Figure 7. ‘The Unmarried Mother’, _Predestination_, publicity still, © Screen Australia (presents), Screen Queensland (in association with), Blacklab Entertainment, Wolfhound Pictures, Stage 6 Films, 2014 (Source: viewed 24 January 2017, [http-//www.imdb.com/title/tt2397535/mediaviewer/rm4270310400](https://http-//www.imdb.com/title/tt2397535/mediaviewer/rm4270310400); International Movie Database 2014).
