--- SOURCE 1: Iranian film shines spotlight on taboo subject of transsexuals ---
URL: https://www.theguardian.com/world/2012/nov/02/iranian-film-taboo-subject-transsexuals

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Guardian article from November 2012 reports on the Iranian film "Facing Mirrors," directed by Negar Azarbayjani, which brings the taboo subject of transsexuality to the big screen in Iran for the first time. The film follows the relationship between Adineh (a wealthy woman who wants to become a man) and Rana (a taxi driver from a conservative background). Despite transsexuality being legal in Iran since a 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini—issued after campaigning by trans rights activist Maryam Khatoon Molkara—the topic remains highly controversial in Iranian society. Iran permits more sex-change operations than any country except Thailand and subsidizes such surgeries. However, the article highlights deep societal contradictions: homosexuality is punishable by death, state support doesn't prevent harassment, and there is widespread confusion between homosexuality and transsexuality. Some parents reportedly force homosexual children to undergo sex-change operations. The film's release created an opportunity for Iranian media to address the issue, including state-run outlets. Experts quoted include producer Fereshteh Taerpour, rights campaigner Shadi Amin (who criticizes the quality of Iranian sex-change operations), and Bronwen Robertson, who notes the immense pressure on young Iranians to conform to societal norms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"I wish she was blind, dead, handicapped but not disgraced." (Adineh's father in the film, summarizing societal attitudes), "At the beginning, it was very strange for me to find out that sex-change operation is permitted in Iran... The authorities give loans and even issue new ID cards after the surgery, something that is not legal in many countries." (Producer Fereshteh Taerpour), "When you're a transsexual, your appearance changes and that's something that many Iranian families can never come to terms with... But when you're gay, your family might tolerate you as long as you keep your sexuality secret." (Soheil, a 33-year-old Iranian who underwent surgery), "In a democratic society, a sex-change operation is an option for transsexuals, but in Iran it's an obligation for their survival." (Shadi Amin, Iranian rights campaigner), "The pressure, from both state and society, on young Iranians to conform to societal norms and adhere to tradition and specific behavioural codes is immense. Therefore, it is not surprising that many young gay and lesbian Iranians, who do not identify as transgender, say they have felt pressured to undergo surgery." (Bronwen Robertson)
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Queer and Trans Subjects in Iranian Cinema - Ajam Media Collective ---
URL: https://ajammc.com/2013/05/11/queer-and-trans-subjects-in-iranian-cinema-between-representation-agency-and-orientalist-fantasies

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Ajam Media Collective, written by a queer Iranian graduate student in the US, critically examines two Iranian films about gender and sexual minorities: "Facing Mirrors" (2011) and "Circumstance" (2011). 

"Facing Mirrors," directed by Negar Azarbayjani, is the first Iranian film featuring a female-to-male transgender main character (Eddy, a pre-op transman). It won awards at over 64 international film festivals including Iran's Fajr Film Festival and San Francisco's Frameline Festival. The film portrays complex, agentic characters navigating transphobia and societal constraints in Iran.

"Circumstance," directed by Iranian-American Maryam Keshavarz, tells the story of two teenage girls in love. The article argues it received far more Western media attention because it conforms to Orientalist fantasies about oppressed Muslim women and queer people. Critics note its inauthentic portrayal of Iranian life (e.g., American-accented Persian, outdated cultural references) and its reduction of Iranian women's struggles to drinking, partying, and cursing the government.

The author argues that "Facing Mirrors" disrupts Orientalist narratives by showing Iranian characters with agency, complexity, and resilience. Despite legal recognition of trans people in Iran (following Ayatollah Khomeini's 1978 fatwa, with government support for surgeries), the film received little Western coverage. Meanwhile, the film was debated extensively in Iran, screened even at Qom's Mofid University, and opened public discourse on trans issues.

A lengthy comments section includes debates about the article's use of "queer" terminology, critiques of Iran's medical-legal framework for trans people (including accusations of forced surgeries and homophobia), and disagreements about the author's Orientalist framing.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The concept of a queer Iranian cinema may sound contradictory or impossible, but that is exactly how one would describe Facing Mirrors (2011), the first movie to feature a female-to-male transgender main character that has been written, produced, and screened in Iran.", "The lack of mainstream coverage of Facing Mirrors in the US stands in stark contrast to the widespread media attention given to Circumstance, which is a direct result of the Orientalizing effect of the Western gaze on Middle Eastern subjects.", "The movie's greatest weakness is the lack of subjectivity of the two protagonists... shown as mere (queer) sexual objects as opposed to subjects of their own destiny.", "The greatest success of the movie, however, is in the fact that it has forever entered Iran's social, cultural, and political public space where it has inserted a thought-provoking and relatable narrative of queerness in the public imaginary.", "Unfortunately, the mainstream Western culture considers such complexity as antithetical to its Orientalist narrative of oppressed Muslim women and queers in need of saving."
</key_excerpts>

<summary>
This is a detailed analysis video from the YouTube channel "POSITIF" (پوزیتیف) about the 1997 Iranian film "Adam Barfi" (آدم برفی / Snowman), directed by Davoud Mirbagheri. The film is one of the most controversial in Iranian cinema history due to its plot involving cross-dressing by star actor Akbar Abdi.

**Key Historical Context:**
- The film was made in 1994 (1373) by Davoud Mirbagheri, with the same cast as his TV series "Imam Ali." Produced by the Howzeh Honari (Art Bureau), it was banned for 3 years.
- A harsh article in Kayhan newspaper by editor Mehdi Nassiri targeted the film for Akbar Abdi's cross-dressing. The film was banned by Ezzatollah Zarqami just before the Fajr Film Festival.
- Mohammad Ali Zaman (director of the Howzeh Honari) lobbied for the film's release, eventually getting it shown to President Hashemi Rafsanjani and Ayatollah Khamenei, who deemed it unproblematic.
- Released in 1997 (1376), it became the year's highest-grossing film, but faced violent attacks from Ansar-e Hezbollah groups (led by Masoud Dehnamaaki and Allah Karam) who physically assaulted cinemas and audiences, including a pregnant woman who suffered a miscarriage.
- The film ran in rotation for 2 years until 1999.

**Plot Summary:**
The story follows Abbas (played by Akbar Abdi), an Iranian man desperately trying to get a visa to the United States. Stranded in Turkey, he meets Iranian acquaintances who suggest his only way to America is to become a woman and marry an American. Abbas transforms into "Dorna" (a female character).

**Analysis Framework:**
The video analyzes the film through multiple lenses:
1. **Sheikh San'an allegory** – The classical Persian story from Attar's Mantiq al-Tayr about a pious sheikh who falls in love with a Christian girl, mirroring Abbas's journey and the fear of Western cultural influence.
2. **Judith Butler's gender theory** – The film is examined through Butler's concept of gender performativity (that gender is a social role performed daily), and the idea of "hacking" gender through signs and repetition.
3. **Ta'ziyeh (Shabih-khani) tradition** – The Iranian passion play tradition where men play women's roles, maintaining a clear distance between performer and role (as opposed to Western mimesis/realistic imitation).
4. **Film Farsi (pre-revolutionary Iranian cinema)** – The film's nostalgic references to the "tipe" (stock characters) of pre-revolution Iranian cinema, particularly through the characters played by Parviz Parastui and Dariush Arjmand.

**Theoretical Conclusions:**
- The film creates a "border zone" identity (liminal space) across three axes: Iran→America (migration), male→female (gender), and old→new Iranian cinema (temporal).
- Turkey serves as the "purgatory" point where all three axes converge.
- The ending requires Dorna (the female persona) to die so Abbas can return to Iran, suggesting that in-between states cannot survive in the film's ultimately binary worldview.
- The film paradoxically operates within Iran's propagandistic framework (the "cultural invasion" discourse) while simultaneously exposing the instability of the very concepts it seeks to defend.

The video was recorded in Mordad 1405 (July-August 2026) and is presented by armia Heydari and Javad Ebrahimi Nejad.
</summary>

## PART I: COMPREHENSIVE LIST OF MENA FILMS WITH TRANSGENDER THEMES, CHARACTERS, OR NARRATIVES

### Iran

**1. *Facing Mirrors* (آینه های روبرو, 2011)**
- Director: Negar Azarbayjani
- Country: Iran
- Year: 2011
- Genre: Narrative Feature
- Summary: The first Iranian film to feature a female-to-male transgender main character (Eddy, a pre-op transman). The film follows the unlikely friendship between Eddie (played by Shayesteh Irani), a pre-op trans man from an upper-class family seeking a passport for sex reassignment surgery abroad, and Rana (Ghazal Shakeri), a religious, conservative taxi driver from a working-class background. Despite initial disgust, Rana eventually accepts Eddie and helps him. The film explores themes of prejudice, acceptance, and challenging superficial judgments. A remarkable scene is when Rana doesn't know how to introduce Eddie to her son—as uncle or as aunt. The film won awards at over 64 international film festivals including Iran's Fajr Film Festival and San Francisco's Frameline Festival (where it won "Best First Feature" in 2012). The film was debated extensively in Iran, screened even at Qom's Mofid University, and opened public discourse on trans issues. The film centers on two characters—Rana and Adineh (Eddie)—who help each other achieve freedom: Rana must defy societal gendered norms to support her family, while Eddie, a transgender man, must defy his family's expectations to live authentically. [Sources: 2, 7, 8, 3, 4, 5]

**2. *Be Like Others* (also known as *Transsexual in Iran*, 2008)**
- Director: Tanaz Eshaghian
- Country: Iran/USA/Canada/UK/France (co-production)
- Year: 2008
- Genre: Documentary
- Runtime: 74 minutes
- Summary: A documentary that explores the lives of transgender women in Iran, focusing on patients at Dr. Bahram Mir-Jalali's Mirdamad Surgical Centre, a sex-reassignment clinic in Tehran. The film highlights the paradox that while homosexual relationships are illegal and punishable by death in Iran, sex reassignment surgery is permitted following a 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini allowing such operations for "diagnosed transsexuals." The documentary follows two main subjects: Ali Askar, a 24-year-old man who doesn't want to become a woman but sees no other option in Iranian society due to his feminine appearance, and Anoosh, another young man ostracized for his femininity. Ali undergoes surgery (becoming Negar) but is disowned by his family, experiences depression, and turns to prostitution. Anoosh becomes Anahita and is initially happy and engaged, though her boyfriend becomes distant after the surgery. Eshaghian's film suggests that many Iranians pursue sex reassignment not because they identify as transgender, but because it allows them to escape persecution for homosexuality. The film won three Teddy Awards at the Berlin International Film Festival, was nominated for the Grand Jury Prize at Sundance, and was nominated for a GLAAD Media Award for Outstanding Documentary. Variety called it "a powerful window into a once-hidden side of the country" and "a model of non-dogmatic filmmaking on a highly charged topic." [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]

**3. *This is Not Me* (2023)**
- Director: Saeed Ghalipour
- Country: Iran
- Year: 2023
- Genre: Documentary/Independent Feature
- Summary: Focuses on the lives of two trans men in Iran as they navigate legal recognition and access to gender-affirming surgery. The film was featured at the Museum of Fine Arts' "Boston Festival of Films From Iran" in late January 2023. Director Ghalipour, speaking from Tehran via translator, noted that while sex reassignment is legally accepted under Islamic law in Iran—making it the only legal form of being queer in the country—trans individuals still face invasive medical checks, court proceedings, and social ostracism. The film highlights the supportive parents of the subjects, but Ghalipour notes this is an exception, as many trans individuals in Iran face suicide due to community rejection. The film is an independent production that has not been approved by Iranian authorities and cannot be screened legally in Iran, reflecting the broader censorship and underground arts scene in the country since the Islamic Revolution. [Source: 10]

**4. *Adam Barfi* (Snowman, 1995)**
- Director: Davood Mirbagheri
- Country: Iran
- Year: 1995 (released 1997 due to ban)
- Genre: Comedy/Drama
- Runtime: 103 minutes
- Summary: The story follows Abbas, a middle-aged Iranian man desperate to leave Iran for America. To obtain a visa, he begins dressing as a woman (transforming into "Dorna") to ensnare an American man. As complications arise, Abbas begins to doubt his plan. The film is described as one of the highest-grossing Iranian films of all time. The film was banned for 3 years, with the ban signed by Ezzatollah Zarqami, and only released after President Hashemi Rafsanjani and Ayatollah Khamenei had a private screening and deemed it unproblematic. Violent attacks by Ansar-e Hezbollah groups (led by Masoud Dehnamaaki and Allah Karam) on cinemas resulted in injuries, including a pregnant woman who suffered a miscarriage—all without the attackers having seen the film. The film creates a "border zone" identity across three axes: Iran→America (migration), male→female (gender), and old→new Iranian cinema (temporal), with Turkey as the purgatory point where all three converge. In the ending, Dorna (the female persona) must die so Abbas can return to Iran, suggesting that in-between states cannot survive in the film's ultimately binary worldview. The film paradoxically operates within Iran's propagandistic framework of "cultural invasion" while simultaneously exposing the instability of the very concepts it seeks to defend. Academic analysis of *Adam Barfi* appears in "Cross-Dressing and Gender (Tres)Passing" by R. Kheshti (2009) and "Transgender Identity in Iranian Cinema" by Kaveh Bassiri (2019). [Sources: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]

**5. *Madmazel Khaleh* (Mademoiselle Khaleh)**
- Identified in Kaveh Bassiri's "Transgender Identity in Iranian Cinema" (2019) as a key film illustrating evolving representations of transgender identities in Iranian cinema. Through close readings of *Baran* and *Dokhtaraneh Khorshid*, the author identifies a "transgender move": a temporary space of political and agential potential sought by both domestic and diasporic spectators in post-1990s Iranian cinema. ## PART II: DETAILED ANALYSIS OF CORE CASE STUDIES (5 Films)

### CASE STUDY 1: *Facing Mirrors* (Iran, 2011, Dir. Negar Azarbayjani)

**(1) Narrative Structure and Plot Summary:**
The film centers on two characters—Rana (Ghazal Shakeri), a religious, conservative taxi driver from a working-class background, and Adineh/Eddie (Shayesteh Irani), a pre-op trans man from an upper-class family seeking a passport for sex reassignment surgery abroad. Their lives meet by chance. Rana must defy societal gendered norms to support her family, while Eddie must defy his family's expectations to live authentically. The story follows the unlikely friendship that develops between them; despite initial disgust, Rana eventually accepts Eddie and helps him. A remarkable scene is when Rana doesn't know how to introduce Eddie to her son—as uncle or as aunt. [Sources: 2, 7, 8, 3]

**(2) Cinematic Techniques:**
Sources note that the film uses intimate framing to capture the emotional journeys of both protagonists. The Ajam Media Collective article notes that the film's greatest weakness is "the lack of subjectivity of the two protagonists... shown as mere (queer) sexual objects as opposed to subjects of their own destiny." However, the film is praised for disrupting Orientalist narratives by showing Iranian characters with agency, complexity, and resilience. The film uses the metaphor of mirrors (as indicated in the title) to explore identity, reflection, and self-perception. [Sources: 7, 2]

**(3) Cultural and National Context of Production:**
In Iran, transgender issues are legally distinct from homosexuality. Following a 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, transgender individuals became officially recognized by the government and permitted to undergo sex reassignment surgery. The government contributes up to half the financial cost of the operation and issues new birth certificates to recognize and reflect the sex change. Iran performs some of the highest numbers of sex reassignment surgeries in the world, second only to Thailand. However, despite government approval, transgender people in Iran face daily harassment, difficulty obtaining work, and family rejection. Homosexuality remains punishable by death. The article notes a contrast with the U.S.: in Iran, the government encourages tolerance of transgender people, whereas in the U.S., the people push the government toward tolerance. The Guardian (2012) quotes producer Fereshteh Taerpour: "At the beginning, it was very strange for me to find out that sex-change operation is permitted in Iran... The authorities give loans and even issue new ID cards after the surgery, something that is not legal in many countries." Shadi Amin, Iranian rights campaigner, states: "In a democratic society, a sex-change operation is an option for transsexuals, but in Iran it's an obligation for their survival." Bronwen Robertson notes: "The pressure, from both state and society, on young Iranians to conform to societal norms and adhere to tradition and specific behavioural codes is immense. Therefore, it is not surprising that many young gay and lesbian Iranians, who do not identify as transgender, say they have felt pressured to undergo surgery." [Sources: 8, 5]

**(4) Engagement with Transgender Identities:**
The film is the first Iranian film featuring a female-to-male transgender main character that has been written, produced, and screened in Iran. It portrays complex, agentic characters navigating transphobia and societal constraints in Iran. The film disrupts Orientalist narratives by showing Iranian characters with agency, complexity, and resilience. The film's greatest success is that "it has forever entered Iran's social, cultural, and political public space where it has inserted a thought-provoking and relatable narrative of queerness in the public imaginary." The film was debated extensively in Iran, screened even at Qom's Mofid University. The director did not use a transgender actor for the lead role (Shayesteh Irani is a cisgender actress). [Sources: 7, 2, 4]

**(5) Critical Reception and Academic Scholarship:**
- The film won "Best First Feature" at the 2012 Frameline Film Festival (the oldest LGBT film festival in the world)
- Won awards at over 64 international film festivals
- Won at Iran's Fajr Film Festival
- The Ajam Media Collective article (2013) by a queer Iranian graduate student provides a critical analysis comparing *Facing Mirrors* to *Circumstance*, arguing that *Facing Mirrors* received far less Western media attention because it disrupts Orientalist narratives, while *Circumstance* conformed to "Orientalist fantasies about oppressed Muslim women and queer people."
- The Yale Review of International Studies article (2019) discusses the film's screening at Yale and its implications for transgender rights in Iran.
- *The Guardian* article (2012) reports on the film's release and the societal contradictions it highlights.
- The Iranian Film Empire blog (2016) discusses the film's themes of prejudice and acceptance.
- Kaveh Bassiri's "Transgender Identity in Iranian Cinema" (2019) contextualizes the film within broader Iranian cinema's treatment of transgender themes.
- The film is cited in the "Handbook of Trans Cinema" CFP (2025) as a key example of Iranian trans cinema. [Sources: 2, 7, 8, 4, 5, 11, 1]

### CASE STUDY 2: *Be Like Others* (Iran/USA, 2008, Dir. Tanaz Eshaghian)

**(1) Narrative Structure and Plot Summary:**
The documentary explores the lives of transgender women in Iran, focusing on patients at Dr. Bahram Mir-Jalali's Mirdamad Surgical Centre, a sex-reassignment clinic in Tehran. The film follows two main subjects: Ali Askar, a 24-year-old man who doesn't want to become a woman but sees no other option in Iranian society due to his feminine appearance, and Anoosh, another young man ostracized for his femininity. Ali undergoes surgery (becoming Negar) but is disowned by his family, experiences depression, and turns to prostitution. Anoosh becomes Anahita and is initially happy and engaged, though her boyfriend becomes distant after the surgery. The film also features Vida, an "alpha-tranny" counselor. The documentary provides an intimate look at young Iranians choosing to undergo sex-change surgery, featuring perspectives from surgeons, Koranic experts, and patients. [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]

**(2) Cinematic Techniques:**
Variety called it "a powerful window into a once-hidden side of the country" and "a model of non-dogmatic filmmaking on a highly charged topic." The film uses intimate observational documentary style, with direct interviews and access to surgical procedures. The Frameline description notes it is "an intimate and unflinching look at life in Iran, seen through the lens of those living at its fringes." The Letterboxd page notes: "I think all the trans women asked in this movie, including one asked while on the literal operating table, said they wouldn't want to go through with the surgery if they were able to have their rights and assimilate into society without it." [Sources: 6, 9, 10]

**(3) Cultural and National Context of Production:**
The film is set against the backdrop of Iran where homosexuality is punishable by death but a fatwa from Ayatollah Khomeini made sex-change operations legal. As one surgeon in the film states: "In the Islamic Republic of Iran, homosexuality is punishable by death. Twenty-five years ago, however, the Ayatollah Khomeini wrote a fatwa pronouncing transsexuality legal and allowing for sex-change operations." The documentary is a co-production between Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States, and France. The film was produced by Forties B, ITVS International, and Necessary Illusions Productions Inc. Languages: English and Persian. [Sources: 6, 8]

**(4) Engagement with Transgender Identities:**
Eshaghian's film suggests that many Iranians pursue sex reassignment not because they identify as transgender, but because it allows them to escape persecution for homosexuality. The film's central argument is that "identifying as transsexual rather than homosexual allows them to live free from harassment." The Supamodu review notes: "It is perfectly accommodating towards transwomen but homosexuality is considered a crime. This leads to many gay men passing as transwomen to not have to deal with morality police. But since legal status is a part of this, some gay men go as far as to have gender reaffirmation surgery which allows them to live freely but not as themselves. Watching people struggle with having to forego one part of their identity to have some space for another is devastating." The film raises complex ethical questions about whether Iran's legal framework for transgender people is actually liberating or coercive, given that some individuals may feel pressured to transition to avoid persecution for homosexuality. The film does not use transgender actors—it is a documentary featuring real transgender individuals. [Sources: 6, 7]

**(5) Critical Reception and Academic Scholarship:**
- Won three Teddy Awards at the Berlin International Film Festival
- Nominated for the Grand Jury Prize at Sundance
- Nominated for a GLAAD Media Award for Outstanding Documentary
- Won a special jury prize at the Berlin Film Festival
- Selected as a Sundance favorite
- Rotten Tomatoes: 7.4/10 IMDb rating from 299 users
- *Variety* praised it as "a powerful window into a once-hidden side of the country"
- The film is discussed in the Letterboxd community as "a rare and illuminating perspective on life in the Islamic Republic of Iran. Reveals the misunderstanding of those who use the example of Iran's state subsidized sex change operations to portray the Islamic Republic as a country that is open to sexual difference. In fact, the compulsion to undergo these operations shows how homosexuality is seen as beyond the pale."
- Kaveh Bassiri's "Transgender Identity in Iranian Cinema" (2019) discusses the film as part of the documentary tradition on Iranian transsexuals that has gained prominence since 2003.
- The film is cited in the "Handbook of Trans Cinema" CFP (2025) as a key example of trans cinema from Iran. [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 1]

### CASE STUDY 4: *Crossing* (Turkey/Sweden, 2024, Dir. Levan Akin)

**(1) Narrative Structure and Plot Summary:**
Lia (Mzia Arabuli), a retired schoolteacher from Georgia, sets out to find her long-lost niece Tekla, a transgender woman. Accompanied by Tekla's former neighbor Achi (Lucas Kankava), she travels to Istanbul, where they meet Evrim (Deniz Dumanlı), a transgender legal advocate and sex worker active in the city's trans community. The film follows Lia's journey from a woman who is "on a mission to do something for her deceased sister" and who "has distanced herself to think life's just something she has to do" to a woman who "starts to come to terms with things in herself." The key thematic "crossing" is a change of mind and heart. The film ultimately questions whether Lia herself needs to be found and forgiven rather than Tekla. [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]

**(2) Cinematic Techniques:**
The film received mixed reviews for its visual style. The Guardian praised it as "a thoroughly intelligent, emotionally engaging and robustly performed movie." The Rotten Tomatoes consensus calls it "a tender odyssey with Mzia Arabuli's wonderful performance as the audience's guide, Crossing marks another humanist triumph for writer-director Levan Akin." However, a negative review from In Review Online criticizes the visual style as "dingy and generic" with excessive handheld camera work, and describes the film's central relationship as relying on "audience-pleasing clichés." Variety notes: "Akin makes a calculated choice to raise awareness of the trans community in Istanbul, but he does so through representation rather than manipulation." Screen Daily highlights "two fierce female characters." Little White Lies describes it as "sweet without being cloying, a love letter to the commonalities between Georgian and Turkish culture, one that encourages empathy and reminds us it's never too late to change for the better." [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 21]

**(3) Cultural and National Context of Production:**
The film is a co-production between Sweden, Denmark, France, Turkey, and Georgia. Director Levan Akin, who was raised in Sweden by Georgian parents, delayed the shoot by a year to conduct proper location research in Istanbul, rewriting the script during that time. Akin's previous film *And Then We Danced* (2019) faced violent protests and backlash from the Georgian Orthodox Church and ultra-conservative groups. Akin received death threats for *And Then We Danced* but chose to make *Crossing* in Turkey nonetheless, prioritizing meaningful engagement with the communities he portrays. The film engages with Istanbul's Lubunca culture (queer slang) and the city's underground trans community. [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]

**(4) Engagement with Transgender Identities:**
The film is groundbreaking for its authentic representation. Akin cast real trans community members both in front of and behind the camera. The key character Evrim, a trans human rights lawyer, is played by trans actress Deniz Dumanli in her first film role. Akin states: "Our main casting person in Turkey was a trans man called Bulut [Sezer] who knew a lot of people in the community. I wanted Evrim to be a resilient character that faces the world with bravado. Deniz really has that spirit within herself. She's so open, so positive, so hungry for life." Akin also hired trans crew members, including an assistant costume designer and a casting person. The film is described as "an uplifting and compassionate portrait of Istanbul's trans community and the fact allies can be found in unexpected places." Akin states: "I wanted to tell a story from the point of view of an older character who's a relative to somebody who's LGBTQI+, and to show it isn't just like, 'Old people don't understand, because they're bigoted.' It's far more nuanced than that." The film's key line: "Lia says, 'We wasted so much time. We could have spent that time together. And for what? I love you regardless.' That's something a lot of us want to hear." [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]

**(5) Critical Reception and Academic Scholarship:**

### CASE STUDY 5: *Adam Barfi* (Snowman, Iran, 1995, Dir. Davood Mirbagheri)

**(1) Narrative Structure and Plot Summary:**
The story follows Abbas (played by Akbar Abdi), a middle-aged Iranian man desperate to leave Iran for America. Stranded in Turkey, he meets Iranian acquaintances who suggest his only way to America is to become a woman and marry an American. Abbas transforms into "Dorna" (a female character). As complications arise, Abbas begins to doubt his plan. The film creates a "border zone" identity across three axes: Iran→America (migration), male→female (gender), and old→new Iranian cinema (temporal), with Turkey as the purgatory point where all three converge. In the ending, Dorna (the female persona) must die so Abbas can return to Iran, suggesting that in-between states cannot survive in the film's ultimately binary worldview. [Sources: 13, 14]

**(2) Cinematic Techniques:**
The film blends comedy, drama, and romance. It is analyzed through multiple theoretical frameworks in the "POSITIF" video analysis (2026): (1) the Sheikh San'an allegory from Attar's Mantiq al-Tayr about a pious sheikh who falls in love with a Christian girl, mirroring Abbas's journey and the fear of Western cultural influence; (2) Judith Butler's gender performativity theory—that gender is a social role performed daily, and the idea of "hacking" gender through signs and repetition; (3) the Ta'ziyeh (Shabih-khani) tradition—the Iranian passion play tradition where men play women's roles, maintaining a clear distance between performer and role (as opposed to Western mimesis/realistic imitation); (4) Film Farsi (pre-revolutionary Iranian cinema)—the film's nostalgic references to the "tipe" (stock characters) of pre-revolution Iranian cinema, particularly through the characters played by Parviz Parastui and Dariush Arjmand. The film is shot by cinematographer Maziar Partow with music by Farhad Fakhreddini. [Sources: 13, 14]

**(3) Cultural and National Context of Production:**
The film was made in 1994 by Davoud Mirbagheri, with the same cast as his TV series "Imam Ali." Produced by the Howzeh Honari (Art Bureau), it was banned for 3 years. A harsh article in Kayhan newspaper by editor Mehdi Nassiri targeted the film for Akbar Abdi's cross-dressing. The film was banned by Ezzatollah Zarqami just before the Fajr Film Festival. Mohammad Ali Zaman (director of the Howzeh Honari) lobbied for the film's release, eventually getting it shown to President Hashemi Rafsanjani and Ayatollah Khamenei, who deemed it unproblematic. Released in 1997, it became the year's highest-grossing film, but faced violent attacks from Ansar-e Hezbollah groups (led by Masoud Dehnamaaki and Allah Karam) who physically assaulted cinemas and audiences, including a pregnant woman who suffered a miscarriage—all without the attackers having seen the film. The film ran in rotation for 2 years until 1999. The film paradoxically operates within Iran's propagandistic framework of "cultural invasion" while simultaneously exposing the instability of the very concepts it seeks to defend. [Sources: 13, 14]

**(4) Engagement with Transgender Identities:**
The film is not explicitly about transgender identity—it is about cross-dressing for instrumental purposes (visa fraud). However, it is a crucial text in the genealogy of gender non-conformity in Iranian cinema. Kaveh Bassiri's "Transgender Identity in Iranian Cinema" (2019) identifies *Adam Barfi* as a key film illustrating evolving representations of transgender identities, noting that MTF (male-to-female) roles in Iranian cinema typically feature comedic elements, while FTM characters often face coercive gender transitions. The film uses a cisgender male actor (Akbar Abdi) in cross-dressing. The critical analysis from the POSITIF channel (2026) argues that the film creates a "border zone" identity but ultimately reinforces a binary worldview by requiring Dorna to die so Abbas can return to Iran. The film is cited in "Cross-Dressing and Gender (Tres)Passing" by R. Kheshti (2009), which examines how the film contributes to the construction of gender and Iran as "transsexual capital of the world." [Sources: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]

**(5) Critical Reception and Academic Scholarship:**

- Subject of violent protests and attacks by Ansar-e Hezbollah
- One of the most controversial films in Iranian cinema history
- Banned for 3 years before release
- R. Kheshti, "Cross-Dressing and Gender (Tres)Passing" (2009, *Hypatia*) - cited by 32 sources

## PART III: ADDITIONAL CONTEXT AND FRAMEWORKS

### Legal and Social Context for Transgender Individuals in the MENA Region

The MENA Trans Archives (Cairo52) is the first and only open-access database dedicated to transgender rights in the MENA region. Key findings:

- **Terminology:** Terms like "gender" and "transgender" are not officially recognized. Instead, terms such as "Sex Identity Disorder," "Sex Change/Transition," "Sex Correction," "Transsexual," "Mukhannath" (effeminate men), "Mustrijla" (masculine women), and "Khuntha" (intersex) are used.

- **Gender-Affirming Healthcare:** Six countries (Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, UAE, Jordan) ban gender-affirming healthcare for transgender individuals, permitting it only for intersex individuals as "sex correction." Iraq is the only exception with a 2002 policy recognizing "transsexualism" as valid.

- **Legal Gender Recognition:** There is a legislative vacuum across the region. Most countries lack specific laws for transgender people, forcing them through lengthy judicial processes. Of 19 identified cases, 73.67% (14 cases) resulted in unfavorable outcomes.

- **Islamic Fiqh:** Prevailing Islamic jurisprudence distinguishes between transgender (viewed as having a mental illness) and intersex (viewed as having a biological condition). The majority of Fatwas (15 of 17) follow this logic, with only two (including Iran's Khomeini) recognizing Gender Identity Disorder as valid.

- **Criminalization:** No country explicitly criminalizes being transgender, but laws against crossdressing, sodomy, public order, and morality are applied to de facto criminalize transgender individuals. Countries like Sudan, Oman, UAE, Kuwait, and Lebanon have explicit laws targeting crossdressing. In 2023, Iraq and Kuwait proposed laws explicitly criminalizing transgender identity. [Source: 4]

The article "Treatment of Transgender Individuals in the Middle East and North Africa" by Lesley Bauer (2024) adds:
- Most MENA states inherited colonial-era laws criminalizing homosexuality, now used to target transgender individuals through vague provisions against "indecent," "immoral," or "unnatural" behavior.
- Almost no MENA states have standardized legal gender recognition processes. Where processes exist, they require surgical/hormonal interventions, expensive forensic medical exams, and can take 3-10 years.
- Notable progress: A 2017 Lebanese appeals court allowed legal gender recognition without surgery; a 2018 Tunisian higher court recognized gender affirming care based on medical necessity.
- Post-Arab Spring (2011), LGBTQ+ civil society movements have grown, with organizations working on decriminalization, legal aid, HIV prevention, media training, and alliance-building. [Source: 2]

### The "Handbook of Trans Cinema" (Forthcoming, 2025-2026)

A Call for Papers (CFP) posted on WikiCFP seeks chapter proposals for "The Handbook of Trans Cinema," edited by Douglas Vakoch. The handbook aims to provide an encyclopedic overview of international trans cinema, organized into three parts: Film Genres (Part I), National Overviews of Trans Cinema (Part II), and Core Concepts (Part III). Specifically, the CFP is seeking chapters on Middle Eastern and North African films with transgender themes for Part II (National Overviews), including chapters on Trans Cinema from Algeria, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, Morocco, Palestine, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, UAE, and others. Several chapters are already confirmed (listed in the CFP), but proposals are still welcome for additional countries. Submission deadline was April 17, 2025; first drafts due October 1, 2025; final versions due December 1, 2025. The handbook already has over 70 confirmed chapters from prominent scholars covering trans films from 6 continents. [Source: 1]

### Academic Scholarship on MENA Transgender Cinema

**Key Works Identified:**

1. **Kaveh Bassiri (2019). "Transgender Identity in Iranian Cinema."** Published in *Global Encyclopedia of Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer (LGBTQ) History*. Examines portrayals of FTM and MTF cross-dressing and transsexuality in Iranian cinema. Key findings: Transgender portrayals often reinforce heteronormativity despite moments of ambiguity and subversion; MTF roles typically feature comedic elements while FTM characters often face coercive gender transitions; key films like *Adam Barfi* and *Madmazel Khaleh* illustrate evolving representations; documentaries on Iranian transsexuals have gained prominence since 2003. [Source: 11]

2. **R. Kheshti (2009). "Cross-Dressing and Gender (Tres)Passing: The Transgender Move as a Site of Agential Potential in the New Iranian Cinema."** Published in *Hypatia*. Cited by 32 sources. Examines *Adam Barfi* and other films. [Source: 12]

3. **"Cross-Dressing and Gender (Tres)Passing: The Transgender Move as a Site of Agential Potential in the New Iranian Cinema" (2020, *Hypatia*).** Through close readings of *Baran* and *Dokhtaraneh Khorshid*, identifies a "transgender move": a temporary space of political and agential potential sought by both domestic and diasporic spectators in post-1990s Iranian cinema. Argues that Iran's censorship codes enforced by the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance have contributed to the emergence of "cross-dressing" or "passing" figures as a ubiquitous trope in New Iranian cinema. [Source: 15]

4. **Maria Abdel Karim (2020). "Queer Representation in Arab and Middle Eastern Films: A Case Study of Women in Caramel (2007), Circumstance (2011), and In Between (2016)."** Published in *Alphaville: Journal of Film and Screen Media*. Examines queer representation in three transnational Middle Eastern women's films. The article argues that while covert representation (Labaki's approach) avoids censorship, overt representation (Keshavarz and Hamoud) is more impactful for social change. None of the films offer a happy ending for queer characters. Emigration (to Dubai, Berlin, or the West) is presented as a common but costly escape route. [Source: 11]

5. **Aaron Jagger (2025). "Tracing the Diasporic Experiences of Transgender and Gender-Nonconforming Palestinians On-screen: Cinema Fouad (1993) and Sultana's Reign (2023)."** Published in *Film Matters* (Volume 16, Issue 3, Dec 2025). Uses queer/trans and post/decolonial theorists including Judith Butler, Hamid Naficy, and Walter Mignolo. Identifies nuance and authenticity as key to representations of diasporic non-Western queerness. [Source: 26]

6. **Murat Akser (2016). "Changing LGBT Narratives in Turkish Cinema."** Published in *Reconstruction: Studies in Contemporary Culture*. Traces the history of LGBT representations in Turkish cinema over approximately 50 years, from 1962 to the present. Documents progression from lesbian to transsexual to homosexual male representations. Notes that LGBT activism gained visibility during the 2013 Taksim Gezi Park protests. [Source: 13]

7. **Zahra Khosroshahi and Sara Saljoughi (2023). "Introduction: Transnational feminist approaches to film and media from the Middle East and North Africa."** Published in *Transnational Screens* (Volume 14, Issue 2, 2023). Argues that a transnational feminist approach brings together divergent fields and has generative possibilities for the contemporary political context. The issue includes five essays analyzing films including *Gilaneh*, *A Moon for my Father*, *The Man Who Sold His Skin*, *Under the Shadow*, and documentaries by Raja Amari. [Source: 3]

8. **Akkadia Ford (2014). "Transliteracy and the New Wave of Gender-Diverse Cinema."** Published in *Fusion Journal* (no. 5). Introduces the Trans New Wave (TNW) as a genre of independent transgender films written, directed, and produced since 2008 outside the mainstream Studio system. Differentiates TNW from New Queer Cinema and from mainstream trans-themed films. [Source: 29]

9. **Akkadia Ford (2019). "Duration, Compression, Extension and Distortion of Time in Contemporary Transgender Cinema."** Published in *Somatechnics* (Vol. 9, No. 1). Introduces the concept of "polytemporality" to denote where multiple time periods overlap in gender-diverse experiences. Analyzes *Change Over Time*, *52 Tuesdays*, and *Predestination*. [Source: 28]

### Key Academic Conferences and Events

- **Columbia University Middle East Institute (2019).** Panel titled "The (R)evolution of Arab Queer Cinema: Queer Representation in Film Pre- and Post-Arab Uprisings." Panelists included Anthony Chidiac, Cyrine Hammemi (coordinator of Mawjoudin/We Exist, the only queer film festival in the Arab world), Sam Abbas (co-founder of ArabQ Films, the first Arab-based LGBTQ-focused production company), and Rolla Selbak. Moderated by Samar Habib. [Sources: 13, 14]

- **Mawjoudin Queer Film Festival (Tunis).** The only queer film festival in the Arab world, coordinated by Cyrine Hammemi. [Source: 13]

- **"Aflamuna" Film Festival (2020).** Online film festival launched by Cinema Al Fouad, the Mawjoudin Queer Film Festival in Tunis, and the platform Jeem, in partnership with Human Rights Watch. Dedicated to Sarah Hegazy, an Egyptian queer activist who died in June 2020 after suffering abuse and torture in Egyptian prisons. [Source: 25]

## PART I: COMPREHENSIVE LIST OF MENA FILMS WITH TRANSGENDER THEMES, CHARACTERS, OR NARRATIVES

### Iran

**1. *Facing Mirrors* (آینه های روبرو, 2011)**
- Director: Negar Azarbayjani
- Country: Iran
- Year: 2011
- Genre: Narrative Feature
- Summary: The first Iranian film to feature a female-to-male transgender main character (Eddy, a pre-op transman). The film follows the unlikely friendship between Eddie (played by Shayesteh Irani), a pre-op trans man from an upper-class family seeking a passport for sex reassignment surgery abroad, and Rana (Ghazal Shakeri), a religious, conservative taxi driver from a working-class background. Despite initial disgust, Rana eventually accepts Eddie and helps him. The film explores themes of prejudice, acceptance, and challenging superficial judgments. A remarkable scene is when Rana doesn't know how to introduce Eddie to her son—as uncle or as aunt. The film won awards at over 64 international film festivals including Iran's Fajr Film Festival and San Francisco's Frameline Festival (where it won "Best First Feature" in 2012). The film was debated extensively in Iran, screened even at Qom's Mofid University, and opened public discourse on trans issues. The film centers on two characters—Rana and Adineh (Eddie)—who help each other achieve freedom: Rana must defy societal gendered norms to support her family, while Eddie, a transgender man, must defy his family's expectations to live authentically. [Sources: 2, 7, 8, 3, 4, 5]

**2. *Be Like Others* (also known as *Transsexual in Iran*, 2008)**
- Director: Tanaz Eshaghian
- Country: Iran/USA/Canada/UK/France (co-production)
- Year: 2008
- Genre: Documentary
- Runtime: 74 minutes
- Summary: A documentary that explores the lives of transgender women in Iran, focusing on patients at Dr. Bahram Mir-Jalali's Mirdamad Surgical Centre, a sex-reassignment clinic in Tehran. The film highlights the paradox that while homosexual relationships are illegal and punishable by death in Iran, sex reassignment surgery is permitted following a 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini allowing such operations for "diagnosed transsexuals." The documentary follows two main subjects: Ali Askar, a 24-year-old man who doesn't want to become a woman but sees no other option in Iranian society due to his feminine appearance, and Anoosh, another young man ostracized for his femininity. Ali undergoes surgery (becoming Negar) but is disowned by his family, experiences depression, and turns to prostitution. Anoosh becomes Anahita and is initially happy and engaged, though her boyfriend becomes distant after the surgery. Eshaghian's film suggests that many Iranians pursue sex reassignment not because they identify as transgender, but because it allows them to escape persecution for homosexuality. The film won three Teddy Awards at the Berlin International Film Festival, was nominated for the Grand Jury Prize at Sundance, and was nominated for a GLAAD Media Award for Outstanding Documentary. Variety called it "a powerful window into a once-hidden side of the country" and "a model of non-dogmatic filmmaking on a highly charged topic." [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]

**3. *This is Not Me* (2023)**
- Director: Saeed Ghalipour
- Country: Iran
- Year: 2023
- Genre: Documentary/Independent Feature
- Summary: Focuses on the lives of two trans men in Iran as they navigate legal recognition and access to gender-affirming surgery. The film was featured at the Museum of Fine Arts' "Boston Festival of Films From Iran" in late January 2023. Director Ghalipour, speaking from Tehran via translator, noted that while sex reassignment is legally accepted under Islamic law in Iran—making it the only legal form of being queer in the country—trans individuals still face invasive medical checks, court proceedings, and social ostracism. The film highlights the supportive parents of the subjects, but Ghalipour notes this is an exception, as many trans individuals in Iran face suicide due to community rejection. The film is an independent production that has not been approved by Iranian authorities and cannot be screened legally in Iran, reflecting the broader censorship and underground arts scene in the country since the Islamic Revolution. [Source: 10]

**4. *Adam Barfi* (Snowman, 1995)**
- Director: Davood Mirbagheri
- Country: Iran
- Year: 1995 (released 1997 due to ban)
- Genre: Comedy/Drama
- Runtime: 103 minutes
- Summary: The story follows Abbas, a middle-aged Iranian man desperate to leave Iran for America. To obtain a visa, he begins dressing as a woman (transforming into "Dorna") to ensnare an American man. As complications arise, Abbas begins to doubt his plan. The film is described as one of the highest-grossing Iranian films of all time. The film was banned for 3 years, with the ban signed by Ezzatollah Zarqami, and only released after President Hashemi Rafsanjani and Ayatollah Khamenei had a private screening and deemed it unproblematic. Violent attacks by Ansar-e Hezbollah groups (led by Masoud Dehnamaaki and Allah Karam) on cinemas resulted in injuries, including a pregnant woman who suffered a miscarriage—all without the attackers having seen the film. The film creates a "border zone" identity across three axes: Iran→America (migration), male→female (gender), and old→new Iranian cinema (temporal), with Turkey as the purgatory point where all three converge. In the ending, Dorna (the female persona) must die so Abbas can return to Iran, suggesting that in-between states cannot survive in the film's ultimately binary worldview. The film paradoxically operates within Iran's propagandistic framework of "cultural invasion" while simultaneously exposing the instability of the very concepts it seeks to defend. Academic analysis of *Adam Barfi* appears in "Cross-Dressing and Gender (Tres)Passing" by R. Kheshti (2009) and "Transgender Identity in Iranian Cinema" by Kaveh Bassiri (2019). [Sources: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]

**5. *Madmazel Khaleh* (Mademoiselle Khaleh)**
- Identified in Kaveh Bassiri's "Transgender Identity in Iranian Cinema" (2019) as a key film illustrating evolving representations of transgender identities in Iranian cinema. Bassiri notes that MTF roles typically feature comedic elements, while FTM characters often face coercive gender transitions. [Source: 11]

**6. *Baran* and *Dokhtaraneh Khorshid* (cited in academic literature)**
- These two films are analyzed in the 2020 *Hypatia* article "Cross-Dressing and Gender (Tres)Passing: The Transgender Move as a Site of Agential Potential in the New Iranian Cinema." The author argues that Iran's censorship codes enforced by the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance have contributed to the emergence of "cross-dressing" or "passing" figures as a ubiquitous trope in New Iranian cinema. Through close readings of *Baran* and *Dokhtaraneh Khorshid*, the author identifies a "transgender move": a temporary space of political and agential potential sought by both domestic and diasporic spectators in post-1990s Iranian cinema. [Source: 15]

### Turkey

**7. *Crossing* (2024)**
- Director: Levan Akin
- Countries: Sweden, Denmark, France, Turkey, Georgia (co-production)
- Year: 2024
- Genre: Narrative Feature/Drama
- Runtime: 105 minutes
- Summary: The film follows Lia, a retired schoolteacher from Georgia, who sets out to find her long-lost niece Tekla, a transgender woman. Accompanied by Tekla's former neighbor Achi (Lucas Kankava), she travels to Istanbul, where they meet Evrim (Deniz Dumanlı), a transgender legal advocate active in the city's trans community. The film had its world premiere on 15 February 2024 at the 74th Berlin International Film Festival, where it opened the Panorama section and won the Teddy Award Jury Prize for LGBTQ-themed films. Critically acclaimed, the film holds a 97% positive rating on Rotten Tomatoes from 60 critics, with the consensus calling it "a tender odyssey" and "a humanist triumph." Metacritic assigned it a score of 83 out of 100, indicating "universal acclaim." The film won several awards including the Guldbagge Award for Best Film, Best Director, and Best Cinematography, the IFFI ICFT UNESCO Gandhi Medal at the 55th International Film Festival of India, and the GLAAD Media Award for Outstanding Film - Limited Release. Director Levan Akin cast real trans community members both in front of and behind the camera during production in Istanbul. The key character Evrim, a trans human rights lawyer, is played by trans actress Deniz Dumanli in her first film role. Akin emphasizes the importance of authentic representation, particularly within Istanbul's Lubunca culture (queer slang). The film is described as an uplifting and compassionate portrait of Istanbul's trans community. [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]

**8. *Your Honor* (2026, in production)**
- Director: Bircan Birol
- Country: Turkey
- Year: 2026 (project)
- Genre: Documentary
- Summary: A Close Up Cinematic Initiative project following Efruz, a trans law student in Turkey who lives under constant threat. The film documents Efruz over the years as her dream of becoming a human rights lawyer is challenged, and the two friends find hope in friendship and resistance. [Source: 18]

### Israel

**9. *Melting Away* (נמס בגשם, 2012)**
- Director: Doron Eran
- Country: Israel
- Year: 2012
- Genre: Narrative Feature/Drama
- Runtime: 86 minutes
- Cast: Hen Yanni as Asaf Shapira / Anna
- Summary: The first Israeli feature film to deal with parents coping with their transgender child. The idea for the movie was conceived after the 2009 Tel Aviv gay centre shooting, when the filmmakers saw parents refusing to visit their injured children at the hospital due to fear of others learning their child was LGBTQ+. Plot: Shlomo Shapira discovers his teenage son Asaf likes to wear women's clothing. With his wife Galia's silent consent, he refuses to let Asaf into the house on a rainy night, hoping the lesson will force him to change. Four years later, Shlomo is dying from cancer. Galia hires a private investigator who finds Asaf, who has transitioned and become a female singer named Anna. Anna visits her father in the hospital disguised as a private nurse, slowly winning his heart, while Galia also gradually accepts her daughter. The film focuses on the gradual rapprochement between parents and child, emphasizing that the parents' adjustment is their own issue to work through. The title refers to a song Anna performs near the end of the film, but also alludes to the difficult and often painful process of dissolving the prejudices, expectations and resentments that stand between parents and children. Awards: Special award for breakthrough performance to Hen Yanni at Tel Aviv International LGBT Film Festival; Audience Award at Boston Jewish Film Festival (2012); Audience Award for Best Narrative Feature at ImageOut: Rochester LGBT Film and Video Festival (2012); Audience Award at Shalom Europa IFF, France (2012); Festival Award at Au fil(m) du temps- IMAJ Israeli Film Festival, Belgium (2011). Hen Yanni was nominated for the Ophir Award for Best Actress. [Sources: 16, 17, 8, 9, 10]

### Lebanon

**10. *Cinema Fouad* (1993)**
- Director: Soueid (full name not specified in sources)
- Country: Lebanon
- Year: 1993
- Genre: Documentary
- Summary: Examined in the academic article "Tracing the Diasporic Experiences of Transgender and Gender-Nonconforming Palestinians On-screen: Cinema Fouad (1993) and Sultana's Reign (2023)" by Aaron Jagger, published in *Film Matters* (Volume 16, Issue 3, Dec 2025). The article traces the diaspora of transgender and gender-nonconforming Palestinians in this documentary. Using queer/trans and post/decolonial theorists including Judith Butler, Hamid Naficy, and Walter Mignolo, the author takes a historical approach to queer Arab identity, navigating white Western assumptions bred from colonialism. The article identifies nuance and authenticity as key to representations of diasporic non-Western queerness, engages with issues of language and assimilation, and calls for a more expansive definition of queer. [Source: 26]

### Palestine / Diaspora

**11. *Sultana's Reign* (2023)**
- Director: Moussally (full name not specified in sources)
- Country: Palestinian diaspora
- Year: 2023
- Genre: Documentary
- Summary: The second film analyzed in "Tracing the Diasporic Experiences of Transgender and Gender-Nonconforming Palestinians On-screen" by Aaron Jagger (2025). The article traces the diaspora of transgender and gender-nonconforming Palestinians in this documentary, made twenty years after *Cinema Fouad* (1993). [Source: 26]

### United Arab Emirates

**12. *Only Men Go to the Grave* (2016)**
- Director: Abdulla Al Kaabi
- Country: UAE
- Year: 2016
- Genre: Narrative Feature
- Summary: A groundbreaking Emirati film that tackles issues of same-sex love, gender identity, sectarianism, and women's rights within a traditional Arab family. The story focuses on a conservative Iraqi family whose secrets emerge after the family matriarch goes blind and dies. Notably, the LGBTQ characters are portrayed as traditional Arab mothers, wives, and caretakers rather than Westernized elites. The film passed state censors to screen at major theaters in Dubai. Al Kaabi says the film's handling of sensitive topics and avoidance of physical intimacy helped it gain approval. The film was awarded best Emirati film at the Dubai International Film Festival in 2016. Egyptian film critic Joseph Fahim called it the first Arab Gulf film to tackle homosexuality candidly, treating it as a matter-of-fact issue rather than a disease. The film was shot in Iran using Iranian actors of Arab heritage and Iraqi actors. Al Kaabi spent six years on the project. [Sources: 21, 22]

### Additional Films Mentioned in Queer Arab Film Lists (AFMI)

The Arab Film and Media Institute (AFMI) maintains a curated list of queer Arab films updated for 2026, featuring over 50 feature narrative films, documentaries, and shorts spanning from 1979 to 2026. While many focus on queer/LGBTQ+ themes broadly (not exclusively transgender), the following are relevant to transgender studies as they push boundaries of gender representation:

- **Layla** (2024, UK/US, Amrou Al-Kadhi) - About a non-binary Arab drag queen

## PART II: DETAILED ANALYSIS OF CORE CASE STUDIES (5 Films)

### CASE STUDY 1: *Facing Mirrors* (Iran, 2011, Dir. Negar Azarbayjani)

**(1) Narrative Structure and Plot Summary:**
The film centers on two characters—Rana (Ghazal Shakeri), a religious, conservative taxi driver from a working-class background, and Adineh/Eddie (Shayesteh Irani), a pre-op trans man from an upper-class family seeking a passport for sex reassignment surgery abroad. Their lives meet by chance. Rana must defy societal gendered norms to support her family, while Eddie must defy his family's expectations to live authentically. The story follows the unlikely friendship that develops between them; despite initial disgust, Rana eventually accepts Eddie and helps him. A remarkable scene is when Rana doesn't know how to introduce Eddie to her son—as uncle or as aunt. [Sources: 2, 7, 8, 3]

**(2) Cinematic Techniques:**
Sources note that the film uses intimate framing to capture the emotional journeys of both protagonists. The Ajam Media Collective article notes that the film's greatest weakness is "the lack of subjectivity of the two protagonists... shown as mere (queer) sexual objects as opposed to subjects of their own destiny." However, the film is praised for disrupting Orientalist narratives by showing Iranian characters with agency, complexity, and resilience. The film uses the metaphor of mirrors (as indicated in the title) to explore identity, reflection, and self-perception. [Sources: 7, 2]

**(3) Cultural and National Context of Production:**
In Iran, transgender issues are legally distinct from homosexuality. Following a 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, transgender individuals became officially recognized by the government and permitted to undergo sex reassignment surgery. The government contributes up to half the financial cost of the operation and issues new birth certificates to recognize and reflect the sex change. Iran performs some of the highest numbers of sex reassignment surgeries in the world, second only to Thailand. However, despite government approval, transgender people in Iran face daily harassment, difficulty obtaining work, and family rejection. Homosexuality remains punishable by death. The article notes a contrast with the U.S.: in Iran, the government encourages tolerance of transgender people, whereas in the U.S., the people push the government toward tolerance. The Guardian (2012) quotes producer Fereshteh Taerpour: "At the beginning, it was very strange for me to find out that sex-change operation is permitted in Iran... The authorities give loans and even issue new ID cards after the surgery, something that is not legal in many countries." Shadi Amin, Iranian rights campaigner, states: "In a democratic society, a sex-change operation is an option for transsexuals, but in Iran it's an obligation for their survival." Bronwen Robertson notes: "The pressure, from both state and society, on young Iranians to conform to societal norms and adhere to tradition and specific behavioural codes is immense. Therefore, it is not surprising that many young gay and lesbian Iranians, who do not identify as transgender, say they have felt pressured to undergo surgery." [Sources: 8, 5]

**(4) Engagement with Transgender Identities:**
The film is the first Iranian film featuring a female-to-male transgender main character that has been written, produced, and screened in Iran. It portrays complex, agentic characters navigating transphobia and societal constraints in Iran. The film disrupts Orientalist narratives by showing Iranian characters with agency, complexity, and resilience. The film's greatest success is that "it has forever entered Iran's social, cultural, and political public space where it has inserted a thought-provoking and relatable narrative of queerness in the public imaginary." The film was debated extensively in Iran, screened even at Qom's Mofid University. The director did not use a transgender actor for the lead role (Shayesteh Irani is a cisgender actress). [Sources: 7, 2, 4]

**(5) Critical Reception and Academic Scholarship:**
- The film won "Best First Feature" at the 2012 Frameline Film Festival (the oldest LGBT film festival in the world)
- Won awards at over 64 international film festivals
- Won at Iran's Fajr Film Festival
- The Ajam Media Collective article (2013) by a queer Iranian graduate student provides a critical analysis comparing *Facing Mirrors* to *Circumstance*, arguing that *Facing Mirrors* received far less Western media attention because it disrupts Orientalist narratives, while *Circumstance* conformed to "Orientalist fantasies about oppressed Muslim women and queer people."
- The Yale Review of International Studies article (2019) discusses the film's screening at Yale and its implications for transgender rights in Iran.
- *The Guardian* article (2012) reports on the film's release and the societal contradictions it highlights.
- The Iranian Film Empire blog (2016) discusses the film's themes of prejudice and acceptance.

### CASE STUDY 2: *Be Like Others* (Iran/USA, 2008, Dir. Tanaz Eshaghian)

**(1) Narrative Structure and Plot Summary:**
The documentary explores the lives of transgender women in Iran, focusing on patients at Dr. Bahram Mir-Jalali's Mirdamad Surgical Centre, a sex-reassignment clinic in Tehran. The film follows two main subjects: Ali Askar, a 24-year-old man who doesn't want to become a woman but sees no other option in Iranian society due to his feminine appearance, and Anoosh, another young man ostracized for his femininity. Ali undergoes surgery (becoming Negar) but is disowned by his family, experiences depression, and turns to prostitution. Anoosh becomes Anahita and is initially happy and engaged, though her boyfriend becomes distant after the surgery. The film also features Vida, an "alpha-tranny" counselor. The documentary provides an intimate look at young Iranians choosing to undergo sex-change surgery, featuring perspectives from surgeons, Koranic experts, and patients. [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]

**(2) Cinematic Techniques:**
Variety called it "a powerful window into a once-hidden side of the country" and "a model of non-dogmatic filmmaking on a highly charged topic." The film uses intimate observational documentary style, with direct interviews and access to surgical procedures. The Frameline description notes it is "an intimate and unflinching look at life in Iran, seen through the lens of those living at its fringes." The Letterboxd page notes: "I think all the trans women asked in this movie, including one asked while on the literal operating table, said they wouldn't want to go through with the surgery if they were able to have their rights and assimilate into society without it." [Sources: 6, 9, 10]

**(3) Cultural and National Context of Production:**
The film is set against the backdrop of Iran where homosexuality is punishable by death but a fatwa from Ayatollah Khomeini made sex-change operations legal. As one surgeon in the film states: "In the Islamic Republic of Iran, homosexuality is punishable by death. Twenty-five years ago, however, the Ayatollah Khomeini wrote a fatwa pronouncing transsexuality legal and allowing for sex-change operations." The documentary is a co-production between Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States, and France. The film was produced by Forties B, ITVS International, and Necessary Illusions Productions Inc. Languages: English and Persian. [Sources: 6, 8]

**(4) Engagement with Transgender Identities:**
Eshaghian's film suggests that many Iranians pursue sex reassignment not because they identify as transgender, but because it allows them to escape persecution for homosexuality. The film's central argument is that "identifying as transsexual rather than homosexual allows them to live free from harassment." The Supamodu review notes: "It is perfectly accommodating towards transwomen but homosexuality is considered a crime. This leads to many gay men passing as transwomen to not have to deal with morality police. But since legal status is a part of this, some gay men go as far as to have gender reaffirmation surgery which allows them to live freely but not as themselves. Watching people struggle with having to forego one part of their identity to have some space for another is devastating." The film raises complex ethical questions about whether Iran's legal framework for transgender people is actually liberating or coercive, given that some individuals may feel pressured to transition to avoid persecution for homosexuality. The film does not use transgender actors—it is a documentary featuring real transgender individuals. [Sources: 6, 7]

### CASE STUDY 3: *Melting Away* (Israel, 2012, Dir. Doron Eran)

**(1) Narrative Structure and Plot Summary:**
Shlomo Shapira discovers his teenage son Asaf likes to wear women's clothing. With his wife Galia's silent consent, he refuses to let Asaf into the house on a rainy night, hoping the lesson will force him to change. Four years later, Shlomo is dying from cancer. Galia hires a private investigator who finds Asaf, who has transitioned and become a female singer named Anna. Anna visits her father in the hospital disguised as a private nurse, slowly winning his heart, while Galia also gradually accepts her daughter. The film focuses on the gradual rapprochement between parents and child, emphasizing that the parents' adjustment is their own issue to work through. The title refers to a song Anna performs near the end of the film, but also alludes to the difficult and often painful process of dissolving the prejudices, expectations and resentments that stand between parents and children. [Sources: 16, 17, 8, 9, 10]

**(2) Cinematic Techniques:**
The review from J. The Jewish News of Northern California notes the film features "consistently solid acting that builds and honors our emotional investment in the characters' destinies." The film is described as "a satisfying, uplifting movie." The director auditioned 120 actors before casting Hen Yanni in the lead role. The film uses a non-linear narrative structure, moving between the past (the rejection) and the present (the reconciliation). The disguise plot—Anna posing as a private nurse—creates dramatic tension. [Sources: 16, 17, 8, 9, 10]

**(3) Cultural and National Context of Production:**
The idea for the movie was conceived after the 2009 Tel Aviv gay centre shooting, when a gunman killed two people and wounded 15 at the Israel Gay Youth Organization in Tel Aviv. The filmmakers were inspired after seeing parents refusing to visit their injured children at the hospital due to fear of others learning their child was LGBTQ+. Director Doron Eran stated: "In 2009, a guy came into a workshop of young gays and lesbians [in Tel Aviv] and he shot them. He killed two of them and 15 of them were wounded... some of the parents don't want to come and visit their children because they don't want their neighbors to see on the TV that their kids are homosexuals and lesbians. That was the idea and motivation behind picking up this script again." Eran also stated: "I have three children and I think that a parent, when you decide to make a kid, you must understand that you must love them with no conditions. That is what the film is about." The film is an Israeli-Canadian co-production. [Sources: 16, 17, 8, 9, 10]

**(4) Engagement with Transgender Identities:**
This is the first Israeli feature film to deal with parents coping with their transgender child. The film uses a transgender actor: Hen Yanni, who plays Asaf/Anna, is a cisgender actress. The film is notable for focusing on the parents' journey toward acceptance rather than solely on the transgender child's experience. The film's key message, as stated by the director, is that parents must love their children unconditionally. The film challenges the stigma surrounding transgender identity within Israeli society, particularly in more conservative communities. The film was screened at community events (including the Jewish Child & Family Services Response program) to raise awareness around LGBTQ topics and spark dialogue about family acceptance. [Sources: 16, 17, 8, 9, 10]

### CASE STUDY 4: *Crossing* (Turkey/Sweden, 2024, Dir. Levan Akin)

**(1) Narrative Structure and Plot Summary:**
Lia (Mzia Arabuli), a retired schoolteacher from Georgia, sets out to find her long-lost niece Tekla, a transgender woman. Accompanied by Tekla's former neighbor Achi (Lucas Kankava), she travels to Istanbul, where they meet Evrim (Deniz Dumanlı), a transgender legal advocate and sex worker active in the city's trans community. The film follows Lia's journey from a woman who is "on a mission to do something for her deceased sister" and who "has distanced herself to think life's just something she has to do" to a woman who "starts to come to terms with things in herself." The key thematic "crossing" is a change of mind and heart. The film ultimately questions whether Lia herself needs to be found and forgiven rather than Tekla. [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]

**(2) Cinematic Techniques:**
The film received mixed reviews for its visual style. The Guardian praised it as "a thoroughly intelligent, emotionally engaging and robustly performed movie." The Rotten Tomatoes consensus calls it "a tender odyssey with Mzia Arabuli's wonderful performance as the audience's guide, Crossing marks another humanist triumph for writer-director Levan Akin." However, a negative review from In Review Online criticizes the visual style as "dingy and generic" with excessive handheld camera work, and describes the film's central relationship as relying on "audience-pleasing clichés." Variety notes: "Akin makes a calculated choice to raise awareness of the trans community in Istanbul, but he does so through representation rather than manipulation." Screen Daily highlights "two fierce female characters." Little White Lies describes it as "sweet without being cloying, a love letter to the commonalities between Georgian and Turkish culture, one that encourages empathy and reminds us it's never too late to change for the better." [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 21]

**(3) Cultural and National Context of Production:**
The film is a co-production between Sweden, Denmark, France, Turkey, and Georgia. Director Levan Akin, who was raised in Sweden by Georgian parents, delayed the shoot by a year to conduct proper location research in Istanbul, rewriting the script during that time. Akin's previous film *And Then We Danced* (2019) faced violent protests and backlash from the Georgian Orthodox Church and ultra-conservative groups. Akin received death threats for *And Then We Danced* but chose to make *Crossing* in Turkey nonetheless, prioritizing meaningful engagement with the communities he portrays. The film engages with Istanbul's Lubunca culture (queer slang) and the city's underground trans community. [Sources: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]

**(4) Engagement with Transgender Identities:**
The film is groundbreaking for its authentic representation. Akin cast real trans community members both in front of and behind the camera. The key character Evrim, a trans human rights lawyer, is played by trans actress Deniz Dumanli in her first film role. Akin states: "Our main casting person in Turkey was a trans man called Bulut [Sezer] who knew a lot of people in the community. I wanted Evrim to be a resilient character that faces the world with bravado. Deniz really has that spirit within herself. She's so open, so positive, so hungry for life." Akin also hired trans crew members, including an assistant costume designer and a casting person. The film is described as "an uplifting and compassionate portrait of Istanbul's trans community and the fact allies can be found in unexpected places." ### CASE STUDY 5: *Adam Barfi* (Snowman, Iran, 1995, Dir. Davood Mirbagheri)

**(1) Narrative Structure and Plot Summary:**
The story follows Abbas (played by Akbar Abdi), a middle-aged Iranian man desperate to leave Iran for America. Stranded in Turkey, he meets Iranian acquaintances who suggest his only way to America is to become a woman and marry an American. Abbas transforms into "Dorna" (a female character). As complications arise, Abbas begins to doubt his plan. The film creates a "border zone" identity across three axes: Iran→America (migration), male→female (gender), and old→new Iranian cinema (temporal), with Turkey as the purgatory point where all three converge. In the ending, Dorna (the female persona) must die so Abbas can return to Iran, suggesting that in-between states cannot survive in the film's ultimately binary worldview. [Sources: 13, 14]

**(2) Cinematic Techniques:**
The film blends comedy, drama, and romance. It is analyzed through multiple theoretical frameworks in the "POSITIF" video analysis (2026): (1) the Sheikh San'an allegory from Attar's Mantiq al-Tayr about a pious sheikh who falls in love with a Christian girl, mirroring Abbas's journey and the fear of Western cultural influence; (2) Judith Butler's gender performativity theory—that gender is a social role performed daily, and the idea of "hacking" gender through signs and repetition; (3) the Ta'ziyeh (Shabih-khani) tradition—the Iranian passion play tradition where men play women's roles, maintaining a clear distance between performer and role (as opposed to Western mimesis/realistic imitation); (4) Film Farsi (pre-revolutionary Iranian cinema)—the film's nostalgic references to the "tipe" (stock characters) of pre-revolution Iranian cinema, particularly through the characters played by Parviz Parastui and Dariush Arjmand. The film is shot by cinematographer Maziar Partow with music by Farhad Fakhreddini. [Sources: 13, 14]

**(3) Cultural and National Context of Production:**
The film was made in 1994 by Davoud Mirbagheri, with the same cast as his TV series "Imam Ali." Produced by the Howzeh Honari (Art Bureau), it was banned for 3 years. A harsh article in Kayhan newspaper by editor Mehdi Nassiri targeted the film for Akbar Abdi's cross-dressing. The film was banned by Ezzatollah Zarqami just before the Fajr Film Festival. Mohammad Ali Zaman (director of the Howzeh Honari) lobbied for the film's release, eventually getting it shown to President Hashemi Rafsanjani and Ayatollah Khamenei, who deemed it unproblematic. Released in 1997, it became the year's highest-grossing film, but faced violent attacks from Ansar-e Hezbollah groups (led by Masoud Dehnamaaki and Allah Karam) who physically assaulted cinemas and audiences, including a pregnant woman who suffered a miscarriage—all without the attackers having seen the film. The film ran in rotation for 2 years until 1999. The film paradoxically operates within Iran's propagandistic framework of "cultural invasion" while simultaneously exposing the instability of the very concepts it seeks to defend. [Sources: 13, 14]

**(4) Engagement with Transgender Identities:**
The film is not explicitly about transgender identity—it is about cross-dressing for instrumental purposes (visa fraud). However, it is a crucial text in the genealogy of gender non-conformity in Iranian cinema. Kaveh Bassiri's "Transgender Identity in Iranian Cinema" (2019) identifies *Adam Barfi* as a key film illustrating evolving representations of transgender identities, noting that MTF (male-to-female) roles in Iranian cinema typically feature comedic elements, while FTM characters often face coercive gender transitions. The film uses a cisgender male actor (Akbar Abdi) in cross-dressing. The critical analysis from the POSITIF channel (2026) argues that the film creates a "border zone" identity but ultimately reinforces a binary worldview by requiring Dorna to die so Abbas can return to Iran. The film is cited in "Cross-Dressing and Gender (Tres)Passing" by R. Kheshti (2009), which examines how the film contributes to the construction of gender and Iran as "transsexual capital of the world." [Sources: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]

**(5) Critical Reception and Academic Scholarship:**

- One of the most controversial films in Iranian cinema history
